During the first 24 hours, engineers surveyed 17 blocks, closed 6 intersections, and noted 28 cracked walls, 14 broken stairwells, and 11 shattered storefronts. None of those figures changed the official count of buildings that had fully collapsed in that first quake: it was 4.

Seismologists then warned the mayor that each following earthquake would cause double the number of collapsing buildings as the previous one because every new quake would further weaken already damaged foundations. Meanwhile, relief teams distributed 250 blankets, 180 bottles of water, and 75 emergency food kits; hospitals treated 23 minor injuries and 2 serious ones; and utility crews restored power to 320 homes by the end of day 2. On the second earthquake, some residents confused partially condemned buildings with collapsed ones, and a separate report listed 8 buildings as unsafe to enter, 5 schools closed for inspection, and 16 aftershocks too small to cause major structural failure. Even so, according to the experts' prediction, the number of buildings that collapsed in that earthquake followed the doubling pattern.

By the time the third and fourth earthquakes occurred, city workers had installed 40 temporary barriers, hung 96 warning signs, inspected 21 parking garages, and logged 13 gas leaks and 7 water-main breaks. One neighborhood association counted 52 cracked chimneys, and a newspaper headline mentioned 64 apartments displaced, though several apartments were inside the same building. Insurance agents opened 118 claims, and a volunteer group served 390 meals over three evenings. Experts still maintained the same rule: each following earthquake had double the number of collapsing buildings as the previous one.

After three more earthquakes, how many buildings had collapsed including those from the first earthquake?

James is a first-year student at a university in Chicago, and at the beginning of each semester he tries to map out every dollar in his spending plan. He lives in a dorm that is a 12-minute walk from his main lecture hall, usually wakes up at 7:15 a.m. for his 8:00 classes, and keeps a spreadsheet with separate tabs for meals, housing, entertainment, transportation, laundry, printing, coffee, and school supplies, even though not every category gets its own official budget share. His student ID number ends in 482, he is taking 5 classes worth a total of 16 credit hours, and he bought 3 notebooks during orientation, 2 folders the next week, and a campus mug for $12. The dining hall serves breakfast from 7:00 to 10:00, lunch from 11:00 to 2:00, and dinner until 8:30, and James sometimes compares meal-plan prices like $8 breakfasts, $11 lunches, and $14 dinners when deciding whether to eat on or off campus.

For the semester, however, the actual budget amount he is working with is $1000 total. Out of that semester budget, he plans to spend 30% of his money on food. He expects to spend 15% on accommodation, even though the housing office also listed several room options costing $850, $920, and $1100 per month for other students. He also sets aside 25% for entertainment, which includes things like occasional movie tickets for $18, concert tickets for $42, streaming subscriptions costing $9.99 per month, and weekend basketball games where snacks can cost another $16. Last semester his older cousin spent 28% on food, 22% on housing, and 10% on textbooks, but James is not using that plan. James also considered buying a used bike for $140 to reduce train rides that usually cost $2.50 each, and he estimates he might do 18 loads of laundry at $2 per wash and $2 per dry over the term, but those details are not part of the percentage breakdown he finally settled on.

James says that after spending 30% on food, 15% on accommodation, and 25% on entertainment, he will use the rest of his semester budget on coursework materials such as textbooks, lab manuals, software access codes, pens, graph paper, calculator batteries, and printing charges. How much money does he spend on coursework materials?

It was Ava's birthday party, and her parents spent all morning getting everything ready. The party was scheduled from 2:00 p.m. to 5:30 p.m., with 18 invitations sent out, although only 14 kids had RSVP'd by Thursday night and 2 more texted that morning to say they were coming late. They hung 27 pastel balloons in three clusters, put 9 paper unicorn cutouts along the wall, set out 16 striped cups, 20 plates, and 24 napkins, and arranged 3 folding tables in the backyard. Ava was turning 8, her cake had 8 candles and 2 extra sparkler candles, and the bakery box said the cake weighed 3 pounds even though it was cut into 12 slices. Her mom also picked up 6 bottles of lemonade at $2 each, 4 cartons of juice boxes with 8 boxes per carton, and a party banner that was on sale from $11 down to $8, but those were part of a different shopping list.

The main event was the candy table and the unicorn piñata. Her parents bought a unicorn piñata for $13 and filled it with all of her favorite treats. At the candy store, they compared several sizes and brands before deciding what to buy. They bought 4 bags of Reese's for $9 per bag, 3 bags of Snickers for $5 per bag, and 5 bags of Skittles for $7 per bag. The Reese's bags each said 12 fun-size cups, the Snickers bags each had 10 mini bars, and the Skittles bags each listed 15 small packets, but the family only cared about the total cost for the piñata and candy. Ava's cousin also brought 2 extra bags of lollipops to share, and there were already 11 chocolate bars left over from last year's Halloween candy in a kitchen drawer, but those were not part of this purchase.

How much did the unicorn piñata and the treats cost altogether?

Carolyn is trying to organize her after-school music routine for the month, and her family keeps a very detailed planner. On Mondays she gets home at 3:40 p.m., has a snack for 15 minutes, and usually starts music at 4:10. On Tuesdays her piano teacher recommends scale warm-ups in groups of 5, while her violin teacher wants bow drills in sets of 8, and on Thursdays she sometimes spends 10 extra minutes putting away sheet music, wiping rosin dust off the violin case, and labeling practice charts. Her piano lesson costs $25 each week, her violin lesson costs $30, and she has 12 songs marked in blue in one binder and 9 pieces marked in red in another. She owns 2 pianos at home if you count the old keyboard in the basement, 1 full-size violin, 3 shoulder rests, 4 music books, and a metronome that can be set to 60, 72, 84, or 96 beats per minute. Last month she missed 2 lessons because of a recital, but this month she plans to follow her regular routine carefully.

For actual daily practice, Carolyn practices the piano for 20 minutes a day. She practices the violin for three times as long as the piano. She practices 6 days each week, usually taking Sundays off, although her calendar also shows 4 school club meetings, 2 dentist appointments, and 1 Saturday recital during the month. Her brother insists that there are sometimes 31 days in a month, but for this schedule Carolyn is planning for a month with exactly 4 weeks. She also tracks that she drinks 2 glasses of water during practice, spends 5 minutes tuning before violin on some days, and once counted 240 total pages across all her music books.

If she practice six days a week, how many minutes does she spend practicing in a month with four weeks?

A student is downloading a project archive from the school server late at night while several other status windows are open on the screen. The archive itself is a single file that is 90 megabytes in size. The download manager shows all sorts of extra information: there are 12 folders inside the archive, 240 images, 18 short videos, and 3 PDF manuals; the compressed version used to be 96 megabytes before a cleanup removed 6 megabytes of duplicate thumbnails; the student's laptop has 512 gigabytes of storage with 147 gigabytes free; the Wi-Fi icon says the router is 8 meters away; and the network dashboard mentions that the internet plan allows up to 100 megabits per second, though the actual download does not follow that number here. A progress bar also notes that the first checkpoint occurs after 60 megabytes have been downloaded, and after that point the transfer behavior changes.

During the first part of the transfer, the file downloads at a rate of 5 megabytes per second for its first 60 megabytes. After those first 60 megabytes are finished, the remaining part of the same 90-megabyte file downloads at 10 megabytes per second thereafter. Meanwhile, the student notices other unrelated numbers on the screen: a cloud backup is paused at 30%, a music playlist has 25 songs totaling 95 minutes, the battery is at 64% with 2 hours left, and last week's download of a different file took 14 seconds because it was only 70 megabytes and used another speed pattern. None of those windows closes the current download manager, and the file continues with the rates already described.

How long, in seconds, does it take to download entirely?

At the school’s annual Pi Day memory challenge, three students—Sam, Carlos, and Mina—were all practicing decimal digits of pi after the 3. The event had several rounds, a poster contest, and a bake sale where mini pies were sold in boxes of 4 for $6, large pies were cut into 8 slices, and one class even hung 31 blue streamers and 14 silver ones around the library. Carlos practiced for 12 minutes before school, 18 minutes during lunch, and wrote his digits on 3 index cards with room for 10 digits each, although he did not necessarily fill every card. Sam brought 2 pencils, 5 notecards, and a stopwatch that showed 3:14 when the bell rang. Mina practiced on 4 different days that week, spending 20 minutes each day, and she also won 2 raffle tickets for correctly naming pi to 10 places during warm-up. In the final memory round, the teacher reminded everyone that leading zeros did not matter because they were reciting digits of pi, not storing locker codes. 

When the scores were recorded, it turned out that Sam had memorized six more digits of pi than Carlos memorized. Mina had memorized six times as many digits of pi as Carlos memorized. The printed results sheet also mentioned that Mina’s total was 24 digits of pi, while another student in a different class had stopped at 21 digits and the judge had checked answers twice using a 30-digit reference sheet. 

If Mina memorized 24 digits of pi, how many digits did Sam memorize?

On a school trip to the seashore, the fifth-grade class arrived at 9:10 a.m. on two buses, one carrying 24 students and the other carrying 27, plus 4 teachers and 3 parent chaperones. The class had 58 paper lunch bags, 61 juice boxes, 2 coolers, and 1 first-aid kit. Before the shell-collecting activity began, the students spent 35 minutes reviewing tide-pool safety rules, 20 minutes sketching the lighthouse, and another 15 minutes eating crackers near the dunes. The beach itself was divided into 6 marked exploration zones, although Alan, Ben, and Laurie stayed mostly around zones 2 and 3 where they noticed 14 pieces of driftwood, 9 smooth black stones, 22 tiny crab holes, and several patches of seaweed. Alan brought a blue bucket that could hold 50 shells, Ben had a mesh bag with a broken strap, and Laurie used a striped pail with room for 40 shells and 3 compartments for sorting by color. During the trip, some students collected sand dollars, some counted gulls, and one group recorded 18 wave sets in 6 minutes for a science worksheet. Ben got a late start because he spent 12 minutes tying his shoe, 8 minutes rinsing sand out of his bag, and 5 minutes helping stack 7 backpacks near the lifeguard stand. Laurie, meanwhile, had already found shells near a rock pool and later traded away 2 pieces of sea glass for a postcard that cost 75 cents in the gift shop, though none of that changed her shell total for the count in question. At the final shell count, Alan and his friends compared what they had collected. Alan collected four times as many shells as Ben did. Ben got a late start and only collected a third of what Laurie did. If Laurie collected 36 shells how many did Alan collect?

Gerald is getting ready for baseball season and has been making a very detailed budget in a notebook. He wrote down that he usually spends $100 each month on baseball supplies, which for him can include things like rosin bags, grip tape, extra socks, replacement batting gloves, practice balls sold in buckets of 12, sunflower seeds, and sometimes a new belt or sliding shorts. Last year he also spent $35 on a team photo package, $18 on sports drinks during a tournament weekend, and $42 on a used equipment bag, but those were separate one-time costs and not part of his regular monthly supplies budget. This year, his baseball season lasts 4 months. During the season, practices are on Tuesdays and Thursdays, games are often on Saturdays, and one month even has 5 weekends, but his main planning number for supplies still stays at $100 per month for the 4-month season.

Because he does not play baseball year-round, Gerald wants to use the months when he is not playing to save up the money he will need. In those off-season months, he plans to do outdoor chores in the neighborhood. Some neighbors ask him to rake leaves, some ask him to shovel snow, and some ask him to mow lawns. He keeps a chart of how long these jobs usually take: raking can take 45 minutes at one house or 90 minutes at a larger yard, shoveling might take 30 minutes for a light snow or 2 hours after a storm, and mowing can take anywhere from 25 minutes to over an hour depending on the size of the lawn. One neighbor has 3 maple trees, another has a corner lot, and another pays on Fridays instead of the day of the job. Gerald even noted that in one especially busy week last year he did 2 raking jobs, 4 mowing jobs, and 1 shoveling job, but that was just a record of a past week.

For his current plan, Gerald charges $10 for each chore he does, whether the chore is raking, shoveling, or mowing. There are 12 months in a year, and since his baseball season is 4 months long, he is not playing baseball during the other months. He wants to know how many chores he needs to average each month during those non-baseball months so that by the time the next season arrives, he has saved enough to cover all of his baseball supplies.

How many chores does he need to average a month to save up for his supplies?

Ann is cutting fabric to make curtains for several rooms in her house and is trying to keep careful notes because she has also been comparing lining materials, trim lengths, rod sizes, and sewing times. The fabric bolt she is currently using is a large rectangular piece that measures 16 feet by 12 feet. It came from a store where bolts were stacked in rows of 8, labeled by color code, and sold for different prices per yard, but Ann already bought this whole piece last week during a sale that ended at 4:00 p.m. She spent part of the morning measuring windows: the living room window is 5 feet wide, the rod is mounted 8 inches above the frame, and she wants extra folds in the finished curtains, but for the fabric she actually cuts a 4 foot by 6 foot rectangle for the living room. For the bedroom, the window itself is narrower, the old curtain panels were each 3 feet long, and she considered adding a 1-foot hem and decorative bands that are 2 inches wide, but the piece she actually cuts for that room is a 2 foot by 4 foot rectangle. On her worktable she also has 3 spools of thread, 12 pins in a pincushion, 2 pairs of scissors, 5 measuring tapes, and a receipt showing she once bought 24 square feet of lining fabric for another project. She writes down several unrelated numbers in her notebook, including a curtain rod length of 7 feet, tiebacks that are 18 inches long, and an estimate that sewing each panel takes 35 minutes. If the bolt of fabric is 16 feet by 12 feet, how much fabric is left in square feet?

Arnel was helping organize school supplies for the start of the semester. On the table were 10 identical boxes of pencils that belonged to him, along with 6 unopened packs of erasers, 12 rulers, 4 jars of markers, and 3 bundles of notebooks tied with blue string. Each pencil box had the same number of pencils in it, although the label on the outside also mentioned things like a batch number of 24, a shelf code of 105, and a price sticker that said $3.50 per box before tax. Arnel first spent 15 minutes sorting the boxes by color, checked off 10 names on a club list, and moved 2 damaged boxes of crayons out of the way, but none of that changed his pencil boxes. He opened all 10 of his pencil boxes, kept 10 pencils for his own homework pouch, and planned to share all the remaining pencils equally among his 5 friends: Ben, Carlo, Dindo, Emil, and Felix. At first they were also talking about borrowing 5 sharpeners, 10 sheets of paper each, and splitting 40 stickers for a poster, but in the end the only thing Arnel actually shared was the remaining pencils. After the sharing was finished, each of his 5 friends got exactly 8 pencils. How many pencils are in each box?

On Saturday afternoon, Caleb went to a warehouse-style grocery store to stock the freezer before a family movie night. He pushed a cart through the frozen aisle for nearly 25 minutes, comparing sizes, flavors, sale tags, and expiration dates. The store had a promotion sign saying that if a shopper bought 6 frozen desserts, they could earn 2 reward points per item, and another sign advertised a weekend special on popsicles: 3 boxes for $9. Caleb ignored the popsicles, even though he noticed 12 different flavors. He also passed shelves with 8 tubs of sorbet priced at $5 each, 7 boxes of ice cream bars at $6 per box, and 5 family-size cheesecakes marked down from $14 to $11. In the dairy section earlier, he had already bought 2 gallons of milk for $3 each, a dozen eggs for $4, and 3 yogurts for $2 each, but those were rung up separately and are not part of this question.

For the frozen desserts he actually chose, Caleb bought 10 cartons of ice cream and 4 cartons of frozen yoghurt. The ice cream cartons were on the top shelf in rows of 5, and each carton of ice cream cost $4. The frozen yoghurt cartons were in a different freezer case, with 9 cartons left in vanilla and 6 in strawberry, and each carton of frozen yoghurt cost $1. Caleb briefly considered buying 2 extra cartons of frozen yoghurt because he had 2 coupons worth 50 cents each, but he decided not to use them and bought only the amounts already mentioned. At checkout, the cashier scanned 14 frozen dessert cartons total, then asked whether he wanted a receipt emailed or printed. Caleb paid with a $50 bill and got change, after tax was added, but tax and payment method do not affect what is being asked here.

How much more did Caleb spend on ice cream than on frozen yoghurt?

On Saturday, Leah spent the morning doing a whole mix of odd jobs around her neighborhood. She watered Mrs. Kim's tomato plants for 20 minutes, brought in packages for the family at house number 18, helped rake 3 bags of leaves for Mr. Alvarez even though it was only early spring, and walked two different dogs on Maple Street, one for 15 minutes and one for 25 minutes. She also helped her next-door neighbor sort a box with 14 old magazines, 9 seed packets, and 6 gardening gloves, though that task was just a favor and not part of what she counted later. By the end of the day, after all the paid jobs were finished, Leah had earned $28 working odd jobs around the neighborhood.

On her way home she passed the corner store, where the chalkboard advertised milkshakes for $4, smoothies for $5, and a special of 2 cookies for $3. She thought briefly about buying gum for $1 and a granola bar for $2, but she did not. She spent a seventh of the money she had earned on a milkshake. After that, she went home, emptied out a pocket that also had 3 buttons, a bus receipt from last Tuesday, and 2 movie ticket stubs that cost $9 each when she bought them a month ago, and then decided to be responsible with the rest of her earnings. Leah put half of what remained after buying the milkshake into her savings account. Her savings account already had $46 in it before this deposit, and her younger brother kept bragging that he had $52 in his own jar, but that did not change what Leah did. She left the remaining money from her odd-job earnings in her wallet.

That evening, while Leah was in the kitchen timing a batch of cookies for 12 minutes and arguing with her cousin about whether 8 p.m. or 8:30 p.m. was too late to start a board game, her dog got ahold of her wallet. The dog dragged it under the table, chewed one corner, and shredded all the money inside except for $1. The wallet also contained a library card, an expired coupon for $2 off a sandwich, 4 pennies, and a punch card from a frozen yogurt shop that was one stamp away from a free topping, but the only thing that matters from the money in the wallet is that all of it was shredded except for $1. How many dollars did Leah lose?

At the community botanical garden, the volunteer team is preparing a flower inventory sheet before the Saturday open house. The gardeners worked in 5 sections, started at 8:00 a.m., took a 20-minute water break, and used 12 green watering cans, 3 wheelbarrows, and 2 hoses while checking labels. Near the entrance there is a stone path with 18 stepping stones, a bench painted last month, and 6 small signs reminding visitors not to pick flowers. In the gift kiosk, seed packets are sold for $2 each, potted herbs for $7 each, and postcards for $1, but those are tracked on a different form. One volunteer counted 14 empty pots stacked behind the shed, another recorded 9 bags of mulch, and the manager mentioned that last spring 15 rose bushes had to be replanted after a storm. This month, however, the current flower bed being counted for the inventory contains 25 roses, 40 tulips, and 35 daisies. The tulips are arranged in 4 rows of 10, the daisies border a small fountain with 8 stones around it, and the roses are in a separate patch beside 3 lavender plants and 11 marigolds that are not part of this particular flower count because they are in another display. The garden map also notes 2 gates, 7 oak trees, 24 tomato seedlings in the education plot, and 30 bulbs reserved for next season, but the inventory question for this flower bed only asks about the flowers already counted here. What percentage of flowers are not roses?

Leo spent a Saturday afternoon working through a long homework assignment that his teacher had organized into three parts on the online class portal. The portal also showed a lot of other information: there were 12 practice questions attached for review, 4 optional challenge problems, and 3 reminder messages from his teacher. Leo sharpened 2 pencils before starting, erased 6 small mistakes during the assignment, and took a 5-minute water break earlier in the day before he even logged in. His desk clock showed 3:00 when he sat down, and the classroom website listed the assignment as due in 2 days at 11:59 p.m. The first part of the assignment had 10 short questions, the second part had 8 medium questions, and the third part had 6 longer questions, although the number of questions in each part did not match how long each part took him. Leo finished the first part of his assignment in 25 minutes. It took him twice as long to finish the second part. During the whole homework session, he glanced at the clock 7 times, drank from a water bottle that holds 16 ounces, and ignored 9 text notifications. If he was able to finish his assignment in 2 hours, how many minutes did Leo finish the third part of the assignment?

Liza was getting ready for a long weekend bake sale and family gathering, so she spent all morning organizing ingredients, labeling containers, and planning several batches of cookies. At the grocery store, she compared 6 different butter brands, noticed that one store special offered 4 boxes for $18 while another sold 250-gram sticks in packs of 8, and even checked whether salted or unsalted butter would be better for her recipes. In the end, for the actual cookie baking she bought 10 kilograms of butter to make cookies. She also picked up 12 kilograms of flour, 7 kilograms of sugar, 3 kilograms of brown sugar, 5 dozen eggs, 4 bags of chocolate chips, 2 jars of peanut butter, 9 bottles of vanilla, and 24 paper baking boxes for packaging. 

Back in her kitchen, she divided her day into 3 baking sessions: one from 8:00 to 10:30, one after lunch from 12:15 to 2:45, and one in the evening after cleanup. She preheated the oven to 350 degrees, lined 8 trays with parchment paper, washed 11 mixing bowls even though she only needed 4, and wrote recipe cards for chocolate chip cookies, peanut butter cookies, sugar cookies, oatmeal cookies, and shortbread. She eventually decided not to make the oatmeal cookies that day because she had only 2 cups of raisins left, and she postponed the shortbread because the decorative tins were still in storage. 

For the cookies she did make, she used one-half of the butter for chocolate chip cookies. Then she used one-fifth of it for peanut butter cookies. After that, she checked what butter was still left in the refrigerator, moved aside 3 unopened cream cheese packages that were for a different dessert, and used one-third of the remaining butter for sugar cookies. She packed the chocolate chip cookies into 6 boxes, the peanut butter cookies into 4 boxes, and the sugar cookies into 5 boxes, with a few broken ones set aside for tasting. She also wrote down that last month she had used 8 kilograms of butter total across 5 recipes, and for next week she expects to need 6 more kilograms if orders increase. 

How many kilograms of butter are left after making those three kinds of cookies?

A Statistics student is preparing a report for class about the average daily allowance of middle school students at a campus that includes Grades 6, 7, and 8. Before doing the final write-up, he organizes his notes in several categories: age, grade level, distance from school, whether students buy lunch or bring food from home, and daily allowance. He first considered collecting data from 72 students, but 12 questionnaires were incomplete because some students wrote their weekly allowance instead of daily allowance, so only the completed surveys were included in the final calculation. The school day starts at 7:30 a.m., there are 8 sections in middle school, and the canteen sells rice meals for $3, sandwiches for $2, fruit cups for $1.50, and juice for $1. Some students said they spend $2 on transportation, some save $1 each day, and a few reported buying snacks 3 times a week instead of every day. In one hallway count, 18 students were carrying packed lunches, 27 bought drinks, and 9 said they usually spend less on Mondays than on Fridays. The student also noted that 40% of those surveyed were from Grade 7, 22 wore school IDs on blue lanyards, and 15 participated in after-school clubs that meet twice a week. None of those details changed the allowance grouping in his summary.

According to his survey, 2/3 of the students receive an average of $6 allowance per day while the rest gets an average of $4 a day. He surveyed 60 students in all. If he surveyed 60 students, what is the total amount of money those 60 students get in a day?

At the indoor fountain in the center court of the mall, Joanne works a repeating cleanup shift where she checks the basin once every hour while music plays over the speakers and nearby stores open and close their gates. The fountain has 4 stone tiers, 3 colored lights on each side, and 8 benches around it, and management keeps track of all kinds of details such as how many shoppers pass by, how many wishes get tossed in, and how often the water filters are changed. On this particular day, the mall opened at 10:00 a.m., the pretzel stand sold 48 pretzels by noon, the toy store started with 120 balloons and gave away 27, and the fountain maintenance log said that yesterday there had been 140 coins removed in total, including 60 pennies, 40 nickels, 25 dimes, and 15 quarters. Joanne also noticed that one child dropped 6 tokens that were not counted as coins, two tourists took 14 photos, and a security guard walked past the fountain 5 times during her shift.

During the first hour, Joanne collected 15 coins. In addition to those, she found 2 paper receipts stuck near the edge, 1 button, and 3 leaves in the water, but those were thrown away separately. For the next two hours, she collected 35 coins from the fountain while hearing the hourly announcements at 11:00 and 12:00, and during that same period the coffee kiosk next to the fountain sold 18 muffins and 22 drinks, one little boy tossed in 9 coins after making a wish, and a couple sitting nearby counted 47 shopping bags between them. Joanne wrote the coin amounts in her notebook with a blue pen that cost $2, even though her coworker used a black pen from a pack of 10.

In the fourth hour, she collected 50 coins from the fountain, but she gave 15 of them to her coworker so she could buy a soda from the vending machine, where soda cost $1.50 and water cost $1.25. The vending machine had 20 sodas at the start of the day and 7 were already gone. Joanne herself had brought a lunch worth $8.75 and had 3 coupons in her pocket that she never used. How many coins did she have after the fourth hour?

Jerry’s two daughters both play softball, but they are on different teams in the same local youth league. One team is the Blue Sparks, whose jerseys are navy with silver numbers, and the other is the Red Comets, whose socks have to be washed separately because the red dye sometimes runs. Their league has 6 teams total, each team keeps a 12-player roster, and the snack stand opens 45 minutes before the first pitch. Jerry usually arrives early enough to unfold 2 camping chairs, carry a cooler with 10 juice boxes and 6 oranges, and chat with 3 other parents about batting orders, weather delays, and whether the field lights will be replaced this year. On Saturdays there are often 4 games scheduled across 2 nearby diamonds, and parking costs $5 unless you have a seasonal pass, which Jerry bought in March for $40.

This season, each of Jerry’s daughters has 8 games on her team’s schedule. One daughter’s team has most of its games on Tuesdays and Saturdays, while the other has more Thursday evening games, and one team even had a preseason scrimmage that lasted 90 minutes and did not count in the official standings. The teams also took separate photo days, one at 9:00 a.m. and one at 1:30 p.m., and each girl needed 1 individual photo and 1 team photo. Jerry also paid $85 for one registration fee, $90 for the other, and another $30 total for socks, belt replacements, and extra hair ties after one equipment bag zipper broke.

During the season, each team practices 4 hours for every game they play. Some practices are split into 2 sessions, some include 30 minutes of fielding stations and 20 minutes of batting cage rotations, and one coach likes to spend exactly 15 minutes on warm-ups before moving to throwing drills. The league handbook is 28 pages long, the outfield fences are 200 feet from home plate, and every team is supposed to have 2 assistant coaches and 1 scorekeeper. Jerry’s daughters each got new bats this year, one costing $70 and one costing $95, although one of them still prefers using an older glove she has had for 3 seasons.

If a game is played as scheduled, each game lasts for 2 hours. A few years ago rain shortened several games to 5 innings, but this season’s official time allotment is still 2 hours per game, and Jerry plans to attend everything for both girls rather than splitting time with their grandfather, who only comes to Sunday doubleheaders. He keeps all the dates on a calendar that already has dentist appointments, a school concert, 2 birthday parties, and a family barbecue marked on it.

If each game lasts for 2 hours, how many hours will Jerry spend at the field watching his daughters play and practice altogether?

A wildlife rehabilitation team is tracking a large bear that is preparing to hibernate for the winter. Based on old records from the region, some bears den for about 5 months, scouts checked 12 possible den sites, and one ranger logged 47 salmon jumps at a nearby river in a single hour. The team notes that this bear began late summer at 680 pounds, was once estimated at 712 pounds after a rainy week, and eventually wants enough fat reserves to meet a seasonal gain target of 1000 pounds before the first deep snow. To monitor feeding, they divide its foraging into end-of-summer foods and autumn foods. At the end of summer, the bear feasts on berries and small woodland animals. During autumn, it devours acorns and salmon. The berry patches were spread across 8 slopes, each survey bucket held 6 quarts, and technicians recorded 240 claw marks near berry shrubs over several weeks. During summer, it gained a fifth of the weight it needed from berries. In autumn, acorn foraging was especially productive: there were 14 oak stands in the study area, some dropping an estimated 90 pounds of acorns per stand, and during autumn, it gained twice that amount from acorns. The river run also attracted many other animals; observers counted 3 eagles, 9 otters, and 26 fish carcasses along the bank one morning. Salmon made up half of the remaining weight it had needed to gain. Small-animal hunting happened mostly at dusk near 4 fallen logs and 2 marsh edges, where motion cameras captured dozens of clips, but the biologists only care about total weight gain by food source. How many pounds did it gain eating small animals?

At a small farm supply warehouse, a shipment of cooking and machine oil was being checked before inventory was updated. The manager had 24 metal cans lined up in 4 rows of 6 cans each on a concrete floor, with labels in red, blue, and green marker from an older sorting system. Some of the cans were dented, 3 had replacement caps, 5 had newer handles, and each empty can would normally weigh 2 kilograms, though none of that matters for the current oil count because all 24 cans together already contain a total of 290 liters of oil. Earlier that morning, workers had unloaded 12 cardboard cartons, used 18 barcode stickers, and recorded batch numbers 104, 105, and 108 for quality control. They also noted that 10 of the cans were a standard measured size for a retail order and each of those 10 cans was holding exactly 8 liters of oil. The other cans were set aside for a separate customer, and those remaining cans were all filled equally, even though their paint markings, lid colors, and shelf positions were different. During the same shift, the warehouse also moved 75-liter drums, checked 6 funnels, and counted 290 bottle caps in a nearby packing area for an unrelated order, which caused some confusion in the paperwork. If 10 of the cans are holding 8 liters each, how much oil is each of the remaining cans holding?

Shawna keeps a detailed fitness journal for the week because she is trying to stay consistent with her home workout routine. Her plan includes stretches, water breaks, and a checklist for different exercises. Every morning she spends 5 minutes warming up, 10 minutes jogging in place, and 3 minutes cooling down afterward. She also tracks pushups, jumping jacks, and planks, even though those are not the focus of this question. On Monday, her notebook says she did 15 jumping jacks, 8 pushups, and 2 one-minute planks before starting situps. Her workout goal for situps is 30. She had hoped to finish all of them on Monday, but she was only able to do 12 situps that day because she got tired early. Since she fell short, she wrote herself a note that she would make up the rest on Tuesday.

On Tuesday, Shawna changed her routine a little. She drank 2 glasses of water before exercising, spent 12 minutes stretching, and did 20 squats, 14 lunges on each leg, and 9 pushups. She also counted 19 minutes of total exercise time before dinner, and her step counter showed 4,300 steps by the afternoon. When it came time for situps, however, she was only able to do 19 situps on Tuesday, even though she had planned to make up everything she missed from Monday. Her weekly chart also shows that Wednesday is usually the day she does yoga for 25 minutes, and on Thursday she normally rests. She has a 7-day calendar on the wall, 3 workout outfits laid out for the week, and 2 towels in her gym bag.

How many situps would Shawna have to do on Wednesday to meet her minimum goal and make up for the ones she didn't do?

James keeps a very detailed weekly planner because he balances two different jobs, tracks his commuting time, and is trying to compare his work income to all of his routine expenses. At his main job, he wears a blue uniform shirt that costs $18 each and black work shoes that cost $45, though those clothing costs are taken care of separately and are not part of this week's pay. The main job is 8 miles from his apartment, and gas for the week came to $32. He usually brings lunch from home 4 days a week, but on Friday he bought a sandwich for $9 and a drink for $3. He also noted that last month he worked 28 hours one week and 34 hours another week, but this week was different.

For his actual pay rate, James earns $20 an hour while working at his main job. The company also gives workers a choice between two break schedules: either one 30-minute lunch and two 10-minute breaks, or one 45-minute lunch, but those scheduling details do not change the hourly wage listed on his pay stub. This week, he worked 30 hours at his main job, spread across 5 days. On Monday he worked 6 hours, Tuesday 5 hours, Wednesday 7 hours, Thursday 4 hours, and Friday 8 hours, for that total.

James also has a second job on weekends and some evenings. At that job, parking costs $6 per shift unless he carpools, and sometimes he sells employee meal vouchers for $2 each to coworkers. The break room there has 12 lockers, 3 vending machines, and a coffee machine that charges $1.50 per cup. Last Saturday he worked one shift that started at 9:00 a.m., and on Sunday he considered swapping a shift with a coworker who works 18 hours a week, but in the end James kept his usual schedule. He earns 20% less while working his second job than he earns at his main job. He works half as many hours at his second job as he works at his main job. Since he worked 30 hours at his main job this week, that means he worked half that much at his second job.

James is also budgeting for other weekly costs: $14 for streaming services, $60 for groceries, $25 for his phone bill contribution, and $40 set aside for laundry and household supplies. He has a rewards card that gives 5% back on certain purchases, and he once calculated that if he saved $75 per week for 12 weeks he could buy a new bicycle for $900. None of those plans changes the amount he was paid for his work this week.

How much does he earn per week?

Lee runs a small neighborhood lawn-mowing service. He keeps a notebook where he tracks all kinds of details from week to week: how many gas cans he filled, how long each mower blade lasted, which streets had corner lots, and whether he had to trim around flower beds, birdbaths, swing sets, or vegetable gardens. He usually starts at 8:00 a.m., takes a 20-minute lunch break around noon, and tries to finish before 6:30 p.m. if the weather holds. On rainy days he sometimes reschedules jobs, and on especially hot days he brings 4 bottles of water, 2 sports drinks, and a cooler with ice packs. His mower uses about 2 gallons of gas during a busy day, and last week gas was $4 per gallon, though he also bought a spare trimmer line spool for $9 and a pair of work gloves for $12.

Some of Lee's customers have small yards, some have large back lots, and a few ask him to edge the sidewalks or blow leaves off the driveway. One customer talked for 15 minutes about fertilizer, another had 7 flower pots lining the porch, and another had 3 dogs that had to be kept inside while he worked. On Monday he completed 4 lawns, on Tuesday 3, on Wednesday 2 because of a brief storm delay, on Thursday 5, and on Friday 2 more, for a total that matched the number of addresses he had written on last week's work page. A few customers asked about monthly scheduling, and one said she might need service every 10 days instead of every 14. He also received two text messages about future hedge trimming, but those jobs were not part of last week's mowing income.

For each lawn Lee mows, he charges $33. Last week he mowed 16 lawns in all. In addition, three customers each gave him a $10 tip for the mowing work. He does not count the value of free lemonade, and no other payments, supplies, or future bookings affect what he earned from mowing lawns last week.

How many dollars did Lee earn mowing lawns last week?

Tara has been comparing several laptop deals for weeks because she needs one for a design class, remote meetings, and storing photos from the 3 memory cards she already owns. One store had a refurbished model for $920 with a 90-day warranty, another had a gaming laptop for $1280 with RGB lights and a free mouse, and an online seller advertised a weekend coupon for $75 off orders over $1500, plus $18 shipping and a possible 7% service fee. Tara also wrote down prices for accessories: a sleeve for $24, a wireless mouse for $36, a keyboard for $58, antivirus software for $49 per year, and a backup drive for $110. She even compared payment plans at two shops: one suggested 18 monthly payments of $72 after a setup fee, and another required 25% down with $55 monthly payments, but neither of those plans matched the model she actually wants.

The laptop Tara has been planning to buy costs $1000. The computer shop that sells that exact laptop accepts payment in installments of $65 per month provided that a 20% down payment is made. Tara has been saving in a jar where she keeps ten $5 bills, twelve $10 bills, and some coins for bus fare, and she is thinking about using some birthday money too. She decides that for the required down payment, she wants to pay an additional $20 beyond that required amount. During the next few months, she also has unrelated expenses like $45 for internet, $30 for printer ink, and $12 each week for coffee near campus, but those are paid from a different budget. If Tara wants to pay an additional $20 for the down payment, how much will her balance be after paying for 4 months?

Jesse and Mia are competing in a week long charity race that runs from Monday through Sunday, and the event handbook says each runner’s goal is to complete 30 miles by the end of the week. The route map is split into colored sections of 1 mile, 2 miles, 5 miles, and a final 10-mile scenic stretch, and volunteers hand out bib numbers, safety pins, and water cups at 7 different checkpoints. Jesse wears bib 14, Mia wears bib 18, and their team table has 24 granola bars, 12 bananas, 8 oranges, and 30 paper cups for the week. On Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, Jesse keeps a very steady pace and averages 2/3 of a mile per day across those first three days, even though her watch also logs 4,000 steps on Monday, 5,200 on Tuesday, and 6,100 on Wednesday. On Thursday, after replacing her shoelaces and switching from her blue shoes to her black shoes, she runs 10 miles. Her family drives 18 miles to watch her at the Thursday checkpoint, and she drinks 3 bottles of water there, but those details do not affect her race mileage. Meanwhile, Mia follows a different strategy: over the first 4 days, she averages 3 miles a day, despite spending 45 minutes stretching on Monday, 30 minutes on Tuesday, 50 minutes on Wednesday, and 40 minutes on Thursday. She also buys 2 energy gels for each of those 4 days at $1.50 each, carries a 9-ounce snack pack, and records lap splits of 12 minutes, 11 minutes, and 13 minutes on one training loop. By the middle of the week, the announcer notes that there are 3 days left in the competition, that 60 total volunteers are helping, that the opening ceremony lasted 25 minutes, and that the runners have already passed a banner at mile 15. If both runners still plan to finish the full 30 miles by Sunday, what is the average of their average that they have to run over the final three days?

On Saturday morning, Elsa and Amalie emptied several jars, pencil cases, coat pockets, and the little ceramic bank on Amalie’s shelf to count their coin collections before going to the toy market. Elsa had already sorted some of her coins into 5 neat stacks of 8 for easier counting, while Amalie liked arranging hers in rows of 9, and there were also old arcade tokens, 12 buttons, 7 foreign coins from a trip, and 3 washers on the table that did not count as part of their real coin totals. Last month, Elsa had traded away 14 stickers for 6 shiny coins, and Amalie had once saved 90 coins before spending some on snacks, but those earlier amounts are not the amounts they have now. Today, the ratio of the number of coins Elsa has to the number of coins Amalie has is 10:45. Together, the two girls have 440 coins in total. 

They are planning a shopping trip with many price tags to compare: a toy drum costs 36 coins, a puzzle costs 28, a stuffed bear costs 55, and a miniature train set costs 84. Amalie is especially interested in toys, and after counting everything carefully, she decides to spend 3/4 of the coins she has on toys. Elsa, meanwhile, sets aside 25 coins for lunch, 18 for bus fare over several days, and thinks about saving half of what remains for a fair next month, but none of that changes Amalie’s count. The shopkeeper also offers a 2-for-1 sticker pack, 4 balloons for 20 coins, and a shelf with 11 toy cars, though Amalie does not necessarily buy any specific combination of those items. 

If the total number of coins they have is 440, and Amalie spends 3/4 of what she has on toys, how many will she remain with?

During a long Saturday morning tide-pool survey at the beach, Carly brought along a laminated species checklist with 18 pictures on the front and 12 more on the back, a bucket labeled with a 3-liter fill line, and 2 mesh bags she never ended up using. She started at 8:15 a.m., checked 4 rocky pools near the jetty, skipped 1 pool because it was too deep, and then spent 35 minutes comparing shell colors with her field guide. Along the way she also noticed 9 crabs, 6 tiny fish, 11 limpets on one rock, and 3 empty snail shells, but she did not collect any of those. She even wrote down water temperatures of 61, 62, and 63 degrees in different spots, and her notebook page was numbered 14.

What she actually collected for her classroom display was this: Carly collected 7 starfish with 5 arms each and one seastar with 14 arms. Her friend thought one of the starfish looked wider than the others, and another had sand stuck to 2 of its arms, but they were still counted the same way. On the walk back, Carly passed 5 warning signs, counted 20 wooden steps up from the beach, and saw a souvenir stand selling postcards for $1 each, toy shells in packs of 8, and plush sea animals for $14. She also remembered that last year her class had drawn 7 starfish on a poster and 1 giant seastar in the corner, though that was only artwork and not part of today's collection.

How many arms do the animals she collected have in total?

At the county harvest fair, three kids—Martha, Tim, and Harry—spent the afternoon helping at the apple display after the morning weighing contest. Martha had already sorted her apples into 4 wooden crates, with 17 apples in each crate, for a total of 68 apples. Next to her display was a chalkboard showing old inventory notes from earlier in the week: 72 bruised apples had been set aside for cider, 14 green apples were used in a pie contest, 9 baskets were stacked near the fence, and each basket could hold up to 12 apples. Tim ignored those notes because they were from a different shipment, but he did compare his own pile to Martha's. Tim had 30 less apples than Martha. Harry, who was helping put labels on smaller bags, had half as many apples as Tim. During the fair, the announcer also mentioned that a nearby orchard had 120 trees, the entry fee was $6 per person, and the apple-tasting booth sold 25 caramel apples before noon and 31 after noon. Martha also planned to save 8 apples for her teacher, give 6 to her cousin, and use 10 for bobbing apples later, but those plans had not happened yet and did not change how many apples she had when Tim and Harry compared theirs to hers. If Martha has 68 apples, how many apples does Harry have?

At a busy Saturday flea market that opens at 8:00 a.m. and closes at 3:00 p.m., Hillary sets up a booth with 24 handmade crafts arranged on 3 shelves, 8 on each shelf. She also brings 2 folding chairs, a cash box containing 15 dollars in small bills to make change, 11 price tags, and a sign she decorated last night using 4 markers and a roll of ribbon that cost her 6 dollars earlier in the week. The booth fee for the day is 10 dollars, parking costs 5 dollars, and she spent 9 dollars on coffee and a muffin before the market started. Her neighbor at the next booth sells knitted hats for 14 dollars each and manages to sell 5 of them before noon, while another vendor across the aisle offers 3 bracelets for 20 dollars. Hillary's own handmade crafts are priced at 12 dollars per craft. During the morning rush, one shopper asks about buying 2 crafts but decides to come back later, another shopper pays with a 50-dollar bill for items from a different booth and causes a line to form, and Hillary spends 6 minutes wrapping one purchase in tissue paper and twine. By lunchtime she has sold 3 crafts, and one especially appreciative customer, after chatting about how long the crafts take to make and admiring several unsold pieces, gives Hillary an extra 7 dollars on top of what she earned from selling the crafts. Later on, after counting only today's profits from sales and that extra gift, Hillary walks over to the bank kiosk near the market entrance and deposits 18 dollars from today's profits into her bank account. She keeps the rest of today's money with her. How many dollars is Hillary left with after making the deposit?

Nancy is setting up a rectangular aquarium for her fish in the living room before the pet store closes at 7:00 p.m. The aquarium stand came with a care sheet reminding her not to overfeed the 8 neon tetras, 2 angelfish, and 1 pleco she plans to keep later, and she has already washed 15 pounds of gravel, arranged 6 plastic plants, and stacked 12 decorative shells near the tank. The tank itself is 4 feet long, 6 feet wide, and 3 feet high, and the instruction booklet says a completely full tank of that size holds a certain number of cubic feet of water. Nancy starts filling the aquarium from a hose that runs at 3 gallons per minute, although she briefly considers using two 5-gallon buckets instead. She fills the aquarium halfway, then hears the doorbell ring because a delivery driver is dropping off 4 boxes: fish food, a net, a thermometer, and replacement filter pads. She goes to answer the door, spends 6 minutes signing for the packages, and also chats with her neighbor about a 20% off sale on aquarium lights. While Nancy is gone, her cat jumps onto the stand, knocks over a bag containing 9 marbles used for decoration, brushes against the aquarium, and tips it enough to spill half the water that is in it onto the floor. Nancy comes back, notices the mess, uses 3 towels and 1 mop to clean up, checks that the filter rated for 40 gallons is still dry, and then resumes filling. Instead of starting over, she triples the amount of water currently in the aquarium. She also measures the room temperature at 72 degrees and wonders whether she should install the 200-watt heater now or later. Ignore the gravel, decorations, fish supplies, cleanup, and all timing details. If the aquarium is 4 feet long, 6 feet wide, and 3 feet high, how many cubic feet of water are in the aquarium?

It is Roger’s turn to provide a snack for the baseball team after the game, and after comparing several options at the sporting goods store and the grocery store, he has decided to bring trail mix instead of orange slices, granola bars, pretzels, or juice boxes. The game starts at 4:30 p.m., the players need to arrive 45 minutes early, and the team usually spends about 12 minutes packing equipment afterward before everyone lines up for snacks near the third-base dugout. Roger first considered buying one large 48-ounce bag for $11.99, but then realized that the team prefers individual portions because they are easier to hand out, create less mess, and fit better in the players’ equipment bags. The brand he chose sells trail mix in cardboard packs, and each pack contains 6 individual pouches. Some nearby brands come in boxes of 4, 8, or 10 pouches, and another warehouse club sells a case of 24 pouches, but Roger is specifically buying the kind that comes in packs of 6 individual pouches.

Roger made a checklist while planning. There are 13 members on his baseball team. In addition to the players, 3 coaches will also be there, and 2 helpers usually stay after the game to organize batting helmets, collect practice balls, and load the collapsible water cooler into the equipment shed. Last week, only 11 players stayed until the very end because 2 had to leave early for music lessons, but this week Roger wants to make sure he brings enough for everyone connected with the team who will be there after the game. The assistant coach also mentioned that there are 14 gloves in the team bin, 3 catchers’ masks in the storage room, 2 extra scorebooks in the office, and 18 bottles of water left over from the previous game, though those supplies are unrelated to Roger’s snack purchase.

At the store, Roger notices a sale sign saying 2 packs for $9, while single packs cost $4.79 each, and he briefly calculates possible totals in his head. He also sees family-size bags marked 20% off, coupon tags worth $1.50, and a limit of 5 discounted items per customer. His mother reminds him to check whether the pouches are peanut-free for one sibling at home, but the team snack rules allow trail mix for this game. Roger puts a few other things in the cart too: 1 bunch of bananas, 2 sports drinks for the ride home, and a box of sandwich bags that contains 40 bags, even though he will not use those for the trail mix because the pouches are already individually sealed. He has $30 with him, the drive to the store takes 9 minutes, and checkout usually takes about 6 minutes unless more than 4 people are in line.

Roger wants every person on the team group after the game to get one individual pouch of trail mix. How many packs of trail mix does he need to buy?

At the end of a 6-month wellness challenge run by a community fitness center, four participants were highlighted in the newsletter. The center had originally enrolled 18 people, though 3 switched to the yoga-only track, 2 joined late in month 2, and 5 were mainly there for blood pressure monitoring rather than weight goals. Weekly meetings were held every Tuesday at 6:30 p.m. for 24 weeks, with optional Saturday walks that averaged 4 kilometers, except on 3 rainy weekends when attendance dropped below 10. The program handbook was 103 pages long, the meal-planning packet listed 27 breakfast ideas, and the gym offered 7 different low-impact classes, but the final article focused only on the weight loss totals of four specific people.

Together, those four people lost a total of 103 kilograms of weight over the challenge. The first person lost 27 kilograms. The second person lost 7 kilograms less than the first person. The third and fourth people followed the same meal plan, each drank 2 liters of water a day, each attended 19 weigh-ins, and they ended up losing the same amount of weight. One participant had started at 94 kilograms, another bought 3 new pairs of workout shoes during the program, one tracked calories for 180 days, and the center sold smoothies for $4 each or 3 for $10 after class. The nutrition board compared meal plans of 1600, 1800, and 2000 calories, and one coach mentioned that losing even 5 kilograms can improve energy levels. None of that changes the combined result reported for these four people.

How many kilograms did each of the last two people lose?

Dale and Andrew stopped at a busy cafe for breakfast just before 9:00 a.m. The chalkboard by the door listed all sorts of morning specials: porridge for £4, tea for £2 a pot, orange juice for £3 a glass, coffee refills for £1, and a full breakfast platter for £11. The cafe also had a note saying that every 6th loyalty stamp earns a free hot drink, although neither of them redeemed any stamps that morning. On another sign, the cafe advertised a weekend brunch deal from 10:30 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., but they arrived too early for that. At the counter, jars of jam were stacked in sets of 8, there were 12 muffins in the display case, and a tray near the till held 15 packets of sugar and 9 stirrers.

The items they actually ordered included toast and eggs. A slice of toast costs £1, and eggs cost £3 each. Dale was hungry after skipping a snack at 7:30, so he had 2 slices of toast and 2 eggs. Andrew had already eaten a banana before leaving home, so he ordered 1 slice of toast and 2 eggs. They looked at the pastry case with 5 croissants, 4 cinnamon buns, and 7 scones, but did not add any of those. One of them considered buying a second drink, and they briefly discussed whether 3 slices of toast would be too much for one person, but they kept their order exactly as planned.

Their server mentioned that yesterday the cafe had sold 24 eggs before noon and 31 slices of toast by lunchtime, and that a delivery that morning brought 5 loaves of bread and 8 dozen eggs. The receipt printer was out of paper for a moment, so the cashier wrote some notes by hand. There was also a donation jar with £6 in coins near the register and a tip guide suggesting 10%, 12%, or 15%, though no tip needs to be considered here. How much did their breakfast cost?

At the end of the summer, a community garden volunteer made a long inventory sheet for the produce harvest before packing everything into crates for a weekend neighborhood market. The garden had 12 raised beds, though only 9 were used for vegetables, and the rest held herbs and flowers. Bed 1 had 3 rows of tomatoes with 18 plants in each row, Bed 2 had 24 carrot clusters, and Bed 3 had onions bundled into 15 bunches of 8 for a school cooking class. The shed had 14 empty baskets, 6 muddy shovels, 3 wheelbarrows, and 27 plant labels left over from spring planting. On harvest day, 8 volunteers arrived at 7:30 a.m., 5 more came at 8:15 a.m., and 2 left early after washing 16 buckets. The weighing table showed 42 pounds of tomatoes, 19 pounds of zucchini, and 31 ears of corn from another section of the garden. There were also 48 marigolds planted around the fence to keep pests away, 11 sunflower stalks near the compost bin, and 4 rain barrels that each held 55 gallons when full.

For the vegetables being counted in the final inventory, the garden produced 237 potatoes. It produced 60 fewer cucumbers than potatoes. It also produced twice as many peppers as cucumbers. Some of the cucumbers were later sorted into 9 pickling jars and 6 salad baskets, and some peppers were separated by color into red, yellow, and green trays, but all of them still counted in the total harvest. Last year the garden had produced 210 potatoes, 155 cucumbers, and 310 peppers, while this year the market planned to charge $2 per pound for potatoes, $1 each for cucumbers in bundles of 5, and $3 for mixed pepper bags; however, the question is only about the number of vegetables grown. If 23 potatoes were set aside for seed stock, 18 cucumbers were washed first, and 40 peppers were displayed in the front stand, those vegetables were still part of what the garden produced.

How many vegetables did the garden produce?

A professional boxer is preparing for an upcoming fight that is exactly 4 months away. At his current medical check-in, the scale shows that he weighs 97 kg. His training camp keeps detailed records of everything: he trains 6 days a week, does 12 rounds of sparring on Mondays and Thursdays, runs 8 km on roadwork days, drinks 4 liters of water on intense training days and 3 liters on lighter days, and usually eats 5 smaller meals instead of 3 large ones. His nutritionist has also written down that his breakfast might include 2 eggs, 1 bowl of oatmeal, and a banana, while lunch sometimes includes 250 g of chicken and 180 g of rice, though those meal details change depending on the week. Last season he fought in the 92 kg class, two years ago he briefly competed closer to 90 kg, and his coach says his walking-around weight used to be over 100 kg during the off-season. The gym membership costs 60 dollars per month, his gloves weigh 16 ounces each for sparring, and he owns 3 pairs of boxing shoes, although he only uses 1 pair in camp. He also has 7 hand wraps in his locker, attends physiotherapy twice a week for 45 minutes each session, and sleeps about 8 hours a night when camp is going well.

For this fight camp, however, the only planned weight change is that he is on a diet that allows him to lose 3 kg per month until the day of the fight. He starts this plan weighing 97 kg with 4 months remaining. How much will he weigh on the day of the fight?

For his birthday, Manny brought treats to school on a Thursday, even though the class had first talked about celebrating on Wednesday after recess. He packed everything in 4 large grocery bags and 2 smaller reusable bags, along with 25 paper plates, 30 napkins, 1 plastic cake server, and 3 unopened juice boxes for himself to save for later. The class had just finished a math quiz with 20 questions, and Mr. Keith had written the day’s schedule on the board: reading from 9:00 to 9:45, science from 10:00 to 10:40, lunch at 11:30, and the birthday snack at 1:15. Manny also brought 3 birthday cookie pies to share with his 24 classmates and his teacher, Mr. Keith.

At first, some students thought there might also be brownies because Manny had mentioned baking 12 brownies the weekend before, but those stayed at home. One of the cookie pies had blue frosting, one had chocolate chips arranged in 5 little circles, and one had 18 candy sprinkles around the edge. The bakery receipt showed a subtotal of $21 before tax, though Manny’s aunt had a coupon for $3 off a different purchase and also bought 2 candles, each marked 99 cents. Mr. Keith reminded everyone that there were 26 desks in the room, though one desk was being used to hold extra crayons, glue sticks, and 7 construction-paper hats left over from an art project. Manny had written his name on the pie boxes with a black marker, and each box was about 10 inches across.

When it was time to serve the treat, the 3 birthday cookie pies were each cut into 10 slices. Manny, his classmates, and Mr. Keith all had 1 piece. Some students asked for milk, but the cafeteria only sent up 8 cartons, and 6 students chose water instead. No one took seconds yet because Mr. Keith wanted to make sure everyone got one first. After everyone listed above had taken exactly 1 piece, how many slices are left?

At the annual school district celebration, James is being honored after a long career that included teaching 5 different grade levels, advising 2 after-school clubs, organizing 14 spring concerts, and once supervising a field trip with 48 students, 6 parent volunteers, and 3 buses. Over the years, he has worked in 4 classrooms, taught in buildings that were 12 miles apart, and kept 27 labeled binders of lesson plans. He usually arrived by 7:15 a.m., taught 6 class periods a day, and drank 2 cups of coffee before lunch. The district newsletter also mentions that he received 8 teaching awards, attended 35 professional development workshops, and wrote recommendation letters for 120 seniors, even though not all of those years were at the same school. James spends 40 years teaching. His partner, who teaches in the neighboring wing, has a different career timeline: she currently teaches 3 sections of literature, coaches 1 debate team, decorates her room with 24 posters, and has 18 desks arranged in 3 rows of 6. She has taught at 2 schools, commutes 9 miles each way, and last semester graded 210 essays and 42 quizzes. She also spent 6 summers running enrichment programs and ordered 15 boxes of classroom supplies this year. His partner has been teaching for 10 years less. Together they are planning a joint retirement display with 50 photographs, 9 certificates, and 4 memory books. How long is their combined experience?

On Saturday afternoon, Jennifer stopped at a large grocery store that had a promotion on canned dairy products. She first picked up 40 cans of milk and put them in her cart. The store had different package signs everywhere: yogurt was 4 for $5, juice boxes came in packs of 8, and condensed soup cans were stacked in towers of 24. Jennifer also compared prices on two milk brands, one costing $2 per can and another $2.25 per can, but she ultimately chose the cans she wanted and had already placed 40 of them in her cart before she ran into her classmate Mark in the dairy aisle. Mark was shopping for a school event and had a list that also included 12 paper plates, 3 bags of ice, 10 napkin packs, and 2 cartons of strawberries, though those items are unrelated to the milk he was buying.

When they met, they briefly talked about how crowded the store was. There were 18 checkout lanes, but only 11 were open. Jennifer mentioned that she had arrived 25 minutes earlier, had spent 7 minutes looking for a basket before switching to a cart, and had already walked through aisles 2, 5, and 9. Mark said he had come in just after soccer practice, where 14 students had attended, and that he still needed to stay under a budget of $150. They also noticed a sign saying customers could buy up to 60 cans during the weekend sale, and another sign advertising a reward of 200 bonus points for spending over $80. None of this changed what they each bought.

As they compared their carts, Jennifer decided to buy additional cans of milk after seeing how many Mark was getting. For every 5 cans of milk Mark bought, Jennifer bought 6 additional cans of milk. Mark purchased 50 cans of milk in total. Jennifer also considered buying 5 bottles of water and 6 granola bars for the ride home, and Mark debated between 4 cereal boxes and 9 bags of pasta, but those choices did not affect the milk count. After paying, Jennifer packed her groceries into 7 reusable bags, while Mark used 6 paper bags and carried one item by hand.

How many cans of milk did Jennifer bring home from the store?

During recess on Thursday, the fourth-grade classes were rotating through several playground stations because the teachers were testing a new activity schedule. There were 28 students on the blacktop, 12 on the swings, 9 waiting for the slide, and 7 playing hopscotch near the painted lines. Sam and Jeff signed up for the skipping competition, which was run beside the basketball court using a clipboard, a stopwatch, and a whistle. The competition was split into four rounds, with a 30-second water break after round 2 and a reminder from the PE aide that shoelaces had to be retied before the final round. Sam wore a red shirt with the number 8 on it, Jeff wore a blue shirt, and the scorekeeper brought 2 pencils, 1 eraser, and 4 blank tally sheets even though only 1 tally sheet was used. Some students were also counting how many total jumps everyone on the playground did that day, but only Sam and Jeff's skipping competition mattered here.

In round 1, Sam completed 1 more skip than Jeff. In round 2, Jeff skipped 3 fewer times than Sam. In round 3, Jeff skipped 4 more times than Sam. In round 4, Jeff got tired after helping carry 6 cones and only completed half the number of skips as Sam. Sam was very steady and skipped 16 times in each round, even though he had practiced 20 skips before recess and said his best ever at home was 24. Jeff had brought a jump rope that cost $9, while Sam's had been borrowed from a bin holding 15 ropes, 3 hula hoops, and 2 beanbags. The recess monitor announced that the whole competition area would close in 10 minutes, but all four rounds had already fit into the schedule.

If Sam skipped 16 times in each round, what is the average number of skips per round completed by Jeff?

Irene works at a neighborhood packaging and shipping store that tracks all kinds of weekly statistics. On the wall by the time clock, there is a chart showing that the store is open 6 days a week, from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Friday and 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. on Saturday. Last week the store processed 214 parcels, sold 36 rolls of tape, 18 padded envelopes, and 42 cardboard boxes, and Irene personally helped 27 walk-in customers on Tuesday alone. She also spent 3 lunch breaks reorganizing shelves, stocked 12 printer-ink cartridges, and counted 95 bubble mailers in the back room after a delivery. Her bus pass costs $25 per week, she bought coffee 4 times at $3 each, and she is saving for a new phone that costs $640. None of those store totals change how payroll works.

For payroll, Irene earns a flat $500 if she works for 40 hours in a week. The manager also noted on the payroll sheet that any time beyond 40 hours is considered overtime, and Irene gets an extra $20 for every hour of overtime. Last week, according to her finalized timecard, Irene worked 50 hours total. On two of those days she stayed 2 hours late, on another day she came in 1 hour early, and the rest of the total was spread across her normal shifts. The store's scheduling software also showed that other employees worked 32, 38, 44, and 41 hours, but Irene's pay should be calculated only from her own hours and pay rules.

If she worked 50 hours last week, calculate her total income.

Paityn is organizing costumes and accessories for a school spirit event, and on Saturday morning she spreads everything out across her room to count it. On one shelf she has 20 red hats and 24 blue hats. In the same room there are also 12 green scarves, 18 pairs of striped socks, 9 costume badges, 6 unopened packs of safety pins with 50 pins in each pack, and 3 storage bins labeled Winter, Parade, and Extras. Last month she had donated 7 old hats and bought 11 new ribbons, but none of that changes the hat count she is using now. She also keeps a notebook where she wrote that red hats usually cost $8 each and blue hats usually cost $6 each, though some were bought during a 25% off sale. 

Her friend Zola is helping from across town. Zola does not have the same collection: she has 4/5 times as many red hats as Paityn has, and she has twice the number of blue hats that Paityn has. Zola also owns 10 red costume capes, 14 blue wristbands, 2 large garment bags, and 30 paper tickets for the event. On Friday she spent 45 minutes sorting clothes, 20 minutes labeling boxes, and 15 minutes texting Paityn about sizes and colors. She almost brought 8 purple hats from drama club, but those are borrowed props and are not included with her own hats. 

The two friends plan to combine all the hats together and then divide the hats equally between themselves so that each has the same number to hand out at the event. They are not separating by color when they split them, and they are only sharing the hats they personally own in the counts described above. If they combine all the hats together and share them equally between themselves, calculate the number of hats each gets.

Hans booked a room in a hotel for a short business trip. The building is advertised as a tidy mid-rise property with 10 floors, and each floor was originally designed with 10 identical guest rooms laid out in the same pattern. The lobby has 2 elevators, 1 service staircase, a breakfast area with 18 tables, and a front desk that rotates between 3 clerks per shift. Check-in begins at 3:00 p.m., check-out is at 11:00 a.m., and guests who arrive before noon can store up to 4 bags at the concierge. On weekdays, breakfast is served from 6:30 to 10:00, while on weekends it runs until 10:30. Room service has 24 menu items, including 6 soups, 8 main courses, and 10 desserts, although hot meals stop at 10 p.m. The hotel also has 40 parking spaces, charges $12 per day for parking, and offers free Wi-Fi on up to 3 devices per room. Hans noticed that the hall carpets were replaced 2 years ago, the windows were cleaned last month, and the keycards must be reprogrammed every 72 hours.

The manager explains that, although the hotel normally has 10 floors with 10 identical rooms on each floor, there was an accident involving plumbing and ceiling damage, so the last floor is completely unavailable for guests until repairs are finished. Maintenance has 5 workers assigned, the estimate is 14 days, and 27 boxes of replacement tile are stacked in storage. No other guests are staying at the hotel tonight, even though 16 reservations had been expected earlier in the week and 9 were canceled. Considering there are no other guests, in how many different rooms could Hans be checked in?

At a class birthday-board meeting in early October, four classmates were comparing their ages by looking only at birth months, not years, because they were all born in different years and the teacher said the chart for this activity should focus strictly on month differences. The board already had 12 month labels, 4 colored magnets, 8 sticky notes, and 2 extra pushpins that nobody ended up using. Jolyn wrote her birthday on a blue card, Therese used a yellow card, Aivo used a green card, and Leon used a red card. Before they got to the actual comparison, they spent time talking about whose birthday falls during the school year, whose family usually buys 6 cupcakes versus 12 cupcakes, and whether summer birthdays feel longer to wait for. Therese mentioned that last year her party started at 3:30 and ended at 6:00, Aivo said he got 5 balloons and 2 wrapped presents from cousins, Leon said his family mailed 4 invitation cards but invited 9 people by text, and Jolyn said she once had a cake with 11 candles even though the conversation today was not about years old at all.

To keep things organized, they made a small comparison table. One note said that Jolyn is 2 months older than Therese. Another note said that Therese is 5 months older than Aivo. A third note said that Leon is 2 months older than Aivo. They also discussed several unrelated birthday details, such as how many months are left until the next holiday break, how many students in class have birthdays in March, and whether being born near the beginning or end of a month changes anything for this chart. It did not, because they were only comparing the age differences in whole months exactly as written on the notes.

After checking the board twice and rearranging the magnets once, they wanted to answer just one comparison: How much older in months is Jolyn than Leon?

On Saturday afternoon, Peter stopped by a neighborhood convenience store on his way home from basketball practice. The store had a big sign advertising fountain drinks in three cup sizes: 12-ounce, 20-ounce, and 32-ounce, and there was also a promotion on bottled water for 2 for $3. Near the register, gum was marked 3 packs for $1.50, candy bars were $1.25 each, and a bag of chips cost $1.75. Peter looked at the cooler first, where sports drinks were priced at $2.49, juice bottles were $1.89, and sparkling water was on sale for $0.99, but he decided he specifically wanted soda from the fountain machine instead. The machine had several flavors, and one sign listed that ice was free, cup lids were included, and refills on a later visit would be half price with a loyalty card. Another sign said the store opened at 7:00 a.m., closed at 10:00 p.m., and had sold 84 fountain drinks the day before. Peter noticed the clerk restocking straws in boxes of 100, with 6 boxes under the counter, and there were 14 empty cups in the small-cup dispenser and 9 in the large-cup dispenser.

Peter checked his pockets and remembered that he had brought $2 with him in total: one $1 bill, 3 quarters, and 5 nickels. He considered buying a candy bar too, but decided not to. He also remembered that last week he had spent $1.75 on a sandwich at the same store and had gotten 25 cents in change, but that was on a different day and with different prices on other items. Today, the soda costs $.25 an ounce. After paying for the soda, Peter leaves with $.50 still in his pocket. He does not buy anything else, even though the cashier mentions a special where 2 cookies cost $1.00 and a hot dog combo costs $4.50. How many ounces of soda did he buy?

John keeps careful records for all of the animals on his small farm. On Monday he noted that his cow had been eating 18 pounds of hay a day, drinking about 12 gallons of water, and spending 7 hours in the pasture and 5 hours in the barn whenever the weather dropped below 40 degrees. The vet had visited twice that month, charging $45 for one visit and $60 for another, and suggested a mineral mix that came in 25-pound bags for $14 each. John also compared the cow with two calves that weighed 185 pounds and 210 pounds, a steer that weighed 950 pounds, and a neighbor's cow that had recently sold for $2.75 per pound after reaching 680 pounds. In last year's county fair, animals in the same class averaged 430 pounds at the spring weigh-in and 590 pounds by late summer, and the blue-ribbon winner produced 6 gallons of milk a day for 9 days in a row.

John's own cow, however, originally weighed 400 pounds. Over time, after following a feeding plan of 8 pounds of grain in the morning and 6 pounds at night, plus occasional supplements sold in 3-pound tubs, the cow increased its weight to 1.5 times its starting weight. John is not selling by the head, by the lot, or by age; he is able to sell this cow for $3 per pound. He also has to think about trucking fees of $75, a market entry fee of $20, and a pen rental fee of $15, although those charges are handled separately from the sale price itself. If he had sold earlier in the season, auction commissions would have been 4%, and if he waits until next month, feed could cost another $90.

How much more is it worth after gaining the weight?

Brandon keeps detailed records for his reptile hobby and small breeding business, and every January he reorganizes everything into labeled binders. In one binder, he listed feeder costs, tank sizes, lighting schedules, and yearly sales. For example, he currently has 14 terrariums in use, although only 9 are full-sized display tanks and 5 are temporary juvenile enclosures. Each full-sized tank uses 2 hides, 1 heat mat, and 1 thermometer, while the juvenile setups share 6 extra water dishes altogether. He buys calcium powder in 3 containers at a time, replaces UVB bulbs every 6 months, and once spent $48 on background decorations even though those did not affect sales. During one busy spring expo, he brought 27 care sheets, sold 11 extra food bowls, and handed out 32 business cards before lunch.
