In summer he tracked hatch dates for 18 clutches, though several eggs were infertile, and he also noted that one rack held 24 tubs while another held only 20 because 4 were being cleaned.

His sales log separates years carefully. Brandon sold 86 geckos last year. He sold twice that many the year before. In the same binder, there are unrelated notes saying he considered keeping back 12 geckos for future breeding, spent $172 on insects over several months, and once discounted 7 older tanks by $15 each at a garage sale. He also wrote down monthly electricity bills of $61, $58, and $64 for different seasons, plus a reminder that a pet show admission fee was $8 per person and parking was $12. None of those notes change the yearly gecko sales totals in the sales log. How many geckos has Brandon sold in the last two years?

Krystian works in the library, where his shift usually starts at 8:15 a.m. and ends at 4:45 p.m., except on the first Wednesday of each month when staff training adds 30 extra minutes. The building has 3 floors, 2 stairwells, 14 public computers, and 6 rolling carts for reshelving. On a typical day he checks due dates, answers questions at the front desk, helps shelve returns from the 900s and 500s sections, prints hold slips, and sometimes refills the copier with paper packs of 500 sheets each. The children’s room had 27 new picture books added this month, the history section is missing 12 call-number labels, and last Tuesday 18 patrons asked about study rooms while 7 asked about printer cards. None of that changes his usual borrowing desk totals.

Krystian keeps a rough summary of how many books he borrows out to patrons. On average, he borrows 40 books every day. That daily average is based on his ordinary workdays, even though some days include extra tasks like processing 16 magazine returns, setting aside 9 interlibrary loan envelopes, or collecting 24 overdue notices from the printer. The library itself is open only from Monday to Friday, even though the return slot can still receive books on weekends, and on Saturdays another employee handles inventory of the 48 atlas volumes and 32 language-learning kits.

Fridays are usually busier because a local school sends students in before the weekend, the reading club of 25 members often meets at 3:30 p.m., and the café next door gives a 10% discount to anyone showing a library card. Because of that Friday rush, Krystian’s number of borrowed books every Friday is about 40% higher than the daily average. On Monday he may also answer 11 account questions, on Tuesday he might sort 35 returned DVDs, on Wednesday he could label 20 donated novels, and on Thursday he sometimes helpfully carries 8 boxes of archives to storage, but his borrowing count still follows the same stated pattern.

How many books does he borrow in a week if the library is open from Monday to Friday?

Every winter, Herman keeps a small notebook by the kitchen window where he tracks all kinds of bird-feeding details. In December, January, and February, he likes to feed the birds that visit his yard, including sparrows, finches, cardinals, and the occasional blue jay. He has 3 bird feeders, 2 hanging near the fence and 1 mounted on a pole, although he does not always fill all of them equally because one feeder spills in windy weather. At the start of winter he buys a 20-pound bag of seed, later picks up another 8-pound bag on sale for $14, and also sets out a suet cake every 6 days. In December he writes down that 11 cardinals appeared on one snowy morning, and on another day he counted 17 small birds and 4 squirrels competing under the feeder. January is colder, so he sometimes wears 2 sweaters, 1 scarf, and insulated gloves when he goes outside, and in February he notices that the sun is up a little longer each week. He even marks on his calendar that December has 31 days, January has 31 days, and February has 28 days that year. Some afternoons he cleans seed shells off the porch, which takes him about 15 minutes, and once a week he rinses the birdbath with 3 gallons of water. He keeps measuring cups in the kitchen drawer: a 1-cup scoop, a 1/2-cup scoop, and a 1/4-cup scoop. Although he uses different seed mixes on some weekends and sometimes refills a feeder that gets knocked sideways, his regular feeding routine during December, January, and February is always the same: he feeds the birds 1/2 cup in the morning and 1/2 cup in the afternoon. How many cups of food will he need for all three months?

John works at a small warehouse job that sometimes tracks speed, accuracy, and attendance separately. On a typical week, the warehouse is open 6 days, employees clock in through a tablet that rounds to the nearest minute, and the break room sells coffee for $2, tea for $1.50, and sandwiches for $6. Last month John worked 22 days total, arrived early 5 times, stayed late 3 times for unpaid cleanup, and used 12 gallons of gas commuting in one week when prices were $3.80 per gallon. The company posts charts showing average box counts per shift, with one team averaging 140 boxes, another averaging 165, and a top team once reaching 200 on inventory day. John usually packs electronics, where some items come in cases of 12, others in crates of 24, and labels are printed in batches of 50. Employees get two 15-minute breaks and one 30-minute lunch, and some workers compare whether they are better off taking the city bus for $4 each way or driving. 

John's base pay arrangement is simple: he makes $80 a day and works for 8 hours. There is also an optional performance bonus program. If he chooses to work hard enough to qualify, he earns an extra $20 for that day. However, hitting the bonus target means his workday becomes 2 hours longer because he spends more time loading, scanning, and double-checking orders before the final truck leaves. Some employees talk about weekly totals like 5-day pay, overtime rules after 40 hours, and monthly budget goals such as saving $300, paying $95 for a phone bill, and spending $120 on groceries, but John's question for today is only about the single day when he decides to go for the bonus. 

How much does John make per hour if he decides to earn the bonus?

Sally and Bob have been talking for months about taking a trip together at the end of the year, and they keep a shared notebook full of ideas. On one page they listed 12 possible destinations, compared 7 train routes, 5 budget airlines, and 3 bus companies, and even estimated that hotel rooms might cost anywhere from $48 to $125 per night depending on the season. Sally wants to visit a beach town with a boardwalk that is 4 miles long, while Bob prefers a mountain cabin area with 9 hiking trails and 2 lakes. They eventually agree that whatever trip they choose, they will both work as babysitters during the year and save half of what they earn specifically for the trip.

To stay organized, Sally babysits for several neighborhood families, including one with 2 children, one with 3 children, and one with twins. She sometimes works weekday afternoons, sometimes Friday evenings, and once in a while on Saturday mornings. One family usually pays her in $1 bills, another rounds everything to the nearest $5, and a third always offers snacks, juice boxes, and leftovers in addition to payment. She also keeps track of things like bus fare to get there, which is $2 each way, and one family lives 6 blocks farther away than the others. Even so, her babysitting pay rate is a steady $6 per day.

Bob babysits too, mostly for relatives and neighbors on the other side of town. One household has a toddler who goes to bed at 7:30 p.m., another has an 8-year-old who needs help with 20 minutes of reading, and another has 4 kids but only hires him on school holidays. He writes down all sorts of notes in his planner: the number of diapers used, the 10-minute walk from the bus stop, whether the children prefer cartoons or board games, and how many hours he stayed. In the summer he babysat near a park with 11 benches and a pond with 14 ducks, and in December he sat for a family that decorated with 200 lights. His babysitting pay rate, however, is a steady $4 per day.

The two friends also make lots of trip calculations that may or may not matter later: if they traveled for 6 days, they guessed they might need 18 meals on the road; if they bought souvenirs, Sally thought she might spend $15 while Bob guessed $20; if they took a train, one route would require 2 transfers and another would leave at 6:45 a.m. They considered putting all their trip money in a jar, then in separate envelopes, then in a savings account that earns a tiny amount of interest, but in the end they simply stick to the same rule all year: each of them saves half of whatever they earn from babysitting for the trip, and the year has 365 days.

If Sally makes $6 per day and Bob makes $4 per day, how much money will they both have saved for their trip after a year?

John is placing a huge supply order for a massive restaurant complex that includes a main dining hall, a banquet wing, a lunch counter, and a catering kitchen. The restaurant serves breakfast from 6:30 a.m. to 10:30 a.m., lunch from 11:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., and dinner from 5:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., and on weekends it also runs a late-night menu until midnight. Last month the restaurant served 18,400 guests, used 2,750 dinner plates, 3,200 cloth napkins, 480 gallons of soup stock, and 1,200 pounds of potatoes in a single festival week. The manager has been comparing vendor quotes: one beef supplier offered brisket at $7.75 per pound with a 1,500-pound minimum, another offered premium cuts at $8.40 per pound plus a $125 cold-delivery fee, and a poultry distributor advertised bulk chicken cases in 40-pound boxes with a temporary rebate of $0.20 per pound on orders above 2,400 pounds. John ignores those alternatives because he has already selected the standard contract items he needs for this order.

For this specific purchase, he orders 1000 pounds of beef for $8 per pound. He also orders twice that much chicken at $3 per pound. The kitchen also happens to have 350 pounds of frozen fish left in storage, 96 cartons of eggs arriving tomorrow, 24 cooks on rotation, and 14 delivery pallets scheduled for the loading dock this week. The accounting office notes that last Tuesday's produce invoice was $4,860, the bakery order for 600 loaves cost $1,200, and the beverage manager budgeted $900 for coffee, tea, and juice refills. The meat deliveries are usually split between two walk-in coolers kept at 34 degrees, and each cooler can hold 5,000 pounds. John also reviewed old records showing that a previous holiday order included 800 pounds of beef, 1,600 pounds of chicken, and 500 pounds of pork, while a different event used 2,200 dinner rolls and 160 pounds of butter.

How much did everything cost?

John has been trying to organize his writing life more carefully this year. He bought 12 new notebooks in January, each with 200 lined pages, even though he mostly types on his laptop now. His desk has 3 lamps, 2 dictionaries, 5 reference books, and a stack of 47 old draft pages from a project he abandoned last summer. On weekdays he wakes up at 6:30 a.m., makes coffee in a machine that can brew 10 cups, answers 18 emails, and spends about 45 minutes outlining chapters before he starts drafting. He also keeps a spreadsheet where he tracks things like chapter titles, word counts, printing costs, and page estimates. Last month he printed 60 sample pages for editing, and his editor sent back notes on 14 chapters, though those notes do not change his current writing pace.

For his new contract, John needs to complete 3 books, and each book is 400 pages long. The publisher offered him $2,000 per book as an advance, plus possible bonuses if he finishes before the end of the 6-month review period. He considered splitting each book into 20 chapters of 20 pages each, but he might rearrange that later. Some chapters may include tables, illustrations, and title pages, and one early outline even listed 24 chapters for the first book and 18 for the second. He has already chosen 9 possible cover designs, compared printing quotes from 4 companies, and priced paper at $8 per ream and ink cartridges at $35 each. None of that changes the amount he actually writes per day.

John's writing routine is very steady: he writes 20 pages a day. He works every day unless he is traveling, and for this project assume he keeps that exact rate the whole time. He told a friend that in a really productive week he can sometimes draft 140 pages, while in a slower month he may spend 3 extra days revising old material, but for these books his actual writing rate remains the same as stated above. How long will it take him to write 3 books that are 400 pages each?

Alice has a coin jar on her dresser that she has been sorting by denomination for weeks. On Monday she counts 48 pennies, 16 dimes, 7 dollar coins from a birthday card, 3 souvenir arcade tokens, and 20 quarters that she has set aside in a small envelope because she plans to trade only those quarters at the bank. The bank is 6 blocks away, opens at 9:00 a.m., and has a coin exchange machine near the front desk with signs listing wrappers for pennies in rolls of 50, nickels in rolls of 40, dimes in rolls of 50, and quarters in rolls of 40. Alice waits behind 4 customers: one cashes a check for $86, one asks for ten $1 bills, one deposits 12 rolls of pennies, and one exchanges $30 in dimes for paper bills. When it is finally her turn, Alice gives the teller all 20 of her quarters and asks to exchange them for nickels. She does not exchange any of the pennies, dimes, dollar coins, or tokens, and she buys nothing on the way home even though the bakery next door advertises muffins for $3 each and coffee for $2.

Back home, Alice pours the nickels onto the table and notices some unusual ones mixed in with the ordinary coins. Her grandfather, who collects coins in 9 binders and once sold a rare dime for $120, examines them and tells her that 20% of the nickels she received are iron nickels worth $3 each to collectors. The rest are ordinary nickels worth face value. Alice lines the coins up in 5 rows, checks them twice, and writes down a few unrelated notes in her notebook about a future garage sale, including prices of $1, $4, and $7 for old books and toys. What is the total value of her money now?

James has a rainwater collection setup behind his garage that includes a main barrel, two older backup barrels he is not using this week, a metal screen to keep out leaves, and a spigot with a short hose. The main barrel is the one he sells water from, and for that barrel he knows that for each inch of rain, he collects 15 gallons of water. He keeps a notebook with lots of weather and yard details. Last week, before this storm, the barrel had been rinsed on Sunday and left empty. On Monday morning the forecast predicted anywhere from 2 to 5 inches of rain, with wind gusts of 18 miles per hour, and James spent 25 minutes cleaning gutters. By the end of Monday, the rain gauge beside the garden showed 4 inches of rain. On Tuesday, after a cooler start with a high of 68 degrees, it rained again, this time 3 inches. On Wednesday there was only a light drizzle of 0.4 inches, but James had already sealed the barrel and did not count that day in this sale. He also recorded that 6 flower pots overflowed, 12 tomato plants needed staking, and his neighbor borrowed 2 watering cans. 

James sometimes uses collected water on his vegetable beds instead of selling it. His garden has 8 rows, and each row is 14 feet long. He once paid $36 for a replacement lid, $9.50 for a new rain gauge, and $14.40 for a hose repair kit. Last month he sold compost for $18 per bag and mulch for $4.75 per sack, but that is separate from the rainwater. He also compared prices with another seller who charged $1.10 per gallon for pond water and with a landscaping company that charged $24 for a 20-gallon tank refill. James, however, can sell his rainwater for $1.2 per gallon. If he sells all the water collected from the Monday and Tuesday rain in the main barrel, how much money did he make from selling all the water?

Nancy, the librarian, was working through one of the rolling return carts just after the library opened at 9:00 a.m. The cart had two sections, a top shelf and a bottom shelf, and she had already spent 15 minutes sorting a separate stack of oversized atlases that were not on this cart. The children's room had returned 17 picture books earlier that morning, the circulation desk had 23 DVDs waiting to be checked in, and a volunteer had left 9 damaged dust jackets on her desk to be repaired later. Nancy also noticed that 3 of the books on another nearby cart were misfiled in the wrong call-number range, and there were 14 reserved books behind the front desk for patrons who were expected after lunch. None of that changed what was on the cart she was shelving now, but it made the morning feel busy.

Starting with the top section of this particular cart, she shelved 12 history books, 8 romance books, and 4 poetry books. A sticky note attached to the cart mentioned that last night another staff member had already removed 7 science books from a different cart, and Nancy briefly compared that note with the reshelving log, which showed 42 total returns processed during the previous hour. She also remembered that the history books belonged on two separate aisles, the romance books were split between paperback and hardcover shelves, and the poetry books went near an endcap display featuring 11 local authors. After clearing the top section, she moved to the bottom section of the same cart.

On the bottom section, half the books were mystery books, which she quickly put back into place first because that section was close to her desk. The other half of the bottom section consisted of other genres. Among those remaining books from the bottom, there were 5 Western novels and 6 biographies, and she shelved all of those remaining bottom-section books after the mystery books. While doing this, she passed a display with 10 new cookbooks, 8 gardening guides, and 6 travel memoirs that had arrived for next week's feature table, and she made a note that fines collected that morning totaled $12.50 in coins and $18 in bills. By the time she finished, one patron had asked for help finding a dictionary, two students had borrowed study rooms, and the printer had produced 27 pages of overdue notices.

How many books did she have on the book cart when she started?

Hector purchased a container of gumballs from a corner candy shop after school. The shop sold small paper sacks of 12 gumballs for $1.50, medium cups of 24 for $2.75, and large plastic containers in assorted colors, and the clerk also had a promotion where every third sticker on a loyalty card earned 10% off a future purchase. Hector spent time comparing grape, cherry, blue raspberry, lemon-lime, and mystery flavors, and he noticed that the display near the register had 9 lollipops, 7 jawbreakers, and 15 wrapped caramels. The candy aisle itself had 4 shelves, each with 8 rows, and one of the signs said that sugar-free gum was 2 packs for $3 while sour belts were marked down by 25 cents. Hector eventually purchased a container of gumballs. Later that afternoon, while standing near the basketball courts where 3 games were going on and 18 students were waiting for turns, he began giving some of the gumballs away. He gave 4 to Todd. A few minutes later, after Todd had already chewed 2 of his and put 1 in his pocket, Hector gave twice as many as he had given Todd to Alisha. Alisha was carrying a backpack with 6 books, 2 folders, and 3 pens, and she said her favorite color was the same as the color of 11 of the gumballs in the machine at the shop. Then Hector gave 5 less than four times as many to Bobby as he had given to Alisha. Bobby had just finished a practice in which he made 14 free throws out of 20, wore jersey number 9, and had brought 3 granola bars, though none of that affected the candy-sharing. After all of this, Hector checked the container and saw that he had 6 gumballs remaining. If Hector had 6 gumballs remaining, what is the total number of gumballs that Hector purchased?

Gail keeps careful notes on her aquarium room because she is always comparing equipment, water use, and stocking plans. She has two fish tanks sitting on different stands: the larger one is on a reinforced cabinet that can hold 500 pounds, and the smaller one is near a shelf with 12 bottles of conditioner, 4 spare filters, and 9 fish nets. She bought the larger tank during a spring sale for $120 off, and the smaller one came with a hood light rated for 18 watts. Every Saturday she changes 25% of the water in one tank and 20% in the other, checks the temperature twice, and records pH values like 7.1 and 7.4 in a notebook with 48 pages. The first tank is twice the size of the second tank. Right now there are 48 gallons of water in the first tank. Last month she considered filling the tanks to 50 gallons and 24 gallons, but she decided to keep the same size relationship as before and only wrote down that the first currently has 48 gallons.

Gail also follows several aquarium rules. She feeds the fish 2 times a day, uses 1 thermometer strip on each tank, and labels fish by species, color, and length. One rule she always uses for stocking is one gallon of water per inch of fish. She has looked at adding fish that are 1 inch, 2 inches, 2.5 inches, and 3 inches long, but for these two tanks she keeps only two-inch fish in the second tank and three-inch fish in the first tank. In one week she might buy 6 plants for the first tank and 8 plants for the second, and she once had 14 fish total before reorganizing everything, but those numbers changed over time as fish were moved, traded, and measured again.

Today she is thinking about how many fish fit under her stocking rule. The second tank has the smaller fish, and the first tank has the larger fish. During feeding, one of the first tank fish eats another. After that happens, how many more fish would Gail have in the first tank than the second tank if one of the first tank fish eats another?

At a busy craft store, the manager spent the evening sorting through the day's register report. The store has several departments that customers often confuse with one another: fabric, jewelry, stationery, seasonal decor, knitting supplies, beads, and a clearance table near the front. There were 12 fabric bolts restocked in the morning, 18 spools of ribbon put on an endcap, 24 greeting cards featured by the entrance, and 9 bracelet kits moved to a lower shelf after lunch. The cashier working the opening shift handled 14 transactions before noon, and the afternoon cashier said the receipt printer jammed twice, once at 1:15 and again at 3:40. A flyer advertised fabric at 20% off, sticker sheets at 3 for $5, and earring hooks in packs of 40 for $6. The store opened at 10 a.m., closed at 8 p.m., and had 4 employees on the floor for most of the day, except during the 2-hour inventory check when 2 more workers helped in back. One customer bought 7 yards of cotton, another compared 5 sketchbooks before choosing 2, and someone else returned 3 unopened paint pens from a purchase made last week. The jewelry counter sold charm chains, clasps, and resin pendants, while the stationery area displayed notebooks, envelopes, planners, washi tape, and gel pens in 6 different colors.

When the owner finally reviewed the actual sales breakdown for today, she noted that the craft store makes a third of its sales in the fabric section, a quarter of its sales in the jewelry section, and the rest in the stationery section. They made 36 sales today. How many sales were in the stationery section?

Marcy is a makeup artist and has agreed to do makeup for her friend's wedding during a long Saturday event that starts with photos at 9:00 a.m., the ceremony at noon, and a reception that runs until 10:00 p.m. She makes a packing checklist the night before because she is bringing 4 brush rolls, 3 mirror lights, 2 cases of foundation in 12 shades each, 18 disposable mascara wands, 24 wedge sponges, 5 setting sprays, 8 powder compacts, 11 eyeliners, 9 blush palettes, and 14 lipstick bullets in assorted colors. She also has 7 unopened lip liners, 10 small sample pots of primer, and 16 packets of blotting papers. Her assistant reminds her that last month at another wedding she used 4 tubes of lip gloss on 12 people, while at a fashion show she packed 15 tubes just to be safe and brought home 3 unopened. This time, however, the only makeup she has limited stock of is lip gloss, so she carefully counts exactly how much she needs.

The bride has 5 bridesmaids, 2 sisters, and 1 mother helping organize the room, and there are 13 place settings at the head table, 6 floral centerpieces, and 120 guests expected overall. The venue charges $250 per hour for extra access, the hairstylist is bringing 18 hairpins per person, and the photographer wants everyone ready 45 minutes early. Marcy's travel case has 6 compartments on the top tray and 8 on the bottom, and she plans to label them by product type so she does not confuse the gloss with the lip oils, of which she has 4 bottles that are not being used. She also sets aside 3 emergency touch-up bags, each containing tissues, cotton swabs, and powder puffs, plus 2 backup kits for the reception.

For the lip gloss specifically, each tube of lip gloss will hold enough lip gloss for 3 people's makeup. Marcy decides to bring 6 tubs of lip gloss, each of which holds 2 tubes of lip gloss, and this will be the exact amount she needs for everyone's makeup. How many people is Marcy painting with makeup?

Ellie has found an old bicycle in a field behind a row of 7 maple trees near a fence with 14 loose boards, and she thinks it just needs some oil to work well again. The bike is muddy from sitting outside through 3 rainy weeks, the chain has 26 visible rusty links, one pedal is missing half its rubber, and the handlebars are turned slightly sideways. She spends 45 minutes brushing off dried grass, pulls 12 burrs out of the spokes, and notices that the bike still has 2 wheels, even though one tire is flat and the seat has a tear about 8 cm long. In her shed she finds 4 different bottles on a shelf: a 50ml bottle of lamp oil, a 30ml bottle of chain oil that is nearly empty, a 100ml bottle of cleaning fluid, and a fresh can of bicycle oil she bought last month for $6.75. She also has 3 rags, 1 hand pump, and a small wrench set with 9 pieces, but none of those amounts changes how much oil the repair itself requires. Ellie remembers that to fix the bicycle properly, she needs 10ml of oil for each wheel. After that, she will need another 5ml of oil to fix the rest of the bike, such as the chain and other moving parts. She wonders whether the oil she has will be enough before she starts. How much oil does she need in total to fix the bike?

Janice works in an office where people are always preparing reports, and today she was finishing a paper for her department. The paper had been started yesterday during a 2-hour writing block, saved in a folder with 12 other drafts, and printed once by mistake on 7 pages before she realized she still needed to revise it. This morning she arrived at 8:10 a.m., checked 34 emails, ignored 5 calendar reminders, refilled her water bottle, and opened the same paper again. Her keyboard has 104 keys, her monitor is 24 inches wide, and the document was using 11-point font with 1-inch margins. None of that changed the typing task itself, but it was part of her normal routine.

Janice can type 6 sentences per minute. Today at work, Janice continued working on the paper she had started typing yesterday. First, she typed for 20 minutes. Then she took a break, during which she spent 12 minutes in the break room, stirred 2 packets of sugar into her coffee, and talked with a coworker about a meeting scheduled for 1:30 p.m. After that, she came back and typed 15 minutes longer. At one point she noticed formatting issues in 9 headings and 3 bullet lists, but those were fixed separately and did not affect the sentence count. She also changed the title twice and moved 4 paragraphs to different pages.

Later, she discovered that some of what she had typed was wrong and had to erase 40 sentences she had typed incorrectly. Before the afternoon meeting, she printed 1 copy for herself and 2 copies for the team, but the number of printed pages is not the same as the number of sentences in the paper. The meeting lasted 45 minutes and included 8 attendees, 3 agenda items, and notes on 14 action points. After the meeting, Janice returned to her desk, answered 6 messages, and then typed for 18 minutes more. By the end of today, after all of that work, revising, deleting, and continuing from yesterday's draft, the paper had 536 sentences in total.

How many sentences did she start with today?

A lakeside park runs several activities every day during the busy season. The snack stand opens at 8:00 a.m., rents out 9 umbrellas, sells juice in packs of 6 bottles, and keeps 14 life jackets for children near the dock while 18 more are stored in a shed. The ticket booth has 3 clerks in the morning and 2 in the afternoon, and the grounds crew cleans 7 picnic tables before the first visitors arrive. There is also a canoe area with 5 canoes, each holding 3 people, and a paddleboard area with 8 boards, although those are managed separately from the sightseeing boat. On Mondays, the first guided nature talk lasts 45 minutes, the second lasts 30 minutes, and a maintenance worker checks 10 dock posts and replaces 4 ropes if needed. A family package includes 2 adult tickets and 3 child tickets, and some visitors buy souvenir postcards at $2 each or lake maps at $5 each.

The sightseeing boat that goes through the lake has its own fixed operating schedule. During one day, there are 4 boat trips through the lake. The boat can take up to 12 people during one trip. Last weekend, one trip left with only 9 passengers because of rain, and another private event reserved 6 seats on a different vessel, but those details do not change the regular daily capacity of this boat. On the second day of this two-day period, the captain still follows the same standard trip schedule, even though 15 students arrive for a field lesson, 11 photographers wait near the pier, and 20 visitors ask about sunset cruises that happen on other dates. How many people can the boat transport in 2 days?

At the county livestock showcase, two neighboring farms, Paddington Farm and Washington Farm, spent the entire morning getting their animals counted, tagged, brushed, and sorted into pens before the judges arrived at 9:30 a.m. Washington Farm brought goats in 7 trailers, although 2 of those trailers were only half full because they also carried feed sacks, water tubs, and 18 folding fence panels. Paddington Farm arrived earlier, at 7:45 a.m., and set up 12 hay nets, 6 mineral blocks, and 4 shade canopies near the goat pens. The registration desk charged $8 per exhibitor wristband, $3 per parking pass, and $12 per extra bale of straw, but those costs were paid separately and did not affect the animal totals. 

In the goat barn, Washington's workers wrote down all sorts of details: 35 goats had blue ear tags, 41 had red ear tags, 28 were scheduled for grooming before noon, and 36 had already been weighed on the digital scale that displays pounds to the nearest tenth. They also noted that 14 buckets were filled with water, 9 buckets were empty, and 5 more buckets were stacked by the wash station. Meanwhile, Paddington's crew checked hoof trims on 22 goats, brushed 31 goats before breakfast, and set aside 17 feed scoops for the afternoon feeding. One volunteer mistakenly counted 40 bags of grain and nearly wrote that number on the goat board before being corrected. 

The farms compared many numbers during the day: Washington sold 16 jars of goat milk soap at the farm stand, Paddington sold 24; Washington's trailer tires were checked at 32 psi, while Paddington's were at 34 psi; one pen held 11 goats temporarily during cleaning, another held 13, and a third was empty because it needed new bedding. The loudspeaker announced 5 youth events, 3 senior events, and 2 team demonstrations. A clerk also recorded that last year Washington brought 132 goats and Paddington brought 171, but this year's official count was different. 

For this year's actual goat totals, the important relationship remained the same all day: Paddington has 40 more goats than Washington. If Washington has 140 goats, how many goats do they have in total?

John went to a large weekend gaming convention and stopped at a vendor booth that sold many kinds of trading card products. The booth had booster boxes with 24 packs each, starter decks with 60 cards, sleeves sold in bundles of 50, binders that held 360 cards, and a sale sign saying that customers who spent over $75 got 2 promo tokens. John had already spent $18 on snacks, $12 on bus fare, and $7 on entry wristbands, and he was comparing whether to buy 8 packs from one series at $3 each or 12 packs from another series at $2 each. He also noticed a display where every 5th customer could roll a die for a prize, and someone nearby was sorting cards into piles of common, uncommon, rare, and foil. After looking through several sets with dragons, wizards, and artifact themes, John finally chose exactly 10 packs of magic cards from the set he wanted. On the wrapper of that product line, each pack clearly contains 20 cards. The set guide at the booth mentioned that, within these packs, 1/4 of the cards are uncommon. John ignored the collector box, the singles case with cards priced at $4, $9, and $15, and the poster listing 16 tournament rounds across 2 days. If he opens all 10 packs he bought, how many uncommon cards did he get?

Happy Street is a short residential road with a speed bump near the corner, 14 mailboxes on one side, 16 on the other, 3 oak trees, and a faded crosswalk that was repainted last spring. A neighborhood volunteer has been keeping a traffic notebook for the entire week because the street is usually quiet compared with nearby Maple Avenue, where over 80 cars can pass in a busy hour. In the notebook, he also wrote down all kinds of related details: the garbage truck came at 7:10 a.m. on Monday and stayed for 12 minutes, the postal van stopped at 9 houses on Tuesday, a plumber parked for 35 minutes on Wednesday, two delivery vans arrived on Thursday, and a moving truck was seen on Friday just after 4:00 p.m. He even noted that 6 bicycles, 4 scooters, and 11 pedestrians used the street on Saturday, and that 3 dogs were walked there on Sunday morning. None of those are the car totals he wants to add, but they are all in the same weekly log.

For actual car traffic, the week looked like this. During the week, the busiest day for cars on Happy Street was Tuesday, when 25 cars passed through. On Monday, the number of cars was 20% less than Tuesday's amount. On Wednesday, 2 more cars went by than on Monday. On Thursday and Friday, it was about 10 cars each day. Over the weekend, traffic dropped to 5 cars per day, even though the corner store at the end of the block was open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Saturday and only until noon on Sunday. The residents' association also mentioned in its newsletter that 42 flyers were delivered during the week, 18 porch lights were replaced this month, and 7 homes are expecting packages next week.

How many cars travel down Happy Street from Monday through Sunday?

Henry was organizing his medication schedule for two weeks while also updating a household budget spreadsheet. On the kitchen counter he laid out 3 weekly pill organizers, even though he only needed 2 of them for this stretch, and each organizer had 7 rows labeled for days and 4 little slots marked morning, noon, evening, and bedtime. He also wrote reminder notes on 14 index cards, set 2 alarms on his phone, kept 1 backup bottle in the cabinet, and used a glass of water at every dose. His pharmacy receipt listed several items from the same visit: vitamins for $12.00, cough drops for $3.75, a reusable pill cutter for $8.50, and a store discount coupon worth $4.00 that applied only to the vitamins. None of that changed the pill plan he actually followed.

For his actual prescription routine, Henry took 9 pills a day for 14 days. Every day, the 9 pills were made up the same way: 4 of the pills were one kind that cost $1.50 each. The other pills were a different kind, and each of those cost $5.50 more than the $1.50 pills. He originally asked the pharmacist whether buying in bottles of 30 instead of 60 would affect the unit price, and the pharmacist mentioned that some customers take 2 pills in the morning and 7 later in the day, but Henry's total for each day still remained exactly the same 9 pills. On one note he even wrote that over a full month of 28 days he would need twice as many pills, but he only followed the plan for 14 days.

Henry also compared this prescription to an older one from last year where he took 6 pills daily for 10 days, with 2 pills costing $2.00 each, but that old information is unrelated to this purchase. During these 14 days, he never missed a day, never changed the dosage, and never substituted a cheaper brand. How much did he spend in total on the pills?

Alyssa, Keely, and Kendall stopped at a fast-food restaurant after a long Saturday of errands, practice, and shopping. Before ordering, they spent several minutes comparing combo meals, coupon deals, and dipping sauce options on the overhead menu. The restaurant had 4 kinds of sauces available that day—barbecue, honey mustard, ranch, and sweet-and-sour—and the cashier mentioned that nugget meals usually came in boxes of 4, 6, 10, 20, or 40. Alyssa originally thought about getting fries and a drink too, Keely was deciding between a sandwich combo and nuggets, and Kendall pointed out that there was a family special advertised for 2 large fries, 3 drinks, and 40 nuggets. They also noticed a sign saying sauces were free up to 6 cups, with extra cups costing 25 cents each.

In the end, the three of them placed one shared nugget order totaling 100 chicken nuggets from the restaurant. They also bought 3 medium drinks, 2 large fries, and 1 apple pie to split later, and the receipt showed a subtotal of $18.75 before tax for the non-nugget items, while a separate promotion took $2 off one part of the order. Alyssa kept track of napkins and counted 17 left in the bag after they sat down. Keely arranged the sauces into 4 little piles, and Kendall joked that if they had ordered 20 more nuggets, they could have packed leftovers for Sunday. None of that changed how many nuggets each person actually ate.

When they started eating, Keely ate twice as many chicken nuggets as Alyssa, and Kendall also ate twice as many chicken nuggets as Alyssa. Altogether, the three girls ate all 100 chicken nuggets they had ordered. How many did Alyssa eat?

Marvin and Tina were selling candy bars to help fund their class trip, which was planned for the last Friday in May. Their teacher had 28 students in the class, 3 parent chaperones had already volunteered, and the trip budget sheet listed costs like $180 for the bus deposit, $12 per student for admission, and $96 for lunches if the class ordered ahead. Earlier in the week, the class had also sold 48 raffle tickets at $5 each and collected 17 permission slips on Monday and 9 more on Tuesday. For the candy-bar fundraiser, there were several flavors in the boxes, including 24 caramel bars, 18 almond bars, and 30 plain chocolate bars per shipment, although students did not all receive the same flavor mix. The candy bars cost $2 each. Marvin kept track of his sales on a clipboard and sold at lunch, after school, and during Saturday soccer games, where he once sold 8 bars in one hour and another day sold 11 before noon, but by the end of the fundraiser Marvin sold 35 candy bars total. Tina sold at the school play, at band practice, and to neighbors on her street. She also made a poster using 6 markers, stood at a table for 4 shifts, and once brought 15 extra dollars in change so customers could pay with larger bills. Her homeroom collected 62 empty wrappers for a recycling contest, and she wrote down 14 names of people who said they might buy later. In the end, Tina sold three times the number of candy bars as Marvin. How much more money did Tina make for the class trip selling candy bars compared to Marvin?

On Saturday afternoon, Paul stopped by a neighborhood grocery shop after checking the weekly flyer and comparing a few prices he had written down from earlier in the week. The shop had a promotion on eggs at $4 a carton, apples at $1 each or 6 for $5, and cereal boxes marked down from $6 to $5. Near the entrance, a sign mentioned that customers who spent over $20 could get a reusable bag for $1, and another sign advertised coffee for $8 per bag or 2 bags for $15. Paul also noticed that milk was $4, cheese was $5, and yogurt was 3 cups for $6. He briefly considered buying bananas that cost $2 per bunch, but he decided not to. In his basket, he put some bread for $2, butter for $3, and juice for two times the price of the bread. He remembered that last week the same juice had been on a buy-one-get-one-half-off offer, but there was no such deal today. Paul had $15 for his shopping, even though he had another $10 bill folded in a different pocket that he was saving for the bus pass he needed on Monday. Before coming to the shop, he had already spent $7 on lunch and had seen a display of notebooks priced at $2 each, 3 for $5. He stood in line behind a customer buying 2 loaves of bread, 1 bottle of oil for $7, and vegetables totaling $9. At the register, the cashier mentioned that the store would close in 45 minutes and that receipts from purchases over $12 could be used for a raffle drawing later in the month. After paying only for the groceries he chose, how much money did Paul have left?

Lilah's family keeps a large digital family gallery organized into albums like birthdays, camping, school plays, pets, sunsets, and vacations. Before their latest trip, the gallery already had 400 photos in it, even though Lilah's mom had recently talked about deleting 35 blurry pictures, restoring 18 old scans, and sorting 62 canyon-themed images into a separate folder. The gallery app also showed 14 albums, 9 shared folders, and 27 favorites, and it had storage space for 2,000 more photos. 

Then the family went on a two-day trip to the Grand Canyon. On the drive there, Lilah counted 6 gas station stops, 3 souvenir shops, 11 postcard racks, and 48 road signs mentioning scenic overlooks. Her dad charged 2 camera batteries, packed 4 memory cards that could each hold 500 photos, and brought 1 tripod, while Lilah carried a phone that already had 275 unrelated pictures on it from earlier in the month. On the first day of the trip, they visited the South Rim for 7 hours, walked 5 miles, bought 8 postcards, and spent $36 on snacks and drinks. During sunset they took half as many photos as they have in the family's gallery. 

On the second day, they woke up at 6:30 a.m., rode a shuttle that made 9 stops, looked through 3 pairs of binoculars at 17 different viewpoints, and spent $24 on breakfast and $42 on souvenirs. Lilah's brother took 15 short video clips, their mom made a list of 12 rock formations to remember, and their dad said the second day felt 2 times busier than the first because of the crowds. Even so, the number of photos they took on the second day was 120 more photos than they took on the first day. 

After the trip, they uploaded every photo from both days into the family gallery, without removing any of the older gallery photos and without counting videos, postcards, or screenshots as photos. If they added all these photos to the family gallery, calculate the total number of photos in the gallery.

Baez keeps her marble collection in a blue tin box with 4 compartments, even though only 3 of them still latch properly. At the start of the week she had sorted her marbles by color: 8 red swirled ones, 6 green glass ones, 5 metallic-looking ones, and 6 plain blue ones, for a total of 25 marbles. She had been planning to trade some of them at recess on Thursday, when 12 students in her class were also bringing collections, and she even wrote down pretend prices of 3 cents, 5 cents, and 10 cents for different styles just for fun, though she was not actually selling them. On Monday she spent 15 minutes counting them, then another 10 minutes rearranging them, and on Tuesday she carried the box in a backpack with 2 notebooks, 3 pencils, and a lunch bag. During the day, she loses 20% of her marbles. She does not lose any more after that, even though later she worries she may have dropped some near the playground where 7 other kids were playing and where she had earlier seen 9 pebbles, 2 bottle caps, and 1 coin on the ground. After she lost that portion, she checked what remained and kept those marbles in her pocket. Then a friend sees her and gives her double the amount that Baez has after she lost them. The friend had originally brought 30 marbles to school, traded away 8, kept 6 favorite ones separate, and still had several left, but only the amount actually given to Baez matters here. By the end of the day, after walking home for 25 minutes and putting the marbles back into the same box, how many marbles does Baez end up with?

Ed keeps careful records for everything in his house because he volunteers at the neighborhood pet fair twice a year and likes to stay organized. On the refrigerator, he has a feeding chart with 7 columns for the days of the week, 3 different brands of cat food he has tried this year, 4 leash hooks by the door, and 12 labeled food containers in the pantry. He also wrote down that one dog eats 2 cups of food a day while the other eats 3 cups, each cat gets half a can in the morning and half a can at night, and each fish tank has a thermometer that usually reads between 74 and 76 degrees. Last month he spent $18 on dog treats, $24 on cat litter, and $35 on aquarium supplies, though some of that included extra gravel for a future tank he never set up. 

In the living room there are 2 large pet beds, 5 cat toys under the sofa, 8 spare filters in a drawer, and 6 framed photos from old trips to the pet store. His dogs are 4 and 7 years old, the cats are all under 5 years old, and the fish were bought over several visits, including one time when he only purchased food and no animals at all. He has 3 windows near the tanks, 2 shelves above them, and 9 small decorative stones around the stand that are not part of any habitat. He even keeps a calendar showing vet visits every 6 months, litter deliveries every 4 weeks, and water-change reminders every Sunday.

As for the pets themselves, Ed has 2 dogs, 3 cats, and twice as many fish as cats and dogs combined. How many pets does Ed have in total?

At the county fair candy booth, a large glass jar of jelly beans is being used for a guessing game. The booth owner spent the morning sorting labels for 12 candy categories, polishing 4 shelves, and setting out 9 scoops, even though only 1 jar is part of the game. A handwritten sign nearby lists all kinds of extra information: last year the booth sold 3,200 lemon drops, 1,875 gummy bears, and 960 lollipops over 8 days; this year they ordered 40 pounds of sugar, 18 pounds of corn syrup, and 6 decorative ribbons for the display. Another note says the jelly bean supplier ships flavors in cartons of 500, with 24 cartons arriving on Tuesday and 16 more expected on Friday, but the game jar was already filled before any of those unopened cartons were counted. The owner also mentions that on a different table there are striped jelly beans in 5 colors, sour jelly beans in 7 flavors, and a clearance bin with 250 mixed candies sold for 4 dollars per bag.

For the jar used in the game, some of the jelly beans are red, while the rest are other colors such as green, yellow, white, and black. Exactly three fourths of the jelly beans in the jar are red. Among the red jelly beans, one quarter are coconut flavored. A separate inventory sheet on the counter mentions that 300 red jelly beans were set aside yesterday for decorating cupcakes, 150 green jelly beans were used in a craft activity last month, and 75 coconut candies of a completely different type were packed into party favors, but none of those are part of the jar in the guessing game. The same sheet also lists sample tasting cups containing 20 cinnamon beans, 20 licorice beans, and 20 buttered-popcorn beans, plus a price sign reading 3 small bags for 5 dollars or 1 large bag for 4 dollars.

During the fair, 750 jelly beans in the jar are coconut flavored. How many jelly beans are there in the jar?

Valerie is sitting at her kitchen table on a Thursday evening trying to finish a whole stack of outgoing mail before the 5:30 p.m. pickup. She spread everything out into labeled piles because last month she mixed a utility envelope with a rebate form and had to redo it. On the table are a roll of address labels with 40 labels left, a sheet of return-address stickers with 18 stickers left, a pen, a book of 20 forever stamps that she bought for $13.60, and 7 loose postcard stamps that she is not using because all of these mailings need regular letter postage unless stated otherwise. She also has 12 blank envelopes, though several are different sizes, and she checked the ZIP codes twice because one rebate center is in a different state than the others. 

For personal mail, Valerie has thank-you cards ready to send for the birthday presents she received from her grandmother, her uncle, and her aunt. Her grandmother sent $25 and a scarf, her uncle sent a board game, and her aunt sent two mystery novels, but Valerie is writing just one thank-you card to each of those three relatives. She thought about also mailing a birthday party photo to each person, but those photos are still on her desk and are not part of tonight's mailing. 

She also has bills to send out. She needs to pay the water bill and the electric bill separately because they go to different processing centers printed on the statements. The water bill is for $38.14, due on the 12th, and the electric bill is for $61.08, due on the 15th. The return envelopes look almost identical except that the electric company envelope has a special notice printed on it and, unlike everything else she is mailing tonight, that electric bill envelope needs 2 stamps. The water bill needs the usual 1 stamp. She briefly considered paying one bill online, but she has not done that, so both bills are being mailed. 

In another pile are rebate forms from recent purchases. Last weekend she bought 4 boxes of cereal during a promotion, 2 packs of batteries, and a printer cartridge, but only some of those purchases came with mail-in rebates and she has already sorted out exactly how many rebate envelopes she needs. Valerie wants to send three more mail-in rebates than she does bills. She also has job applications to mail. At first she planned to hand-deliver some resumes, but instead she counted out complete application packets, each with a cover letter, resume, and references page clipped together. She has twice as many job applications as rebates to mail. Some applications are to bookstores, one is to a library, and another is to an office supply store, but that does not affect postage because each application packet goes in its own standard envelope and needs the usual 1 stamp. 

On her calendar, she wrote reminders for garbage day, her cousin's recital, and a dentist appointment at 9:00 a.m. next Tuesday. She also has 6 incoming letters to open, 3 magazines on the counter, and 2 coupons she might mail later for a store sweepstakes, but none of those are part of what she is about to send now. She double-checks that every piece of outgoing mail tonight needs 1 stamp except the electric bill, which needs 2. How many stamps does she need if everything needs 1 stamp except the electric bill, which needs 2?

At a large aquarium preparing for its 10:00 a.m. public feeding show, the staff are reorganizing several habitats. The building has 12 exhibit zones, 4 backup filtration rooms, and a gift shop that sold 86 plush sea turtles last weekend. One hallway display features seahorses, another has 18 moon jelly tanks, and the tropical wing keeps water at 78 degrees while the cold-water wing stays near 52 degrees. In the middle of all this, one keeper is working only with the clownfish and blowfish population.

The aquarium holds an equal number of clownfish and blowfish altogether. Earlier in the morning, the blowfish were checked one by one because 7 had special feeding tags, 9 were due for water-quality observation, and 3 of the labels on the holding bins had to be replaced. After the check, 26 of the blowfish stay in their own tank, while the remaining blowfish swim into a nearby display tank that already has decorative coral arches, 14 shells, and 2 thermometer probes mounted on the back wall.

To make the display look balanced for visitors, an equal number of clownfish join the blowfish in the display tank. The clownfish came from a separate tank that had 5 artificial anemones, 8 hiding caves, and a posted cleaning schedule for Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. However, once the pumps are adjusted and the fish settle, a third of these clownfish swim back into their own tank. None of the seahorses, tangs, lionfish, or jellyfish are involved, even though nearby signs list 24 reef fish in one habitat, 32 freshwater fish in a classroom exhibit, and 6 rescued turtles in rehabilitation.

If the aquarium holds a combined total of 100 fish, how many clownfish are now in the display tank?

Jeanette is practicing her juggling for the school variety show, and she keeps a very detailed notebook about it. On the first page she lists all kinds of things that do not directly affect her juggling progress: she owns 7 beanbags, 4 tennis balls, 3 rings, and 2 scarves, although she does not use all of them every week; her practice timer is set for 18 minutes on Mondays, 22 minutes on Wednesdays, and 25 minutes on Saturdays; the talent show is 9 weeks away; she practices in the gym where the ceiling is 24 feet high; and last month she dropped a ball 11 times in one session but only 6 times in another. She also notes that her friend Mara can already juggle 8 objects, her coach charges $15 per lesson, and a new set of colorful juggling balls costs $12 for a pack of 3 or $20 for a pack of 6. Jeanette even records that during one week she spent 35 minutes stretching, 40 minutes warming up, and 45 minutes cooling down across all her sessions, and that she drank 5 bottles of water one week and 7 the next.

Despite all those extra notes, Jeanette's actual improvement pattern is simple: each week she can juggle 2 more objects than the week before. She starts out juggling 3 objects. If she practices for 5 weeks, how many objects can she juggle?

Jessa is organizing a school celebration day and has been making lists all afternoon. First she checked the kitchen inventory: there are 4 unopened bags of flour, each labeled 5 pounds, 3 partial bags with about 2 pounds each, 6 dozen paper liners, 2 extra muffin pans that hold 12 cupcakes each, and 1 large cooling rack that fits 24 at a time. She also wrote down that the bakery supply store sells frosting tubs for $7 each or 3 for $18, sprinkles in 8-ounce jars, and candles in packs of 10, even though she may not need any of those. The school office reminded her that dismissal is at 3:15, lunch starts at 11:40, and the buses line up in 2 rows of 6. In the hallway, there are 5 bulletin boards for student art, and the fourth-grade wing has 3 classrooms side by side, each with 30 students. On the other side of the gym, the P.E. teacher said the P.E. class meeting for the celebration has 50 students. Jessa briefly considered making cookies too, since a recipe card on the counter says 24 cookies need 2 cups of sugar and 1 cup of butter, while her cupcake recipe makes 18 cupcakes per batch and uses 2 eggs, 1 cup of milk, and 2 cups of flour. She has 36 eggs in the fridge, 2 gallons of milk, 9 lemons for decoration, and 14 napkin packs with 20 napkins in each. Last year she made treats for 2 third-grade classes of 28 students, and the year before that she helped with 4 fifth-grade classes of 27 students, so she wants to be careful with her count this time. If every student in the fourth-grade classes and the P.E. class is supposed to get exactly one cupcake, how many cupcakes does she need to make?

Carrie recently started a part-time job at a neighborhood outdoor and bike shop that is open 6 days a week, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Saturdays. During her training, she learned the store carries 42 helmets, 18 locks, 27 water bottles, and 15 different bike seat covers. The shop manager also mentioned that last month the store sold 12 mountain bikes, 9 road bikes, and 14 kids' bikes, and that employees get a 10% discount on accessories but not on full bikes. Carrie usually brings a lunch that costs her family about $3.50 to make, and on two Fridays she bought smoothies for $4 each, but she decided not to spend any of her pay because she wants to save for something specific.

Her schedule is steady: she works 35 hours each week, even though some coworkers work 20, 24, or 30 hours. She earns $8 an hour. She has now been working there for a month. In the store, she has been comparing several bikes: one costs $385 before tax, another costs $440 with a basket included, and the model she really wants is priced at $400. She wrote down a few other numbers too, like a $25 bell, a $16 bottle cage, and a $32 light set, just in case she decides to accessorize later. She has saved all of the money she earned since starting the job. How much money will she have left over after she buys her bike?

At a restoration site for an old fortress, Stella and Twinkle are helping load a flatbed truck with stone blocks that will be taken to a repair yard. The truck itself is marked with a maximum payload corresponding to 6000 stone blocks for this particular type of block. Earlier that morning, the site manager checked 12 pallets, counted 500 blocks on each full pallet, noted that 2 pallets were only half used from the previous day, and updated a clipboard that also listed delivery times of 7:00 a.m., 9:30 a.m., and 1:15 p.m. The workers wore orange vests, 8 pairs of gloves were handed out, 3 wheelbarrows had to be moved out of the way, and a forklift with a lifting limit of 1800 kilograms sat unused because the access ramp was blocked. None of that changed the hand-loading plan.

Stella and Twinkle begin filling the truck by hand. Each person loads stone blocks at a rate of 250 blocks per hour. They keep that pace steadily for four hours, stopping only for brief water breaks that are already included in the work schedule. During those first four hours, one supervisor records 2 safety checks per hour, a supply tent sells bottled water for $2 each, and a nearby crew sorts 900 smaller bricks into stacks of 30, but Stella and Twinkle continue loading the truck at the same rate.

After the four-hour mark, 6 other people arrive from another section of the site. Those 6 additional workers also load blocks at the same rate of 250 blocks per hour per person. The expanded team keeps working until the truck reaches its capacity of 6000 stone blocks. For reference, the lunch bell rings at noon, the return trip for the truck usually takes 45 minutes, the fuel log shows 18 gallons used that week, and another truck on site can carry only 4200 blocks, but this truck is the one being filled.

How many hours did filling the truck take?

For a quarterly board meeting, a company reserved its large conference room and had the facilities team set up 40 identical chairs in neat rows. The room itself could hold 120 people standing, had 10 windows, 4 doors, 8 ceiling lights, 2 projectors, and 6 wall outlets, and the staff spent 3 hours arranging name cards, water bottles, notepads, and microphones before the meeting began at 9:00 a.m. Each of the 40 chairs placed in the room was a wide chair designed with a seating capacity of 2 people per chair, even though some of the smaller side chairs stored along the wall could seat only 1 person each and were not part of the arranged set. The company had exactly as many board members as the seating capacity of those arranged chairs. In addition, 12 trays of pastries were delivered, each tray originally holding 15 pieces, 18 bottles of sparkling water were chilled, 24 printed agendas were left over from the previous quarter, and 3 late vendors came by the wrong entrance before the receptionist redirected them.

The chairs were arranged across 5 rows, although two rows had 8 chairs each, one row was temporarily shifted 2 feet closer to the screen, and a center aisle 3 feet wide was left open for walking. Of the 40 arranged chairs, 2/5 were not occupied during the meeting. Every one of the remaining chairs that was occupied had exactly two people sitting in it. Some attendees arrived 20 minutes early, the finance packet had 64 pages, the legal appendix had 18 pages, and the presentation deck contained 27 slides, but none of that changed the seating situation.

Calculate the number of board members who did attend the meeting.

At a weekend comparison-shopping event, a family is trying to decide where to buy sparkling water for an upcoming neighborhood picnic. They already know they need the same brand and flavor no matter where they shop, because the party planner rejected the lemon variety, the berry variety, and the 24-can sampler pack. One store is a bulk warehouse that charges a $5 parking fee unless you spend over $100, opens at 8:30 a.m., and sells giant pallets stacked 6 cases high. At that warehouse, a case of the sparkling water they want contains 48 cans and costs $12.00 per case. The family also notices nearby signs for paper plates at $7.50 for 50, napkins at $3.25 for 100, and juice boxes at 10 for $8.00, but they are only comparing the sparkling water right now.

On the same day, the local grocery store down the street is running several beverage specials: 2-liter soda for $2.50 each, energy drinks for $3.00 apiece, and flavored seltzer in a mix-and-match display. The grocery store has the exact same sparkling water the family wants, but it only has 12 cans available, and the price for that offer is $6.00. The store closes at 9:00 p.m., has 14 checkout lanes though only 5 are open, and limits shoppers to 4 sale items in some aisles, but there is no special coupon involved for this sparkling water.

The family writes down a lot of numbers from both stores, including distances of 11 miles to the warehouse and 2 miles to the grocery store, a warehouse membership cost of $60 per year, and a picnic guest list of 36 people expecting about 2 cans each. Ignore everything except the price comparison being asked. How much more expensive, per can, in cents, is this deal at the grocery store?

Joy is spending the afternoon making yarn balls for her cat, who has a habit of batting anything round under the couch and then losing interest after about 12 minutes. She bought yarn from a craft store that sells it in 9-foot sample bundles, 27-foot mini skeins, and 54-foot jumbo skeins, and she sorted the colors into 6 piles on the floor: blue, red, yellow, gray, green, and striped. Before she started winding the play balls, she measured out extra lengths for other projects: 14 feet for a scarf fringe, 8 feet for wrapping a package, and 5 feet that got tangled around a chair leg and had to be cut off. Her cat already had 4 old yarn balls in a basket, though 2 were partly unraveled, and there were also 3 plastic toy mice, 1 bell ball, and a scratching post in the room. 

Joy decided to make 3 new yarn balls for the cat. She wanted the sizes to follow a particular pattern even though she experimented with winding speed, tension, and color order. The first ball used alternating blue and gray stripes and took her 9 minutes to wind. The second ball was wound more tightly, used two shades of red, and she almost made it match one of the old store-bought balls that had a circumference of 11 inches. The third ball was made from yellow yarn, then wrapped with a thin green layer, and she briefly considered adding another 6 feet to make it look more even, but she did not. 

For the actual sizes of the 3 new balls, the first ball is half the size of the second ball. The third ball is three times as large as the first ball. She used 27 feet of yarn for the third ball. How many feet of yarn did she use for the second ball?

Haley’s family keeps a very detailed growth chart on the kitchen wall next to a calendar, a ruler marked in both inches and centimeters, and a list of old measurements from different years. On the same wall, there are notes saying that Haley’s baby cousin was 18 inches long at birth, her older brother grew 2 inches last year, and their dog’s leash is 36 inches long. There is also a school health record showing Haley weighed 45 pounds at one visit, 48 pounds at another, and that she outgrew a pair of 22-inch rain boots storage bins labeled by season. Her parents also wrote down that one shelf in her room is 30 inches high, her desk is 24 inches tall, and a sunflower she planted grew 5 inches in one month during summer. Last year, they compared her height with a stack of 4 books that was 12 inches tall and with a toy box that measured 21 inches across. On a nearby page, someone converted 20 inches to centimeters, and another note says there are 12 months in a year and 10 school months in the academic calendar. They even recorded that over 6 years, the family added 3 photo frames per year to the hallway wall, and that Haley has 10 favorite storybooks on the bottom shelf, 7 on the middle shelf, and 8 on the top shelf.

Ignoring all those other household measurements and records, suppose Haley herself grows at the rate of 3 inches every year. If she is currently 20 inches tall, what will be her height after 10 years?

At a large off-campus housing complex near the university, the student services office is updating records for several apartment buildings before the fall semester. Building A has 48 units, Building B has 52, and together they can house up to 300 students if every bedroom is filled. Some apartments are doubles, some are singles, and a few have converted study rooms that can temporarily be used as extra bedrooms. Last year, one floor averaged 6 residents per suite, another averaged 4, and the resident assistant mentioned that 17 students moved in early during orientation week while 9 moved out before classes even began. Bob lives in Maple Hall, where rent is $640 per month plus a $35 utility fee, and his apartment has already split the cost of a $120 microwave, a $48 router, and two $15 lamps. John lives across the courtyard in Cedar Hall, where the laundry room has 14 machines, quiet hours begin at 10:30 p.m., and the front desk logged 27 maintenance requests in September, including 8 for leaky sinks and 5 for broken blinds. During roommate matching, the housing coordinator noted that some students requested morning roommates, 23 requested quiet roommates, and 11 specifically asked for a pet-free apartment. Bob has 10 roommates. John has five more roommates than twice as many as Bob. If Bob has 10 roommates, how many roommates does John have?

On a chilly autumn night, three neighborhood cats sat on a long wooden fence behind a row of backyards, all facing the bright full moon over the alley. The fence had 12 posts, 11 gaps between the posts, and a missing slat near the vegetable garden. A porch light across the street flickered every 10 seconds, a sprinkler had run for 18 minutes earlier in the evening, and somewhere nearby a wind chime rang 4 times whenever the breeze picked up. Mrs. Ortega, who lived in the blue house with 7 flowerpots on the back steps, said the cats had been visiting for 9 nights in a row. One of the cats was orange with 5 stripes on its tail, another wore a red collar with a bell, and the third had one white paw and had knocked over 2 empty watering cans before jumping onto the fence. A dish by the porch still held 14 pieces of dry food, though 6 had already been eaten, and a neighbor had left out 3 saucers of water, each filled halfway. At 8:15 p.m., the cats finally settled down and began meowing at the moon.

The first cat meowed 3 times per minute. The second cat meowed twice as frequently as the first cat. The third cat meowed at one-third the frequency of the second cat. During the same 5-minute stretch, a dog barked 8 times from two houses away, a train horn sounded once, and 4 upstairs windows turned off one by one. One child on a balcony tried to count all the nighttime sounds, starting over after reaching 20, while another guessed there would be 30 cat meows before the church clock struck the quarter hour. The moon was almost full for the 13th night of the lunar cycle, the temperature had dropped 6 degrees since sunset, and the street had 17 parked cars, including 2 red ones, 1 silver van, and a bicycle leaning against a mailbox.

What is the combined total number of meows the three cats make in 5 minutes?

A school principal is organizing an overnight field trip and is trying to finalize the hotel booking paperwork before the district office closes at 4:30 p.m. The class has 30 students going on the trip. Earlier in the week, 32 permission slips were handed out, 31 were returned, and 1 student who originally planned to go had to stay home because of a family event, so only the students in the class who are actually attending need hotel space. The principal has already arranged for 2 teachers and 1 parent chaperone to stay in separate adult rooms paid for under a different line of the travel budget, so those adults are not part of the student room count. The bus leaves at 7:15 a.m., the museum tour starts at 10:00 a.m., dinner is scheduled for 6:00 p.m., lights-out is supposed to be at 10:30 p.m., and breakfast vouchers are provided for 33 travelers total, but the principal is currently focused only on how many student hotel rooms to reserve.

The hotel the school usually uses offers standard rooms with two queen-size beds and one pull-out couch. According to the hotel manager, each queen-size bed can fit two students, and the pull-out couch can fit one student. That means the principal wants to know how many such rooms are needed so that all of the students in the class can sleep in the rooms. The principal briefly compares this to another nearby hotel that has rooms with one king bed and two cots for a different price, and also notes that the current hotel charges $129 per room before tax, plus a $40 refundable key-card deposit per floor, with towels stocked in sets of 5 and 3 extra blankets available at the front desk, but none of those details affect the sleeping capacity.

For rooming preferences, 12 students requested to be with their lab partners, 8 asked for rooms near the ice machine, 5 are allergic to feather pillows, 6 need early medication reminders, and 9 packed board games. The principal also has a packing checklist showing 30 lunches for the trip out, 30 museum tickets, 30 matching T-shirts, and 15 pairs of binoculars to share. On a previous trip, 28 students stayed in 6 smaller rooms at a different hotel where each room fit fewer students, and last month another grade level booked 7 rooms for 34 students at a lodge with bunk beds. None of those arrangements match this hotel's setup.

If each room in this hotel has two queen-size beds that can fit two students each, plus a pull-out couch that can fit one student, how many rooms does the principal need to book to fit all of the students in the class?

Dan owns an ice cream shop on a busy boardwalk, and on a hot Saturday he keeps careful notes about everything: he opens at 11:00 a.m., closes at 9:00 p.m., has 4 employees on the early shift and 3 on the late shift, and stocks 180 waffle cones, 140 cake cones, 12 tubs of vanilla, 10 tubs of chocolate, and 8 tubs of strawberry. A chalkboard near the register advertises milkshakes for $5, sundaes for $6, bottled water for $1, and a family special of 3 toppings for $1 extra, although some customers skip toppings entirely. He also tracks that 17 customers asked for napkins, 9 asked for extra sprinkles, 6 changed their minds about flavors, and 14 paid with $10 bills. The shop had a morning delivery fee of $18, he tipped the delivery driver $4, and later he counted $63 in small bills and $21 in quarters in one drawer before restocking it with change. Dan even remembers that 5 customers bought milkshakes, 8 bought sundaes, 11 bought bottled water, and 2 children dropped their cones and had them remade.

Despite all that, Dan's cone promotion stayed the same as always: every sixth customer gets a free ice cream cone. Regular ice cream cones cost $2 each. By the end of the day, he had sold $100 worth of cones. If he sold $100 worth of cones, how many free ones did he give away?

Ali had a collection of seashells that he had been sorting all summer after visiting three different beaches with his family. He kept the shells in 6 labeled jars on a wooden shelf, although some jars were only for display and some still had old labels from last year. On Monday he spent 45 minutes washing shells in a blue bucket, and on Tuesday he spent another 35 minutes arranging them by color: white, tan, pink, striped, spiral, and broken pieces he planned to glue later. He had once collected 24 tiny shells in a single afternoon, 16 large conch pieces on another trip, and 12 smooth gray shells that he decided not to trade, but after combining everything into one main collection, Ali started with 180 seashells. At a neighborhood craft day, 14 children came by the table, though only 9 actually asked about shells, and Ali set out 50 shell-shaped stickers, 8 trays, and 3 price cards that said 2 dollars, 5 dollars, and 10 dollars for different souvenir bags he was not using that day. He then gave away 40 seashells to his friends. Later that evening, his 3 brothers visited while carrying 2 toy buckets and 1 net from the beach, and although they argued over 18 shiny shells and 6 striped ones, Ali simply gave 30 seashells to his brothers. After that, he counted the remaining shells while sitting beside 4 piles of sand dollars, 7 postcards, and 20 polished stones that were part of a different collection. The next morning he decided to sell half of the remaining seashells at a small stand near the boardwalk, where the table rental was 15 dollars, parking cost 10 dollars, and he sold lemonade for 1 dollar per cup to 22 people, but those sales were separate from the shell count. If he sold half of the remaining seashells, how many seashells did he have left?

Mitchell was spending the afternoon studying for a big test using a thick review book that had a table of contents, chapter summaries, practice questions, and sticky notes marking several sections. She began earlier in the day with a detailed schedule written on a notepad: review vocabulary for 15 minutes, organize pens into 3 cups, refill her water bottle twice, and finish as much reading as possible before dinner at 6:30. Her desk had 4 highlighters, 2 blue pens, 6 sharpened pencils, and 11 index cards already filled with formulas. The book itself had chapters of equal length, and Mitchell had even written in the margin that every chapter was 40 pages long. Before the clock reached 4 o'clock, she had already completed reading ten full chapters of the book. During that same stretch of studying, she also underlined 18 definitions, solved 12 practice problems from another worksheet, checked the time at 1:30, 2:15, and 3:40, and ate 8 crackers, but those tasks were separate from the reading total.

Right when the clock struck 4:00, she was partway through chapter 11 and had read 20 pages of that 11th chapter. On her study planner, chapter 11 was labeled as including 5 diagrams, 2 recap boxes, and 1 mini-quiz, though none of that changed how many pages she had actually read by then. After 4 o'clock, instead of finishing the remaining pages of chapter 11, she skipped ahead in her studying plan and read 2 more complete chapters of the same book. She did not go back to the unread part of chapter 11 afterward. Her phone alarm went off at 4:45, she drank another half bottle of water, and she briefly counted 40 flashcards for a different subject, but the question is only about the pages she read in this book.

If each chapter in the book had 40 pages, calculate the total number of pages that Mitchell had read altogether?

On Saturday morning, James went to a warehouse grocery store to stock up for several upcoming meals. He pushed a cart through the meat department after first passing displays of chicken marked $3.99 per pound, pork shoulder value packs labeled 6 pounds each, and ground turkey trays on a buy-2-get-1 promotion. He had also clipped a store coupon for $8 off a purchase over $80, checked the weekly ad that listed ribeye steaks at $12 per pound, and noticed that some family packs had bright orange stickers showing they had been marked down by 10% if purchased before 2:00 p.m. The store opens at 7:00 a.m., and James arrived at 9:15 a.m. after buying 2 loaves of bread for $3 each, 3 bottles of marinade at $4.25 each, and a bag of charcoal weighing 16 pounds.

For the cookout, James decided not to buy the chicken wings in 10-pound cases, the seafood platter for $24, or the bacon that came in 1-pound packs. Instead, he bought 5 packs of beef, and each of those packs weighed 4 pounds. The price of beef was $5.50 per pound. He also picked up paper plates in a pack of 40, napkins in packs of 100, and 2 bags of ice at $2.50 each, but those were rung up separately on another receipt because his friend was reimbursing him for party supplies. One sign in the aisle mentioned a limit of 8 meat packages per customer, and another sign advertised that shoppers who spent $150 would earn 300 reward points. James briefly compared the beef packs to larger trays weighing 5 pounds each and to premium cuts priced at $7.25 per pound, but he stayed with the original beef selection.

How much did he pay?

At Westfield Elementary, Class 5B has a homeroom board with 40 student name cards clipped to it for the day. The classroom itself has 42 chairs because 2 are spare, 20 desks arranged in 5 rows of 4, 8 windows, 3 wall fans, and a shelf with 18 math workbooks and 22 reading folders. On this particular morning, the school bus that serves the neighborhood has 48 seats, but only 37 students from various classes rode it. The attendance clerk starts work at 7:30 a.m., the first bell rings at 7:55, assembly ends at 8:10, and the canteen begins selling snacks at 8:15. In Class 5B, 6 students brought lunch boxes, 11 ordered milk, 9 usually buy noodles on Wednesdays, and 14 have library books due this week. The class teacher collected 35 homework notebooks, though 4 of those belonged to students from another section by mistake and were returned later. There are also 10 students on the red house team, 12 on blue, 9 on green, and 9 on yellow for sports day.
