For attendance, however, the class officially has 40 students in total. If 1/10 are absent, then only the remaining students are present at school that morning. Of the students who are present, 3/4 are in the classroom during roll call, while the rest of the present students are in the canteen buying food before the next activity. The canteen menu that day lists sandwiches for $3, fruit cups for $2, and juice boxes for $1, and the canteen has 24 stools, 6 tables, and 2 serving lines, but those details do not affect the class count. How many students are in the canteen?

On the first Saturday of summer break, a couple planned a full day at a large amusement park with their two children. They left home at 8:15 a.m., packed 4 water bottles, 2 rain ponchos, sunscreen SPF 50, and 6 granola bars, and argued for 20 minutes about whether to bring the stroller they had not used in 3 years. The older child, who is 10 years old, wanted to ride the roller coaster with a 48-inch height minimum, while the younger child, who is 6 years old, was more excited about the carousel that runs every 15 minutes. Before reaching the gate, they spent $18 on parking, passed a sign advertising season passes for $249 each, saw a family bundle meal deal for $42, and noticed lockers renting for $9 for small, $12 for medium, and $15 for large. A nearby booth also listed souvenir photos at 2 for $25, refillable drink cups for $17 each, and arcade cards starting at $20.

At the ticket window, the posted regular admission price was $109 per person. There was also a senior discount, a twilight entry price after 4:00 p.m., and a promotion for online buyers that had ended the previous Thursday, but none of those applied to them. The cashier explained that children below 12 years old get a $5 discount off the regular ticket price. Since both children were under 12, their tickets qualified for that reduction, while the two adults paid the regular price. The family briefly discussed whether the 10-year-old would count as an adult next year, and the 6-year-old asked if being almost 7 changed anything, but the cashier said the policy was strictly based on being below 12.

The couple considered buying fast passes priced at $35 extra per person, but decided not to. They also did not buy the map for $3, the unlimited ride wristband upgrade, or the snack voucher worth $14. One parent held a $500 bill ready while the other checked the children's heights: 44 inches and 52 inches. After the cashier totaled only the admission tickets, they handed over $500. How much change will they receive?

Kennedy and Benedict are comparing houses while getting estimates for flooring, paint, heating, and property taxes. Kennedy's place has a 2-car garage, 5 exterior doors, 18 windows, and a backyard patio that measures 240 square feet, while Benedict's place has a shed, a fenced garden, and a driveway that was resurfaced last year for $3,600. Kennedy just replaced 1,200 square feet of old carpet with hardwood in some rooms, painted 9 rooms over 3 weekends, and pays $425 per month for utilities on average in winter, though summer is closer to $310. Benedict has been looking at renovation quotes too: one contractor offered $12 per square foot for tile in the kitchen, another estimated $8,400 for roofing work, and his annual property tax bill is $2,950. Their real estate agent also mentioned that homes on the street recently sold for $215,000, $228,000, and $241,000, and that one nearby house has 2,400 square feet spread over 2 floors. Kennedy's lot is 0.31 acres, Benedict's is 0.24 acres, and both homes are within 6 miles of downtown. Kennedy's living room alone is 320 square feet, the upstairs hallway is 90 square feet, and the basement storage area is used for 14 plastic bins and 3 bicycles. Benedict has 4 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms, and a laundry room with space for 2 machines, and he once measured 150 square feet of deck boards for a repair project. None of those details settle the comparison they care about now: Kennedy's house is 600 square feet larger than 4 times Benedict's house. If Kennedy's house is 10000 square feet, how many square feet is Benedict's house?

Loraine makes wax sculptures of animals for a weekend nature-center craft fair. She keeps her wax in labeled drawers with 6 colors, 8 scent tags even though the wax is unscented, and 24 reusable paper wrappers from earlier projects. On Friday evening she spent 35 minutes organizing her worktable, lining up carving tools in 3 rows of 5, setting aside 7 metal stamps, and sorting old order forms for turtles, foxes, birds, and bears. She had originally bought 40 sticks of wax earlier in the month, used 9 sticks on practice flowers that were not animals, gave 3 sticks to her cousin for a candle project, and later found 11 leftover wrappers in a bin. For this particular batch of animal sculptures, however, she followed her usual rule: large animals take four sticks of wax each and small animals take two sticks each. She also wrote down several production notes: one school wanted 14 blue ribbons for display labels, another customer asked whether 5 owl sculptures could be gift-boxed, and the craft fair opens at 10 a.m. and closes at 4 p.m. on both Saturday and Sunday. Loraine made three times as many small animals as large animals. When she checked the wax used just for the small animals in this batch, she recorded that the small animals used 12 sticks of wax. She packed the finished pieces into 4 cartons, put 6 price tags in each carton, and taped a receipt showing booth fee $18 and parking $7. How many sticks of wax did Loraine use to make all the animals?

Three families rented a large beach house together for a 7-day vacation from Saturday check-in to the following Saturday checkout. Family A brought 2 boogie boards, 1 striped umbrella, and 3 coolers; Family B packed 4 folding chairs, 6 snorkel masks, and a deck of 52 cards; Family C arrived later with 5 bags of groceries, 2 sand buckets, and 8 paperback novels for the adults. Each family has 4 people, although one grandparent only stayed indoors during the hottest afternoons, two children preferred the pool to the ocean, and one adult spent an entire morning on a work call. The rental came with 12 regular bath towels already folded in the upstairs closet, 9 hand towels in the bathrooms, 6 kitchen towels near the sink, and even 3 emergency blankets in a hallway cabinet, but the beach rules for the house were very specific: every person used 1 oversized beach towel per day and then got a fresh one the next day instead of reusing the old one. The host also mentioned that the washer has a quick cycle of 38 minutes, a heavy cycle of 54 minutes, and a sanitize cycle of 71 minutes, and that detergent pods are sold in packs of 24 at the market down the road for $11 per pack or 3 packs for $30. During the week, the group did 2 restaurant dinners, cooked breakfast in the house all 7 mornings, bought 18 bottles of water, 4 bags of ice, and 21 pieces of fruit, and paid a $250 cleaning deposit plus a $90 linen fee that covered sheets and pillowcases but not beach towels. On day 3, it rained for 2 hours in the afternoon, and on day 5, they drove 14 miles to a boardwalk arcade where they spent $36 on games and won 127 tickets. At the end of the trip, all of the oversized beach towels used during the 7 days needed to be washed. The washing machine can hold 14 oversized beach towels per load. How many loads of laundry will it take to wash all the oversized beach towels?

At a neighborhood supermarket during a weekend breakfast promotion, the dairy aisle has several kinds of milk on sale signs and shelf tags. Whole milk usually sells for $3 per gallon, 2% milk usually sells for $3.25 per gallon, almond milk is marked at $4.50, and half-gallons of chocolate milk are 2 for $5. For this promotion, however, a gallon of whole milk is being sold for $2 per gallon, with a limit of 6 gallons per customer, although the store has 24 gallons left on the shelf and 12 more in the cooler. Nearby, cereal is displayed on an endcap with signs showing family size, regular size, and variety packs. One brand of cereal has a manufacturer coupon for 50 cents, another has a buy-4-get-1-bowl offer, and a box of cereal in the deal you want is sold at a discount of $1 per box. The regular shelf prices of the cereals range from $3 to $6, but not all of them are discounted equally. 

A shopper making a breakfast-stock-up list plans meals for 7 mornings, has already bought 2 bananas for $1, skipped the orange juice priced at $4, and noticed eggs are 18 for $5. She decides to buy 3 gallons of whole milk and 5 boxes of cereal. She does not use loyalty points, paper coupons, or tax calculations, and she ignores the prices of bread, fruit, and yogurt even though they are listed nearby. How much will you save via discounts if you buy 3 gallons of whole milk and 5 boxes of cereal?

Janice works in a downtown building with a lobby, a basement mailroom, a parking level, and six office floors above ground. Her own office suite is on the third floor, where the accounting team keeps 12 binders of invoices, 4 backup keyboards, and a coffee station that gets restocked every Tuesday and Thursday. The building opens at 7:00 a.m., the security desk changes guards every 8 hours, and the elevator can carry up to 10 people at a time, although it is often crowded between 8:30 and 9:15. The stairwell has signs at every landing, there are 18 steps in each flight, and the maintenance crew mops the stairs twice a day. Janice usually brings a lunch in a blue bag, sometimes stops in the lobby to pick up one of the 6 packages delivered that morning, and occasionally chats with coworkers from the second and fourth floors.

Because her office is on the third floor, getting there by stairs requires walking up 3 flights of stairs. On one particularly busy workday, she has several reasons to move around the building: she arrives in the morning, later goes out for a coffee run, returns for a budget meeting at 10:00, heads down again to meet a client in the lobby at 1:30, comes back up afterward, and near the end of the day goes down once more before leaving. She also makes other trips during the day, but for those she rides the elevator instead of using the stairs. Altogether, in that single day, she goes up the three flights of stairs 5 times, down the three flights of stairs 3 times, and uses the elevator the remainder of the time. Her smartwatch records steps, the elevator display shows floor numbers in red, and the building manager notes that the round-trip elevator ride from the lobby to the third floor takes about 42 seconds.

How many flights of stairs does Janice walk (up and down) in a single day?

On Friday night, Fern was working the front entrance at the 7:40 p.m. showing of an R-rated movie at the old downtown theater, where the lobby had 3 poster cases, 2 soda fountains, 4 ticket scanners, and a snack counter advertising popcorn combos for $9, $12, and $15. The manager had reminded the staff twice during the 6:55 p.m. briefing that everyone needed both a ticket and a valid ID, even though some students kept arguing that the late show on Thursdays had looser rules. Earlier that evening, 18 college students, 7 parents, and 11 teachers had already gone in through a different line, and one broken scanner had delayed entry by 9 minutes. A janitor was mopping aisle 5, the theater had 14 rows with 16 seats each, and the box office sold 63 medium drinks and 41 large drinks before the first previews started. None of that changed Fern's actual ID-checking counts for the three visiting high school groups.

Three schools arrived by bus after a film-club event. Riverside High came in 3 buses carrying a total of 120 kids; some wore red wristbands from the earlier event, 35 had preordered concessions, and 12 had accidentally lined up in the wrong queue at first. Fern denied 20% of the 120 kids from Riverside High for not meeting the age requirement.

West Side High arrived next. Their group had 90 kids total, along with 5 chaperones who were not part of the student count, and their students had bought 48 small popcorns, 27 candy boxes, and 19 glow keychains from the lobby stand. Although their bus driver said they had left campus at 6:10 p.m. and hit 2 red lights and a train crossing, Fern still denied 70% of the 90 kids from West Side High.

Mountaintop High was the last school to reach the theater. Their bus had to park in the overflow lot near screen 6, and their 50 kids spent several minutes reorganizing themselves because 8 students had digital tickets, 14 had paper printouts, and the rest were on a group reservation list. Half the 50 kids from Mountaintop High were denied.

At the end of this whole process, after the previews had already started and after the assistant manager counted 6 unopened candy cartons and checked the 2 emergency exits, Fern wanted to know one thing: How many kids got into the movie?

Larry keeps a detailed routine chart for taking care of his dog because his vet once suggested consistency. On weekdays, Larry usually wakes up at 6:30 a.m., leaves for work at 8:15 a.m., gets home a little after 5:45 p.m., and tries to keep the dog on the same schedule even on weekends. The dog has 3 favorite toys in the living room, 2 water bowls in different parts of the house, a leash that is 6 feet long, and a bag of treats with 40 biscuits that Larry is supposed to use sparingly. The dog weighs 28 pounds now, though last year he weighed 25 pounds, and Larry buys a 15-pound bag of food about every 6 weeks when it is on sale for $24 instead of the regular $30. He also once compared 4 different brands of dog shampoo, and he keeps grooming appointments every 8 weeks, which usually last 45 minutes, though that is handled by the groomer, not Larry. 

Every day, Larry spends half an hour in the morning walking and playing with his dog, and then later that same day he spends another half an hour walking and playing with him again. He also spends a fifth of an hour every day feeding his dog, including scooping food, refreshing water, and putting the bowl away afterward. On rainy days, the walk may be slower, and on sunny days they may stop near the park bench by the 2 oak trees at the end of the block, but the total scheduled times stay the same. Larry once tracked 7 days in a row in a notebook, and on one Saturday he also spent 20 extra minutes washing the dog's blanket and 10 minutes searching for a missing tennis ball under the couch, but those chores are not part of his usual daily dog-care time described here. 

How many minutes does Larry spend on his dog each day?

A cleaning company is preparing a product demonstration for a chain of office buildings, schools, and gyms, and the training packet for the sales team is full of details. The company currently sells two sanitizer sprays in its basic hygiene line, although it also has 3 surface wipes, 4 concentrated refill options, and 2 seasonal scented products that are not part of this demonstration. In last quarter's catalog, Spray A was packaged in 12-ounce bottles sold in cases of 24, while Spray B came in 16-ounce bottles sold in cases of 18. The company tested the products in 8 different rooms over 6 weeks, with technicians visiting every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, usually at 9:00 a.m. and again at 2:30 p.m. On average, each technician carried 3 clipboards, 2 pairs of gloves, 1 timer, and 6 labeled test strips. Some rooms had 40 desks, some had 25 chairs, one lobby had 14 windows, and a storage area had 9 shelves holding 72 spare bottles. None of those logistical details changed the final germ summary in the report.

For the actual germ-kill comparison in the report, one spray kills 50% of germs, and another spray kills 25% of germs. The report also notes that 5% of the germs they kill are the same germs, because some germs are affected by both sprays. The marketing manager nearly confused this with a separate note saying that 5 out of every 100 customer surveys mentioned bottle design, and another note saying that a discount of 25% was offered to schools ordering more than 50 units, but those notes were from different sections of the packet. In the warehouse, 150 bottles were labeled for Region 1, 225 for Region 2, and 175 for Region 3, and the company expected 80 attendees at the demonstration, with 20 sample kits for managers and 60 for custodial supervisors. A budget sheet listed $500 for signage, $250 for travel, and $125 for refreshments. During setup, workers arranged 10 tables with 6 chairs each, and each chair had a printed brochure describing contact times of 30 seconds, 1 minute, and 5 minutes for different surfaces. Another page described a trial in which contamination counts started at 10,000 on one test panel and 8,000 on another, but those figures were used only to illustrate measurement procedures.

After all of the scheduling notes, bottle counts, room inventories, budgets, percentages from unrelated sections, and overlapping test documentation, the question in the training packet remains: What percentage of germs would be left after using both sanitizer sprays together?

Early on Saturday morning, Toby is standing by the local pond near the wooden dock, trying to estimate the number of goldfish there for a nature notebook he keeps. The pond has 4 benches around it, 2 signs warning visitors not to feed the ducks, and a path that loops around it in about 12 minutes if he walks quickly. Last week he came at 8:30 a.m., but today he arrived at 9:15 a.m. He brought a small container with 30 fish pellets, although he knows he is not supposed to use them, and he also packed binoculars, a pencil, and 3 different colored pens for sketching what he sees. There are 6 ducks near the reeds, 9 lily pads close to the shore, and 2 dragonflies hovering above the water. A park worker told him that the pond is about 5 feet deep near the edge and 11 feet deep toward the middle, and that some koi were moved out of the pond 2 years ago, leaving only goldfish now. Toby also remembers that on a school worksheet he once saw a chart saying that fish near the top are easier to count when the sun is out, though clouds can make reflections worse.

Today, Toby is only counting goldfish. He knows that only 25% of the goldfish are at the surface and the rest are too deep below the surface to be able to see. While scanning the pond carefully and double-checking that he is not counting any orange leaves or bright reflections, he counts 15 goldfish. Some are near the dock, some are near the reeds, and he writes several side notes in his notebook, including the water temperature of 68 degrees, the date, and the fact that he spent 20 minutes observing before making his estimate. He wonders how many fish might be deeper down where he cannot see them from the bank. If he counts 15 goldfish, how many are below the surface?

The owner of a Turkish restaurant was getting ready for a large community celebration weekend and spent the entire previous day planning traditional dishes. She reviewed menus for lentil soup, stuffed grape leaves, rice pilaf, shepherd’s salad, trays of baklava, and several kinds of kebab. On her prep sheet, she noted that 180 guests were expected for lunch, 40 more might stop by after the afternoon music performance, and the dining room had already been rearranged from 22 tables into 18 larger table groupings. She also checked that there were 96 plates, 140 tea glasses, 12 copper serving trays, 8 trays of bread, and 24 pounds of onions in storage. Her spice inventory listed 3 jars of sumac, 5 tins of paprika, 2 sacks of rice weighing 25 pounds each, and yogurt delivered in 6 large tubs. None of that changed her main concern, though: she needed enough ground beef for the traditional dishes she planned to cook.

Because one supplier had been unreliable during last year’s festival, she decided not to rely on a single source. Instead, she ordered ground beef, packaged uniformly in four-pound packages, from three different butchers across town. One butcher was near the produce market and usually opened at 6:30 a.m.; another was closer to the spice bazaar and charged a separate delivery fee of $12 on small orders, though that fee was waived this time; the third butcher usually made evening deliveries after finishing wholesale accounts. Her notebook also mentioned prices from earlier in the week: one shop had quoted $7 per pound for lamb, another had offered 15 pounds of chicken at a discount, and a different invoice from the restaurant’s freezer listed 32 pounds of ground beef left over from a previous month that had already been fully used and was no longer available.

The following morning, while the kitchen staff were chopping tomatoes, soaking chickpeas, and baking 48 rounds of flatbread, the first butcher delivered 10 packages of ground beef. A couple of hours later, just after a tea break in which 9 staff members each drank 2 small glasses of tea, 7 packages arrived from the second butcher. During the afternoon, other deliveries came and went: 14 cartons of yogurt were checked against an invoice that actually listed 12, 5 crates of eggplants were stacked by the back door, and 3 servers folded 60 napkins each. Finally, the third butcher’s delivery arrived at dusk, around the time the owner was counting 50 dessert plates and confirming a musician’s 7:00 p.m. arrival.

If all the ground beef delivered by the three butchers weighed 100 pounds, how many packages did the third butcher deliver?

On Saturday, James planned a long TV-and-snacks afternoon. He started by checking the guide at 1:00 p.m. and noticed that there were reruns, bonus clips, and a 5-minute commercial-free preview for one game show, plus a 10-minute behind-the-scenes segment for another later that evening, but he did not count those extras as episodes. He made a bowl of popcorn with 3 tablespoons of butter, poured 12 ounces of soda over ice, and set out 4 cookies, although he only ended up eating 2 of them before the second show. He also flipped through 18 channels before settling in, wrote down 6 possible Final Jeopardy categories from memory, and texted 3 friends about whether they preferred puzzles or trivia. The cable bill is $84 per month, the streaming service costs $12 more, and his remote has 44 buttons, though some are worn out. 

What he actually watched was this: James watched 2 episodes of Jeopardy and 2 episodes of Wheel of Fortune. Each episode of Jeopardy is 20 minutes long, and each episode of Wheel of Fortune is twice as long as a Jeopardy episode. Earlier in the week he had also watched 1 baseball game that lasted 3 hours and 15 minutes, and he once read that a special tournament version of one of these shows can run 60 minutes, but neither of those applied here. One of the 2 Jeopardy episodes had contestants with scores of $4,800, $7,200, and $12,400 going into Final Jeopardy, and in one Wheel of Fortune episode the winner earned $38,000 after solving 5 toss-up puzzles and buying 7 vowels. During commercial breaks James muted the TV 9 times, stood up twice to refill his drink, and checked the microwave clock, which was 6 minutes fast. He had originally planned to stop after 90 minutes so he could do 25 math problems and fold 14 shirts, but he finished everything he intended to watch first. How many hours did he watch TV?

Every Saturday morning, the three kids in the Harper house follow a detailed chore board that hangs on the refrigerator next to last month's electricity bill, a soccer practice calendar, and a coupon for $4 off laundry detergent. Richard usually starts by making his bed with 2 pillows, folding 3 blankets, stacking 7 comic books, and putting 12 toy cars back into labeled bins before vacuuming the rug. On weekdays he leaves for school at 7:45 a.m., gets home at 3:20 p.m., and spends 18 minutes on homework before piano practice, but none of that changes the fact that Richard can clean his room in 22 minutes. Cory is much more particular about organizing things: she sorts 16 hair clips by color, lines up 9 stuffed animals on one shelf, wipes down a desk with 4 drawers, and sometimes opens the window for 5 minutes to air out the room. Last week she spent $6 on new storage baskets and found 11 old stickers under her bed. Cory takes 3 minutes more than Richard to clean her room, while Blake, who keeps 8 action figures, 5 baseball caps, 14 trading cards, and a hamper that holds 20 shirts, can clean his room 4 minutes more quickly than Cory. Blake also claims he works fastest on Tuesdays, slower on Thursdays, and once timed himself using a digital stopwatch that counted seconds, but his actual cleaning rate for this problem is unchanged. Their family has a routine where bedrooms are cleaned twice a week, even during weeks when there are 5 school days, 2 weekend days, 1 library trip, and 3 basketball practices. If each child cleans only his or her own room and they all stick to the family schedule of cleaning their rooms twice every week, how many minutes do all three spend cleaning their rooms each week?

On Saturday morning, Mary spread out her art supplies across the kitchen table before her school poster project. She had a 24-slot crayon box, although not every slot was filled, plus 2 broken crayon wrappers she planned to throw away, 4 pencils, 1 eraser shaped like a star, and 6 markers that she was not allowed to use for this assignment. In the crayon box, some colors were missing completely, and several crayons were different shades from one another. Among the crayons she actually had with her, Mary counted 5 green crayons and 8 blue crayons of different shades. One green crayon was dark forest green, one was light green, and the others were other shades; the blue ones included sky blue, navy, and several others. On a shelf nearby, her younger brother had his own separate pack of 10 crayons, including 2 red and 3 yellow, but those were not Mary's. Earlier in the week, Mary had used 2 orange crayons down to stubs and had already removed them from the box, and last month she donated 7 old crayons to her classroom supply bin. 

While Mary was organizing everything by color, Becky came over to help. Becky brought 3 sheets of poster board, 12 stickers, and 1 glue stick, and she asked whether she could borrow a few crayons. Mary gave out 3 green crayons and 1 blue crayon to Becky. Mary did not give Becky any pencils, markers, wrappers, poster board, or crayons from anyone else's box. After that, Mary continued arranging the crayons she still had left on the table for her drawing. How many crayons does she have left?

On Saturday, Winwin went with her cousins to a neighborhood spring fair that had 12 game booths, 3 food stalls, and a small lottery table near the entrance. She arrived at 10:15 a.m., bought 2 raffle snacks for $3 each, and later spent $8 on lemonade for her group, although her cousin paid her back $4 before they left. At one booth, signs advertised prizes of $10, $20, $50, and $100, and another poster explained that some winnings could be affected by taxes and fixed administrative charges depending on the amount. Winwin checked her wallet twice because she had brought $30 in cash, a $15 gift card for the fair arcade, and 6 one-dollar bills she was saving for bus fare, but she never used the gift card at the lottery table. After waiting behind 4 people, she bought a lottery ticket during the 11:00 a.m. drawing and ended up winning $50 in the lottery. The booth attendant reminded winners that there was a 20% tax on the winnings and also a separate $5 processing fee for preparing the payout receipt. The receipt itself had other information on it too, including ticket number 2481, booth code 7B, and the note that prizes under $10 were paid in coins while larger prizes were paid in bills. Winwin briefly wondered whether to spend some of her money on a souvenir hat priced at $12 or on 3 postcards for $2 each, but before doing anything else, she wanted to know how much money from the lottery she was actually able to take home. Winwin won $50 in a lottery. She paid 20% for the tax and she paid $5 for the processing fee. How much was she able to take home?

At a big family birthday gathering on Ernesto's side of the family, people kept comparing everyone's ages, heights, and party jobs, which made the conversation surprisingly confusing. Ernesto just turned 11 years old this week, and his cake had 11 candles, though only 10 stayed lit because one kept going out. Jayden helped set up 24 balloons, 6 paper streamers, and 3 tables with 4 chairs at each table. Ernesto's aunt brought 2 pizzas cut into 8 slices each, and Jayden ate 3 slices while Ernesto ate 2. Their cousin Mia is 14, their neighbor Leo is 9, and their grandfather is 68. The party started at 3:00 p.m., the games lasted 45 minutes, and 17 guests signed the birthday card. Ernesto received 5 toy cars, 2 books, and a $20 bill, while Jayden brought a gift bag with 1 card, 2 packs of stickers, and 4 markers. Someone also mentioned that in 3 years, Ernesto will be 14, and another relative said that at that same time Jayden will be half of Ernesto's age. Ignore the chatter about pizza slices, candles, chairs, cousins, and gifts, and focus on the age statement: in 3 years, Jayden will be half of Ernesto's age. If Ernesto is 11 years old, how many years old is Jayden now?

Angela is a bike messenger in New York, and her Wednesday route is unusually busy because several offices changed their delivery windows after a morning rainstorm. She starts her shift at 8:15 a.m. in Midtown with a thermos of coffee, 2 spare bike tubes, a U-lock, a phone battery pack charged to 91%, and a paper route sheet clipped to her bag even though she also uses an app. By noon she expects to cross 4 borough boundaries, ride about 18 miles, stop at 11 office buildings, and use 3 different elevators that are notoriously slow. Her company handles many kinds of deliveries: legal envelopes, flower bundles, pharmacy pickups, catered trays, documents, keys, small retail parcels, and meal orders from restaurants. That morning, one dispatcher mentions 12 document envelopes for another rider, 5 canceled flower drops, 9 coffee cartons going to a film set, and a same-day invoice worth $48.75, while Angela herself notices that the app shows $6.50 toll reimbursement, 14 pending notifications, and 3 customers requesting "leave at front desk." At one stop she picks up 7 insulated drink carriers that belong to a different courier team, and at another she passes a shelf holding 16 unclaimed packages from the previous day. Her backpack can safely hold up to 35 pounds, though today she is carrying only 22 pounds at the moment. She usually averages 10 miles per hour in traffic, but on avenues with green lights she can briefly reach 16 miles per hour.

For Angela's own assigned deliveries today, the dispatcher cares about only two categories for her final count: meals and packages. She needs to deliver 8 times as many packages as meals. Altogether, the total number of meals and packages she needs to deliver is 27. Some of the meal orders are from deli counters, some are boxed lunches, and some package drop-offs are padded mailers while others are small cartons, but those details do not affect the count. If she needs to deliver 27 meals and packages combined, how many meals does she deliver?

Keiko keeps very detailed phone notes because she is trying to lower her screen time. On the bulletin board above her desk, she has a weekly planner with 7 days marked out, a reminder that her phone battery lasts about 18 hours on standby, and a sticky note showing that her family text plan allows 500 messages per month before any extra charge. Last month she sent 286 messages total, her brother sent 143, and their mother sent 92. She also wrote down that on Monday of this week she charged her phone to 100%, on Tuesday it dropped to 64% by dinner, and on Thursday she spent 25 minutes turning off old notifications from 14 apps. None of that changed the count she recorded in her message log.

In her actual weekly log, Keiko wrote that last week she sent 111 text messages. She also noted several other communication details: 36 of last week's messages were to one friend about homework, 12 were group-chat replies, 9 were reminders to her soccer team, and 4 were messages she drafted twice because of autocorrect mistakes. This week, after trying to estimate her usage, she wrote that she sent 50 fewer than double the number of text messages she sent last week. She almost compared that to the 2 hours she spent on calls this week and the 17 photos she shared, but those were tracked separately and not part of the text-message total.

Keiko also keeps receipts in the same notebook: a phone case cost $22, earbuds were discounted from $40 to $28, and she paid $15 for a charging cable. Her school days start at 8:10 a.m., soccer practice runs 90 minutes, and she set 3 daily alarms on her phone. Even so, the question in her notebook is simply this: How many text messages did Keiko send last week and this week combined?

At the annual community media fair, the local newspaper set up a booth advertising several subscription options and promotional bundles for new and returning readers. A weekend-only print plan was listed at $36 for 6 months, a digital-only student plan was advertised at $5 per month, and a family bundle that included the Sunday magazine and coupons was marked as saving 20% compared with buying two separate accounts. One sign mentioned that last year 1,250 households renewed, another said the paper prints 48 pages on weekdays and 72 pages on Sundays, and a flyer on the table listed optional puzzle books for $12 each or 3 for $30. There was also a chart showing that home delivery is available 7 days a week in 14 nearby neighborhoods, and a small poster noted that early-bird visitors between 9:00 a.m. and 11:00 a.m. could enter a drawing for a $50 gift card if they filled out a 3-page survey.

Among all these offers, the booth representative points out one specific deal: a one-year subscription to the newspaper is offered with a 45% discount. The regular price of that one-year subscription is $80. Some customers at the booth are comparing that discount with a different promotion from last month that took $18 off a premium package, while others are calculating sales tax on souvenir mugs priced at $8 each, but those are separate items and not part of this subscription price.

How much does the discounted subscription cost if a subscription normally costs $80?

On a busy Tuesday, Tim's cat bit him while he was trying to separate the cat from a torn bag of treats. Earlier that morning, Tim had already spent $18 on cat litter, $7 on bandages, and $11 on antiseptic cream from a pharmacy that was running a buy-2-get-1-free promotion on travel-size items. He had also just renewed his own health insurance for a monthly premium of $240 and his pet insurance for $35 per month, after comparing plans with deductibles of $250, $500, and $1000. The clinic receptionist told him that urgent care closes at 8 p.m., regular appointments are every 20 minutes, and a tetanus shot can sometimes cost $45, though that was discussed only as a general policy. Tim first went to his doctor, where the visit itself cost $300. His health insurance covered 75% of that doctor's visit. Afterward, he took the cat to the veterinarian. The cat's visit cost $120, and his pet insurance covered $60 of that veterinary bill. On the way home, Tim considered stopping for a $14 sandwich and a $3 coffee, but he skipped both because he was already thinking about expenses. The vet waiting room had 6 dogs, 4 cats, 2 birds, and a poster advertising annual checkups for $95, dental cleanings for $210, and vaccines in packages of 3 for $75. Tim's cat weighs 12 pounds, is 4 years old, and usually eats 2 cans of food a day from cases of 24 cans that cost $36. Tim also remembered that last year he paid $80 out of pocket for flea treatment and $150 for blood work, but none of that was part of today's charges. How much did he pay?

At a family financial-planning workshop held on a Saturday morning from 9:00 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., several parents compared the savings accounts they had opened for their children. The presenter handed out worksheets showing sample balances like $150, $275, $400, $550, and $800, along with example annual rates of 3%, 5%, 8%, 10%, and 12%. One page also mentioned monthly deposits of $20, $25, and $40, and another showed what would happen over 1 year, 2 years, 3 years, and 5 years under simple interest versus compound interest. During a break, Ariella mentioned that she had recently paid a $35 bank fee on a different account, deposited birthday money of $60 into her daughter's emergency jar, and set aside $18 each week for groceries. Daniella said she had once considered moving money into a certificate paying 6% for 18 months, but decided not to because she wanted easy access to cash for school supplies that cost $47, $29, and $16.

For their sons' savings accounts specifically, Ariella has $200 more in her son's saving account than Daniella has in her son's savings account. Ariella's account earns her simple interest at the rate of 10% per annum. Daniella has $400 in her son's account. At the same workshop, someone else mentioned earning $80 in interest on $500 over a different time period, and another parent compared two banks that charged $2 monthly service fees unless the balance stayed above $300. None of those accounts are the ones being discussed here.

Ariella and Daniella also talked about how one son is 8 years old and the other is 10, how they each receive birthday checks from relatives—sometimes $25, sometimes $50, occasionally $100—and how one child spends $12 a month on comics while the other saves loose change in a jar that already contains 147 quarters, 36 dimes, and 19 nickels. Ariella keeps a color-coded notebook with 24 entries per page, 3 pages for each child, and annual goals of saving $1,000 by high school. Daniella uses a spreadsheet with columns for date, deposit, withdrawal, interest, and notes, and she highlighted balances at the end of January, June, and December.

Ignoring all unrelated examples and side details, if Daniella has $400, how much money will Arialla have after two years?

At the end of the harvest week, Colby spent all of Saturday working through the rows of his mango orchard. He has 12 mango trees in total, although only 9 produced well this season, and he used 6 woven baskets that can each hold up to 15 kilograms. His cousins helped for 4 hours in the morning and 3 more in the afternoon, and they also sorted out bruised fruit for jam, counted empty crates, and cleaned tools before sunset. By the time everything was weighed on the large hanging scale near the shed, the total mangoes Colby harvested came to 60 kilograms. Earlier in the week he had expected maybe 54 kilograms because one tree flowered late, but the final total was higher. He wrote the weights in a notebook next to other orchard details such as 18 ladders borrowed over the season, 24 watering turns completed that month, and 3 sacks of fertilizer used back in June.

On market day, Colby loaded fruit into blue crates that each hold 5 kilograms, though one crate was left half-filled just to balance the truck. The market itself opens at 7:30 a.m., charges a stall fee of $12, and usually buys mangoes alongside papayas, bananas, and avocados. Colby sold 20 kilograms to the market. After that, he looked at what was left and decided to support local families by selling the remaining half to his community during the afternoon pickup, where neighbors arrived in groups of 2, 3, and 5 and some also asked about next week's harvest. His community orders were packed into smaller bags labeled by street, and one neighbor even asked whether the fruit came from the eastern grove or the western grove.

For packing records, Colby also noted that small mangoes often go 10 to a kilogram while larger ones can be fewer, but for this particular accounting problem, each kilogram contains 8 mangoes. He wants to finish his inventory sheet before dinner, after also setting aside 4 kilograms of leaves for compost and checking 7 unused twine rolls in the shed, neither of which changed the harvest total already recorded.

If each kilogram contains 8 mangoes, how many mangoes does he still have?

George was getting ready for a long trip and stopped at a highway convenience store just before the 8:15 a.m. bus departure. He spent several minutes comparing food options because the trip would last 6 hours, with a 20-minute stop after about 140 miles. On one shelf, the store had 3 kinds of juice, 5 brands of milk, and a refrigerated case with 12 sandwiches, including turkey, ham, egg salad, and vegetarian. A promotion sign said that buying any 2 snacks gave 10% off a third snack under $3, but George did not use that deal. Another sign advertised coffee for $2, tea for $1.50, and muffins for $3 each or 2 for $5. He also noticed that family-size juice packs cost $9, small yogurt cups were $1.25 each, and bottled water was 3 for $6, though he did not choose any of those.

For his trip, George bought exactly three items: a bottle of juice, a sandwich, and a bottle of milk. The sandwich was for $4. The juice was two times more expensive than the sandwich. The bottle of milk cost was 75% of the total cost of the sandwich and juice. George had originally brought $20 in cash, plus 8 quarters and 3 one-dollar bills in a side pocket, and he wanted to save enough money for a locker that might cost $2 later. He also checked the nutrition labels: the sandwich had 420 calories, the juice bottle contained 16 ounces, and one milk option had 2% fat while another had whole milk. The cashier rang up another customer ahead of him for $13.75, and the customer behind him was buying 2 energy bars at $2.50 each and a banana for $0.89.

Ignoring taxes and all the other items George looked at but did not buy, how much did George pay for his food?

On a rainy Saturday afternoon, a young girl is sorting beads for a craft table at a community fair. In front of her are several containers: one jar labeled blue with 23 blue beads in it, one jar labeled yellow with 16 yellow beads, a tray holding 12 red beads left over from last week, a packet of 9 green beads she decides not to open, and a string of 18 striped beads already sewn onto an old bracelet. She also has 4 empty cups, 2 plastic spoons, 5 paper labels, and a bowl decorated with 7 painted flowers around the rim. She checks the wall clock, which reads 3:15, and writes the date on a name card before beginning.

She pours the 23 blue beads and the 16 yellow beads into the bowl and mixes them together thoroughly. She does not add the red, green, or striped beads, because those are for different projects later in the day. Her friend suggests making 4 piles of 8, but she ignores that idea. Instead, she divides the total number of beads in the bowl into 3 equal parts and lines the parts up on a mat. Then, wanting the parts to end up smaller before a later decoration step, she removes the same number of beads from each part and sets those removed beads aside in a tiny box that already contains 11 buttons and 3 sequins from another activity. After removing those beads, she doubles the number of beads remaining in each part by pairing each remaining bead with one matching bead from a separate practice stash. Now there are 6 beads in each part.

She is also keeping notes in a notebook where she has written that last month she used 14 beads per bracelet, sold 8 bracelets, charged $6 for each, spent $9 on ribbon, and sorted supplies into 10 drawers. None of that changes what she has just done with the bowl.

How many beads were removed from each part?

Jerome is preparing for a long charity bicycle ride that follows a 150-mile route from one end of the county to the other. Before he leaves, he checks all kinds of details: his bike has 27 gears, both tires are pumped to 85 psi, he packed 3 water bottles holding 24 ounces each, 2 spare tubes, 1 mini pump, 6 energy bars, and a rain jacket. His cycling computer says his practice rides last month were 18 miles, 22 miles, 15 miles, 31 miles, and 14 miles, although those training distances are separate from this trip. The event handbook says rest stops are placed about every 25 miles, volunteers begin setting up at 6:30 a.m., and riders pay a $40 registration fee unless they raised at least $200 in donations. Jerome also made a meal plan: oatmeal for breakfast on 7 mornings, pasta the night before day 1, and sandwiches cut into halves for lunch. He even wrote down hotel prices for nearby towns: $89, $104, and $97 per night, though he may not need them.

For this particular trip, Jerome's goal is to complete exactly 150 miles in total. He has decided on a simple schedule for most of the ride: he wants to ride 12 miles each day for 12 days. On some earlier vacations he once rode 13 miles in a day, and on another weekend he averaged 12 miles per hour for part of a morning, but those are not part of this plan. He also noticed that if he stopped at every rest area, he would take 5 breaks a day of 10 minutes each, and he estimated he might burn around 600 calories on shorter rides and closer to 900 on longer ones. His map packet includes 14 pages, the cue sheet lists 32 turns, and one scenic detour would add 8 extra miles, but he is not taking that detour.

After following his plan of riding 12 miles a day for the first 12 days of the 150-mile trip, how long will he ride on the 13th day to finish his goal?

Mario’s barbershop has a long list of posted prices and promotions that regular customers constantly talk about. A beard trim is usually $12, a shampoo add-on is $6, kids’ cuts are $14 on Tuesdays before 3 p.m., seniors get $3 off on Wednesdays, and there is a loyalty punch card that gives every 8th haircut half off, although Mario says hardly anyone remembers to bring it. The shop opens at 9 a.m. on weekdays, 8 a.m. on Saturdays, and closes early at 4 p.m. on Sundays. On the wall near the register there is also a note that haircuts are 50% more expensive during the weekends because of higher demand. Last month, Mario bought 3 new barber chairs for $240 each, replaced 2 mirrors, ordered 48 bottles of hair product, and raised the price of hot towel shaves from $10 to $11.50. He also keeps track of tips in a separate jar, and on one busy weekend he gave 27 haircuts, 9 beard trims, and sold 14 styling products. 

This week, Mario was comparing receipts and noticed that for his last haircut, which he got on Monday, he paid $18. He did not get a shampoo, beard trim, shave, gel, or any other extra service, and there was no coupon involved. Since the day before Monday was Sunday, he wondered what the same haircut would have cost the day before under the weekend pricing rule. How much he would have paid the day before?

John throws a large neighborhood block party on a Saturday that is supposed to run from 2:00 p.m. until 9:00 p.m., although setup starts at 10:30 a.m. and cleanup usually takes another 90 minutes. He and 3 other people are the main organizers, but there are also 12 neighbors who volunteered to bring folding chairs, 8 kids helping decorate with 5 strings of lights, and 2 people in charge of music who made a playlist with 47 songs. Last year the party had 86 guests, this year they expect around 110, and the rain date is the following Sunday. They reserve 14 tables, borrow 36 chairs, put out 9 coolers, and hang 24 paper lanterns. A local store offers burger buns in packs of 8 for $4 per pack, but those are being donated by a bakery, along with 18 trays of cookies and 6 sheet cakes, so John does not pay for those. There is also a debate about whether to rent an extra grill for $65, but one neighbor lends them a second grill for free, so no rental happens.

For the food they do pay for together, the organizers buy 100 pounds of burgers at $3 per pound. They also buy $80 of condiments and propane to cook everything. John splits that shared cost equally with the 3 other people organizing the party. Separately, John also buys all the alcohol himself, which costs $200, even though one guest later brings 2 unopened soda cases and another brings 3 bags of ice. Someone keeps track of wristbands and says adults get red bands, kids get blue bands, and 75 cups are used by 5:00 p.m., but none of that changes the purchases. There are also coupons worth $10 off decorations and a previous year's leftover napkin supply of 300 napkins, but those are unrelated to the main purchases here.

How much did John spend altogether

At a lengthy town council meeting about the town’s annual finances, officials reviewed a stack of reports covering everything from road repainting to library hours, seasonal flower planting, trash pickup routes, and the replacement schedule for 18 park benches, 42 streetlights, and 6 decorative fountains. One committee mentioned that last year the town collected $31 million in taxes and $2 million in permit fees, while another presentation noted that this year they expect 4 summer festivals, 3 farmers markets each month from June through September, and maintenance for 27 miles of sidewalks. The parks department requested $1.5 million for tree trimming, playground mulch, and repairing 9 broken sprinklers, and the transportation office discussed a separate grant of $8 million for road resurfacing that cannot be used for other purposes. Meanwhile, the school district slide deck listed 14 schools, 620 teachers, 11 bus routes, and cafeteria upgrades costing $400,000, and the police department report listed 12 patrol cars due for replacement over the next 3 years, along with overtime figures from holiday weekends. After all of these presentations, the mayor summarized the actual town budget for the year: the town’s annual budget totals $32 million. Of that amount, half of the budget goes towards policing, and $12 million goes towards education. The council then asked the finance director to state how much money remains for managing public spaces, including routine upkeep of plazas, parks, lawns, and other shared outdoor areas. How much money is left for managing public spaces?

Daniel keeps a meticulously cataloged video game collection in a room with 6 shelves, each shelf divided into 4 sections, although a few sections are reserved for strategy guides, empty collector's edition boxes, and old console manuals. On the wall he has posters from 9 different franchises, and in one drawer he stores 27 controllers, 14 charging cables, 8 memory cards, and 3 headsets. None of that is part of the game count, but it makes the room look more crowded than it is. His spreadsheet also tracks release year, genre, whether a game was bought new or used, and which system it belongs to: 92 are for one console, 88 for another, 61 are handheld titles, 54 are PC games in boxes, and the rest are spread across retro systems. Some games came with steelbooks, some with maps, and 18 were gifts from relatives over the years, though Daniel still records every game in the same master inventory.

According to that inventory, Daniel has a collection of 346 video games. Of those 346 games, 80 were games Daniel bought for $12 each during launch-week purchases, midnight releases, and special editions that also happened to include things like preorder bonuses, reversible covers, or soundtrack coupons. At one point he considered selling 24 duplicate titles for $9 each, but he never actually included any sales in this calculation. He also once budgeted $150 for gaming accessories in the same month he bought several of these games, and he spent another $36 on shelf labels and protective plastic cases, but those expenses are tracked separately from the games themselves.

After accounting for the 80 games that cost $12 each, Daniel looks at the rest of his collection. Of the remaining games, 50% were bought for $7 each, often during weekend sales, used-game promotions, and buy-two-get-one events where the average receipt totals looked confusing because taxes, coupons, and store credit were involved. The rest of the remaining games—all others not already counted in the $12 group or the 50% of the remainder bought for $7—had a price of $3 each, mostly from clearance bins, garage sales, and bundle leftovers. Daniel's notes also mention that 40 of the cheapest games came in worn cases, 22 had no manuals, and 17 were part of mixed lots, but each of those games still counts as exactly one game in the collection.

If Daniel also visited 5 different game stores over 3 months, used 2 loyalty cards, and made purchases on 11 separate Saturdays, how much did Daniel spend on all the games in his collection?

James joins the varsity football team at the start of the fall and quickly becomes the star player everyone talks about. Before the season begins, the team has 48 players on the roster, 11 starters on offense, 11 on defense, 3 special teams units, 5 coaches, 2 trainers, and practices 4 afternoons each week for 2 hours at a time. Their stadium has 6 entrance gates, 24 rows on each side, and tickets cost $12 for students and $18 for adults, though attendance varies depending on weather. The booster club sells 350 programs at the opener, the marching band has 72 members, and the concession stand orders 500 hot dogs, 420 sodas, and 275 pretzels for the first home game. James wears jersey number 12, his team uses a playbook with 96 offensive plays, and in one newspaper profile they mention that he ran 40 yards in 5.1 seconds and lifted weights 3 mornings a week during preseason.

Once the season starts, James is unbelievably productive on offense. He scores 4 touchdowns per game, and each touchdown is worth 6 points. The season lasts 15 games in total, including rivalry games, homecoming, and playoffs. In some games the coaches decide to go for 2 after a touchdown, and during the season James manages to score 2-point conversions 6 times altogether. In one game he scores 3 touchdowns in the first half and 1 in the second; in another game the team wins by 14 points; and in yet another the defense records 2 interceptions and 4 sacks. The kicker also makes several extra-point kicks during the year, the team averages 28 first downs per game, and James gains more than 1,200 all-purpose yards, but those details are just part of his amazing season summary.

By the end of the year, people start comparing James to the program's all-time greats. The old school record for points scored in a season was 300 points. The trophy case also holds 9 district titles, 4 regional plaques, and a faded championship banner from 1998, and the athletic director mentions that last year's team finished 10-5. James wants to know exactly how far past the old scoring mark he finished. How many points did James beat the old record by?

Buddy keeps his baseball card collection in a binder with 6 plastic pages, and each page has 9 pockets, although some pockets are empty because he sorts cards by team, year, and whether they are shiny. On Monday after school, before reorganizing anything, Buddy has 30 baseball cards in his collection. That same evening he spends 45 minutes alphabetizing player names, sets aside 8 duplicate cards he is thinking about trading later, counts 14 cards from pitchers and 16 from batters, and notices that 5 cards have bent corners while 25 do not. None of that changes how many cards he owns on Monday: he has 30 baseball cards.

On Tuesday, Buddy brings his binder to lunch. His friend shows him 24 football cards and 18 basketball cards, and another student offers to trade 3 rare cards for 6 common ones, but Buddy says no. Later that day Buddy loses half of his baseball cards. He also checks the binder and sees that 10 card pockets on the first few pages are still open, 2 pages are partly filled, and 1 page is completely empty because he moved some non-baseball cards out last week. By Tuesday night he writes in a notebook that he had started the week with 30 baseball cards on Monday and that on Tuesday he lost half of them.

On Wednesday, after finishing homework at 4:30, Buddy goes to a card shop that sells packs for $3 each or 4 packs for $10. He brings $20, spends $6 on sleeves, sees a display of 50 vintage cards, and notices a sign advertising 12% off team posters. He does not buy posters. Instead, on Wednesday Buddy buys 12 baseball cards. At home he compares them with 7 cards he got last month, 9 cards he keeps in a separate box, and 4 cards featuring his favorite team mascot. He also writes down jersey numbers from some players: 27, 42, 11, and 8.

On Thursday morning, Buddy plans how to arrange his collection again. He thinks about making rows of 5 cards, then columns of 3 cards, and then grouping cards by division with 15 American League cards and 13 National League cards if he includes a few old extras from another folder that are not part of the cards counted in his main collection. He buys a third of what he had on Tuesday. He also passes a store window showing 33 autograph cards, 21 commemorative coins, and 6 binders on sale, but those are unrelated to what he actually purchases that day. How many baseball cards does he have on Thursday?

Manex is a tour bus driver for a regional sightseeing company that runs several loop trips every week. On the day in question, he starts with 48 passengers even though the bus has 52 seats, and before leaving the depot he spends 15 minutes checking the mirrors, 10 minutes reviewing the route card, and 5 minutes making sure the microphone works. The company keeps records showing that the bus gets about 6 miles per gallon on highways, the fuel tank was topped off with 40 gallons that morning, and parking at the destination lot costs $18 for buses, though the company prepaid it. The route sheet lists a standard outbound drive of 55 miles to the destination. Because of roadwork near a bridge, however, Manex is instructed to return to the starting point by a different road that is 10 miles farther than the outgoing route. Along the way there are 7 traffic lights in town, 3 toll signs he does not use, and 2 scenic pull-offs where other drivers sometimes stop, but on this tour he only follows the assigned distances. The passengers spend money at the destination gift shop, where postcards cost $2 each, keychains cost $5, and lunches average $14, and the museum there stays open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Manex himself remains at the destination for 2 hours before heading back. His company estimates his average driving pace for scheduling by saying he can drive 1 mile for 2 minutes. Last month he drove 12 similar tours, and one of them had a detour of 8 extra miles, but not this one. If his bus number is 27, his employee badge number is 314, and he writes down odometer readings before and after every trip, how long will it take the bus driver to do the entire tour in hours?

Grandpa Lou keeps a handwritten TV log in a blue notebook by his recliner. He mostly likes the Hallmark channel, although he also flips past the weather report at 6:00, the local news at 6:30, old western reruns that come on for 1 hour blocks, and an occasional baseball pregame show that can run 30 minutes before first pitch. On the shelf next to him are 18 DVDs, 7 mystery novels, 3 pairs of reading glasses, and 2 remote controls, only one of which still has working batteries. His granddaughter once tried to organize his week by color-coding all the channels: Hallmark in red, sports in blue, news in black, and movies recorded on the DVR in green. The DVR currently shows 11 saved programs, but some are only 42 minutes long, some are 60 minutes, and one holiday special is 2 hours. None of that changes his Hallmark habit: every Hallmark movie he watches is a full-length movie lasting exactly 90 minutes, not counting the 5 minutes he usually spends making tea before one starts or the 10 minutes he sometimes spends looking for the remote afterward.

On Tuesday, after lunch at 12:15 and before calling his brother at 8:00 p.m., Grandpa Lou watched several full-length movies on the Hallmark channel. Altogether, his Hallmark viewing time that day added up to 4 hours and 30 minutes. Earlier that same Tuesday he had also listened to a 15-minute farm report, sorted 24 coupons, and microwaved soup for 3 minutes, but those were separate activities. He did not count commercials, station promos, or the 20 minutes he dozed in his chair during the afternoon because he only records completed full-length movies in his notebook.

On Wednesday, his routine was busier: he watered 9 tomato plants, spent 45 minutes at the hardware store, and mailed 6 letters after buying 12 forever stamps. He also watched Hallmark on the same channel again, and on that day he watched twice as many movies as he did on Tuesday. A neighbor later mentioned that Wednesday's lineup included one sequel, two winter-themed romances, and a marathon advertised as lasting 9 hours, but Grandpa Lou's notebook still only counts the number of full-length 90-minute Hallmark movies he actually watched.

What is the maximum number of full-length movies Grandpa could have watched during these two days?

Janet runs a small film studio that keeps unusually detailed production notes. Her previous movie was a 2-hour film that premiered on a Friday after 14 weeks of editing, used 6 principal actors, 18 extras, 4 camera operators, and 3 sound technicians, and had scenes shot across 5 indoor sets and 2 outdoor locations. The production binder says the crew typically worked 10-hour days, broke for lunch after 5 hours, rented 12 lights at $40 each per day, and used 8 microphones, 3 drones, and 2 backup generators. That older movie sold 9,000 opening-weekend tickets, its poster campaign cost $12,000, and 1,500 commemorative programs were printed, although none of those figures affect filming time. The important production note about that previous movie is that it was 2 hours long, and it cost $50 per minute to film.

Now Janet has filmed a new movie. Early planning documents mention several comparisons with the old project: the new movie had 20% more speaking roles, 3 fewer night shoots, 4 more costumes per lead actor, and a soundtrack containing 15 songs instead of 12. The catering budget rose from $800 per day to $1,100 per day, location permits cost a total of $7,500, and the studio booked 9 vans instead of 6 for transportation. One memo says the final cut includes 144 scenes, while another notes that the raw footage lasted 310 minutes before editing. The new marketing team also proposed ticket prices of $12 for adults and $8 for children, plus a merchandise line with mugs priced at $14 and shirts priced at $22. Despite all these details, the actual filming relationship is simple: the new movie is 60% longer than Janet's previous 2-hour movie.

On the cost side, accountants tracked many categories separately. Makeup expenses averaged $900 per week, insurance cost $18,000 for the whole production, and a storage warehouse charged $600 per month for props. Camera rental packages were renegotiated midway through shooting, with one quote of $2,400 per week and another of $2,850 per week depending on lens selection. A separate note says the previous movie's set-construction budget was $24,000 and the newest movie's set-construction budget was $31,000. However, when Janet compared direct filming cost rates, the newest movie cost twice as much per minute to film as the previous movie.

What was the total amount of money required to film Janet's entire newest film?

Silvia is organizing food for a long Saturday community workshop and is comparing several bakery options before placing an advanced order. The bakery she uses has a printed flyer that mentions a few policies: weekday pickup starts at 7:30 a.m., Saturday pickup starts at 8:00 a.m., coffee travelers serve 12 people, fruit tarts must be ordered 48 hours ahead, and advanced orders over $50.00 receive 10% off. There is also a note that disposable serving trays cost $1.50 each, compostable plates come in packs of 20, and a catering assistant can help load orders of more than 8 boxes. Silvia writes down a lot of information while planning because 24 people are expected, 3 volunteers are arriving early, and the event lasts 4 hours with a 15-minute break after the second session.

On one page of her notes, she lists items she considered but does not end up choosing for this order: 1 spinach pie for $14.00, 2 loaves of sourdough at $6.00 each, 12 muffins at $2.50 each, 3 fruit cups at $4.00 each, and 2 coffee travelers at $18.00 each. She also sees that mini danishes are sold by the dozen for $24.00, sandwich platters start at $42.00, and gluten-free scones are $3.50 each. Last month, she had spent $56.00 on a different order and got a discount, and earlier this week her friend mentioned spending $49.50 and missing the discount by just fifty cents. Silvia also has a separate shopping list for jam jars, napkins, and orange juice totaling $27.25 from another store, but that is not part of this bakery order.

For the actual bakery order she places in advance, Silvia orders 2 quiches for $15.00 each, 6 croissants at $3.00 each, and 6 buttermilk biscuits for $2.00 each. She does not add the optional tray liners, does not order coffee, and does not change the quantities after submitting the form. How much will her order be with the discount?

At Borris liquor store, the owner keeps unusually detailed notes about grape use, deliveries, storage, and future planning. In the front display, he currently stacks 18 empty decorative wine crates, each labeled with old vineyard names, and in the back room he has 24 reusable plastic bins, though only 15 of those are used for actual grape sorting. His supplier drives in every 3 weeks during the harvest season, usually arriving around 7:30 a.m., and charges a flat delivery fee of $12 per trip plus different rates for red, white, and table grapes depending on weather. Last year, one invoice listed 35 kilograms of a darker variety for tasting events, another listed 22 kilograms of a sweeter variety for special orders, and a separate note mentioned that 8 kilograms spoiled during a heat wave because the cooler briefly stopped working. The cooler was later repaired for $180, and Borris also bought 6 new oak shelves that can each hold 40 bottles. None of that changes his standard production record, which says that the store uses 90 kilograms of grapes every 6 months for its regular liquor production schedule.

Borris is now reviewing his annual plan. He opens a ledger that also includes other numbers: 52 weeks in the year, 2 main holiday rushes, 4 seasonal tasting weekends, 300 bottles already labeled, and 120 corks left over from spring. He is considering redesigning the labels, which would increase printing costs by 15%, and he is also thinking about extending Saturday hours from 8 hours to 10 hours during the summer. His assistant suggests ordering 10 extra boxes just in case, and another note says that each storage pallet fits 50 kilograms, although one pallet is currently occupied by empty glass bottles. There are also old handwritten reminders like "subtract 5 kilograms for samples" and "reserve 12 kilograms for private events," but those notes belong to discontinued promotion plans and not to the new production change he is evaluating.

What Borris actually wants to decide is this: his store currently uses 90 kilograms of grapes every 6 months, and he is thinking of increasing his production by twenty percent. How many grapes does he need in a year after increasing his production?

Mel and Katherine are filling out a family event planning sheet for a big birthday season. Katherine has already been to 19 birthday parties in her life, keeps 24 candles in a drawer for emergencies, and once baked 36 cupcakes for a cousin's celebration, while Mel prefers making 18 paper decorations and tying balloons in groups of 6. Their aunt keeps reminding everyone that a dozen means 12, because last year she ordered 2 dozen plates, 3 dozen napkins, and 4 dozen forks for a picnic that lasted 5 hours and started at 2:00 p.m. On the refrigerator there is also a list showing Katherine's shoe size, Mel's favorite number, the ages of three younger cousins, and the fact that the family photo album has 27 pages with 8 pictures on each page. None of that changes the relationship between the sisters' ages: Mel is three years younger than Katherine. Suppose Katherine reaches two dozen years of age during the summer, after sending 14 invitations, receiving 11 cards, and stacking 2 layers on her cake with 12 strawberries around the edge of each layer. When Katherine is two dozen years old, how old will Mel be in years?

At the end of the summer harvest, James goes through his small orchard and gathers every piece of fruit from his 2 trees before the weather changes. He keeps a notebook where he records all sorts of details: one tree is near the fence and gets 7 hours of sunlight, the other is closer to the shed and gets 6 hours; he used 4 ladders during the season, 2 watering cans, and 3 bags of compost; each tree was watered 5 days a week for 12 weeks; and last year he had 3 trees but one died in a storm, so this year he is working with only the 2 trees he currently harvests from. During the harvest he sorts fruit into 8 baskets, checks 11 branches for damage, and throws away 9 bruised fruits, but then he focuses on the seeds for planting next season.

From the fruit collected from these 2 trees, he counts that each tree has 20 plants' worth of fruit to process for seeds. He also notes some other gardening numbers in the same notebook: a garden center nearby sells seed trays in packs of 10, young saplings cost $6 each or 2 for $11, fertilizer comes in 15-pound bags, and James has room for 50 pots on one bench and 18 on another. He labels rows A through F, plans to space future trees 12 feet apart, and estimates that if every seed grew he would need 40 markers, though he only has 27 left from spring. None of that changes what he actually does with the seeds he gets from this harvest.

For the actual planting, each plant yields 1 seed, and James decides to plant 60% of those seeds. He saves the rest in envelopes, placing 5 envelopes in one drawer and 7 in another, and writes the date on each packet. How many trees did he plant?

Kyle was organizing a craft display for the school arts fair and spent most of Saturday afternoon comparing storage containers for the origami stars he planned to fold. At the first shop, he looked at short jars, tall jars, plastic tubes, and several kinds of glass bottles with handwritten labels. One shelf had 8 blue bottles on sale for $4 each, another had 6 square jars that could hold 12 paper cranes each, and a clearance bin had mixed containers priced 3 for $10. Kyle also checked a note in his phone where he had written that last month he folded 27 stars, 14 hearts, and 9 paper flowers, although those old decorations were for a different event and were not going into these new bottles. After measuring ribbon lengths of 18 inches, 24 inches, and 30 inches for possible decorations around the bottle necks, he finally bought 2 glass bottles that can hold 15 origami stars each. The cashier wrapped them in 2 layers of paper and put them in a bag with a receipt showing the store opened at 9:00 a.m. and closed at 8:00 p.m.

Later that day, Kyle stopped by another craft store because he realized he wanted more matching containers for the same display. He ignored some larger bottles that could hold 20 stars each, a set of mini bottles sold in packs of 4, and a display of 5 decorative corks for $6. He also noticed sticker sheets with 36 gold stars, 48 silver stars, and 60 alphabet labels, plus a sign advertising 25% off beads if you bought at least 2 packs. None of that changed how many origami stars the matching bottles themselves could hold. At this second store, he bought another 3 identical glass bottles. When he got home, he lined up all the glass bottles on a table next to 7 rolls of washi tape, 11 markers, and 4 unfinished greeting cards, then started planning how many origami stars he would need if he wanted every glass bottle he bought completely filled.

How many stars must Kyle make to fill all the glass bottles he bought?

Mark is setting up a tiny backyard "pet field day" on a Saturday afternoon. He has been timing all sorts of things with a stopwatch: his hare can sprint 10 feet per second on the straight practice lane, while his turtle crawls 1 foot per second on the same kind of surface. Mark originally marked off several distances with chalk and tape for different events: a 5-foot warm-up lane near the porch, a 12-foot lane by the garden hose, a 20-foot main race lane across the patio, and even a 30-foot lane he decided not to use because it ran too close to the flower bed. He also put small flags every 2 feet, bought 3 carrots for the hare, washed the turtle's shell for 4 minutes, and wrote down lap times from earlier practice sessions, including 2 seconds, 6 seconds, and 20 seconds for unrelated drills. The hare's water bowl holds 16 ounces, the turtle's dish holds 8 ounces, and Mark spent $10 on chalk, $1 on lettuce, and $20 on a folding table for keeping score. He invited 4 neighbors to watch, set out 2 lawn chairs, and planned races at 1:00, 1:10, and 1:20, though only the final official race matters here. For the official event, both pets are racing toward the same finish line in a 20-foot race. Mark wants the race to end in a tie, so he is considering letting the slower turtle begin moving before the hare starts. If they're going to run a 20 foot-race, how much of a head start (in seconds) does the turtle need to finish in a tie?

At Glenn’s local movie theater, the posted weekly promotion board is crowded with details. On Mondays, standard movie tickets cost $5 each. The same board also says children under 6 get in free before noon, seniors save $2 on the first Tuesday of every month, 3D showings add $4 per ticket, and the theater charges $8 for a small popcorn combo, $12 for a large combo, and $3.50 for bottled water. Matinee times start at 11:30 a.m., evening shows begin after 6:00 p.m., and parking in the attached garage is $2 for the first hour and $1 for each additional hour, though validation can reduce that on weekdays.

Glenn notices that on Wednesday, regular movie tickets cost twice as much as they do on Monday. On Saturday, regular movie tickets cost five times as much as Monday’s price. The theater has 14 screens, shows 6 different films this week, and Glenn spends a while comparing runtimes: one movie is 92 minutes, another is 104 minutes, another is 118 minutes, and the one he wants to see has 2 preview trailers totaling 7 minutes. He also checks the rewards app, which says he has 120 points, and that 500 points can be redeemed for a free soda. Last month he went to the movies 3 times, but this week he only plans 2 visits.

On Wednesday he goes to one movie, and on Saturday he goes to one movie. He thinks briefly about buying snacks, since candy costs $4, nachos cost $6, and a refillable bucket is $15, but he decides that is unrelated to what he wants to know. If Glenn goes to the movie theater on Wednesday and Saturday, how much does he spend?

Conner has a dune buggy that he rides in the desert, usually on a long training loop near the dunes outside town. The buggy has oversized tires, a reinforced roll cage, a 14-gallon fuel tank, a bright orange flag on a whip antenna, and a speedometer that reads up to 120 miles per hour. Before one ride, he checks the tire pressure in all 4 tires, packs 3 bottles of water, 2 granola bars, a toolkit with 11 wrenches, and an extra pair of goggles because the forecast says the temperature could reach 92 degrees by noon even though it was only 68 degrees at sunrise. His route map shows flat stretches, steep-looking downhill sections, and long uphill climbs, and the whole practice area is divided into 9 marked zones, although he only uses 6 of them on this trip. On flat sand, his dune buggy can ride at a speed of 60 miles per hour. On downhill slopes, it can race at 12 miles per hour faster than it can when it is on flat sand. On an uphill incline, it travels at a speed 18 miles per hour slower than when it is riding on flat sand. During this outing, Conner spends one-third of the time on flat sand, one-third of the time on uphill slopes, and one-third of the time on downhill slopes. He also makes 2 brief stops earlier in the morning to tighten a loose strap and brush sand off a headlight, but those stops are not part of the riding intervals being compared. Last weekend he covered 180 miles total over 4 hours on a different route, and his friend Mason claimed his own buggy averages 54 miles per hour over mixed terrain, but Conner says that course had softer sand and more turns. A mechanic had once suggested gear settings for cruising at 35, 50, and 65 miles per hour in different conditions, and Conner wrote those down on a note card tucked into the glove compartment next to a receipt for $27 of fuel and a park entry pass numbered 2481. If Conner rides his dune buggy one-third of the time on flat sand, one-third of the time on uphill slopes, and one-third of the time on downhill slopes, what is his average speed in miles per hour?

A neighborhood grocery store keeps detailed weekly records for its baking supplies. On Mondays, the manager checks the shelves, where sugar is stocked next to flour, salt, and rice. The store carries sugar in several formats for display purposes: large 1-kilogram family bags for festival season, decorative 500-gram jars near the tea aisle, and small packets placed by the checkout counter for customers who only need a little. Last month, the store ordered 12 cartons of tea, 18 bottles of cooking oil, 45 bars of soap, and 30 kilograms of rice, and it also rearranged Shelf 4 so that 8 rows were used for baking items instead of 6. The sugar supplier delivers on Tuesdays and Fridays, and each delivery truck can carry up to 200 kilograms, although the truck is usually only half full because it also brings lentils, beans, and spices.

In the weekly sales report, the cashier notes that the store sells 20 packets of sugar every week, and each of those packets contains 100 grams of sugar. For comparison, the same report says the store also sells 14 packets of flour at 1 kilogram each, 9 jars of honey at 250 grams each, and 24 snack bars at 50 grams each. During a holiday promotion, customers who bought 3 packets of sugar got a coupon worth $2 off their next purchase, but the promotion did not change the total weekly count of sugar packets sold. The owner is trying to convert the sugar sales amount into kilograms for inventory planning, because the storeroom labels bulk goods in kilograms rather than grams.

A store sells 20 packets of 100 grams of sugar every week. How many kilograms of sugar does it sell every week?

James decides to replace his car after spending several weekends comparing models, reading fuel-economy charts, and visiting three different dealerships. His old car originally cost $20,000, had 84,000 miles on it, got about 28 miles per gallon on the highway and 22 in the city, and had just received $1,200 worth of maintenance over the last year, including new tires that cost $640 and brakes that cost $310.
