He had also been paying $145 per month for insurance, around $90 per month for gas, and a $25 monthly car wash membership he forgot to cancel for 2 months. The dealer who eventually bought it mentioned similar cars on the lot were listed anywhere from $18,500 to $21,400 depending on trim, color, and condition, and James had gathered trade-in quotes of $14,700, $15,200, and $16,100 from other places. In the end, he sold his $20,000 car for 80% of its value.

For the replacement, James considered a sedan with a sticker price of $27,500, an SUV listed at $32,000, and the car he really wanted, which had a sticker price of $30,000. The salesperson talked about dealer fees of $495, documentation paperwork taking 2 hours, an optional warranty for $1,800, all-weather mats for $220, tinted windows for $350, and a maintenance package covering 3 years or 36,000 miles. James also compared financing offers of 4.9% for 60 months versus 5.4% for 72 months, and he calculated monthly payments on a note pad while drinking the dealership's free coffee. After negotiating back and forth for 90 minutes, he was able to haggle to buy the $30,000 sticker price car for 90% of its value.

He paid no attention to the blue-book printout showing depreciation by year, the estimated resale value after 5 years, or the chart comparing registration costs of $180, $210, and $240 in neighboring counties. Assuming only the sale of his old car and the negotiated purchase of the new one matter, how much was he out of pocket?

The Saturday before Mother's Day, Simon went with a handwritten list to a large garden center that had several seasonal promotions posted everywhere. One sign near the entrance advertised tomato starter trays for 3 for $15, another offered mulch at 4 bags for $20, and a hanging banner mentioned that loyalty members earned 25 points for every $10 spent. A smaller chalkboard by the register said the store opened at 8:00 a.m., closed at 6:00 p.m., and would have a planting workshop at 1:30 p.m. Simon arrived at 9:15 a.m., spent 12 minutes looking at herbs, and compared lavender in 4-inch pots for $3.75 each with rosemary in 6-inch pots for $5.25 each before deciding those were not what his mom wanted.

He was really there to buy flowers that his mom could plant for Mother's Day. The garden center was offering 10% off all purchases that day, including annuals, perennials, and shrubs, although fertilizer, gift cards, and delivery fees were listed separately on another sign. Simon noticed that flats of marigolds were marked 20% off if you bought 2 or more, daisies were $1.75 each or 8 for $12, and ceramic planters ranged from $18 to $42 depending on size. He also saw seed packets priced at 4 for $5, potting soil at $8.99 a bag, and gardening gloves for $6.50 a pair. His mom already had gloves, a trowel, and two unopened bags of soil in the garage, so he skipped all of those.

In the flower section, Simon picked out exactly 5 pansies at $2.50 each. He also bought 1 hydrangea that cost $12.50. Then he chose 5 petunias that cost $1.00 each. He briefly considered buying 2 extra begonias at $3.25 each and a watering can for $14, but he put them back on the shelf. Near checkout, there was a sign saying plastic trays were refunded at $0.10 each if returned later, and another notice saying deliveries under 5 miles cost $7 while deliveries from 5 to 10 miles cost $12, but Simon was carrying everything himself. The cashier rang up his flowers with the storewide 10% discount.

Simon had brought a wallet containing one $50 bill, two $10 bills, three $5 bills, and four $1 bills, but he decided to pay with a $50 bill. If he paid with a $50 bill, how much change would Simon receive back from his purchase?

Colton was organizing his giant sticker collection on a Saturday afternoon after cleaning out 6 desk drawers, 2 plastic bins, and a backpack pocket. His whole collection included sharks, turtles, whales, and dolphin stickers, but for this trade he was only counting the dolphin stickers. He had 72 dolphin stickers at the start of the afternoon. Earlier that week, he had already sorted them into 9 equal mini-piles of 8 just to count them, and he wrote the total on a notepad next to a list of 14 sea animal names. He also had 18 shark stickers, 24 turtle stickers, and 30 whale stickers in separate envelopes, plus 5 glitter stickers he was not trading at all. 

At lunch, 3 friends stopped by while Colton was labeling folders with blue and green markers. He gave 4 dolphin stickers each to those 3 friends. One of those friends also brought 7 shells, another had 2 toy submarines, and the third had a notebook with 40 blank pages, but none of that changed Colton's dolphin sticker count except the stickers he handed out. After that, Colton packed some stickers into 4 sandwich bags, checked a trade list with 12 names on it, and counted 8 unopened sticker packs on his shelf, each pack containing 6 stickers, though he did not open those packs.

Later, he also gave his friend Mandy 2 more than he gave his three friends total. Mandy was wearing a dolphin T-shirt with 2 fins on the picture and carrying 3 folders, and she asked whether the stickers were from the ocean set of 50 or the deluxe set of 60, but Colton only cared about how many dolphin stickers he was giving away. Then he gave Justin 10 less than Mandy. Justin had 10 baseball cards in his pocket, arrived 15 minutes after Mandy, and had already traded away 4 robot stickers to someone else earlier that day.

By the end of the afternoon, Colton had also counted 27 sticker backs on the table, 11 empty sleeves in a binder, and 3 pencils he used to record trades. How many stickers does Colton have left?

At the start of the semester, Derek sets aside $960 specifically to cover his book-related shopping before classes begin. He makes a detailed plan because his campus bookstore has a 3-day rush period, is open from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m., and is offering 10% off university hoodies, buy-2-get-1 notebooks, and a rewards program that gives 40 points for every $100 spent. Derek also compares prices at three places: the campus bookstore, an off-campus shop 2 miles away, and an online seller that charges $6.99 shipping unless an order is over $75. On his checklist, he has 5 courses, 4 required textbooks, 2 recommended reference books he decides not to buy yet, 8 pens, 6 highlighters, 3 folders, 2 binders, 1 calculator battery, and a backpack that costs $48, though that backpack is part of a separate clothing-and-gear budget and not part of this money.

Before shopping, Derek writes all sorts of numbers in his planner: one biology textbook is marked $210 new or $140 used, a literature anthology is $95, an access code would be $82 if purchased alone, and loose-leaf paper is sold in packs of 150 sheets. His roommate says he spent $1,120 last fall, while Derek's cousin only spent $720 because she rented books for 16 weeks. Derek also notes that tuition is due in 12 days, parking costs $180 for the semester, and his meal plan has 14 swipes left this week. None of that changes the way Derek uses this particular $960 fund.

When he finally shops, Derek spends half of that $960 on his textbooks. After that, from the money still left, he spends a quarter of what is left on his school supplies. He pays with exact amounts from this budget and does not add tax, shipping, or any purchases from other budgets to these calculations. What is the amount of money Derek has left?

At the end of 2017, a forestry survey team recorded that a certain tree in a research park was exactly 100 meters tall. The park keeps many unrelated records as well: the tree stood in plot 12 of section B, inspectors visited 4 times that year, the path around the plot was 250 meters long, and the nursery nearby planted 100 saplings, of which 18 were pines, 27 were maples, and 55 were oaks. The survey report also mentioned that the tree's trunk circumference was 8 meters, the observation platform beside it was 15 meters high, and the team spent 3 hours and 20 minutes collecting data on a windy afternoon in 12°C weather. In 2018, the park's maintenance budget increased by 10%, fertilizer orders rose from 40 bags to 44 bags, and visitors bought 219 tickets in spring and 241 in summer. None of those records changed the growth rule for this tree: it will grow 10% more than its previous height each year. By the end of 2018, a nearby smaller tree that had started at 50 meters also followed its own schedule, and a different tree on the opposite side of the park grew by 12 meters after pruning, but this particular tree always grows by 10% of its own previous year's height. In 2019, workers replaced 2 ladders, repainted 6 signs, trimmed branches from 14 shrubs, and measured shadows at 9 a.m., noon, and 3 p.m. The research station itself is open 365 days a year, except for 6 public holidays, and the tree is watered every 3 days with 120 liters each time during summer. From the end of 2017 to the end of 2019, following the same yearly rule that each year its height becomes 10% more than the previous height, how long has the tree grown from 2017 until the end of 2019?

Lisa and Carly go shopping together at a large outlet mall on a Saturday that has a back-to-school sale, a winter clearance rack, and a loyalty-points weekend all happening at once. They arrive at 10:15 a.m., park in section C near entrance 4, and first stop for pretzels that cost $6 each, although Carly uses a coupon so they do not split that evenly. Lisa is carrying a gift card with $25 left on it from her birthday, and Carly has $90 in cash plus a debit card, but neither of those details changes what each actually spends on clothing. At the first store, signs say t-shirts are 2 for $18, jeans are marked down from $55 to $32, and coats range from $60 to $120 depending on brand. Lisa tries on 5 t-shirts, 3 pairs of jeans, and 2 coats before deciding what to buy. Carly compares 4 different coat colors, checks 6 sale tables, and spends 20 minutes deciding whether to buy boots, but she ultimately does not include boots in the totals asked about. 

For the clothing purchases that matter here, Lisa spends $40 on t-shirts. After that, she spends half of this amount on jeans and twice this amount on coats. Meanwhile, Carly spends only a quarter as much as Lisa on t-shirts, but she spends 3 times as much as she herself spent on t-shirts on jeans and a quarter of the amount Lisa spent on coats on coats. 

Along the way, the cashier mentions that if they had spent $200 before tax they would have received a free tote bag, and the sales tax in the area is 8%. Lisa also notices a rack with scarves priced at $12 each or 3 for $30, and Carly briefly considers buying 2 belts at $14 apiece. They also pass a sign advertising that members earn 1 point per dollar and that 100 points gives $5 off a future visit. After shopping, they meet two friends in the food court at 1:30 p.m., where smoothies cost $7, fries cost $4, and combo meals are $11. None of those purchases are part of this question. 

In dollars, how much did Lisa and Carly spend in total?

A small poultry farm on the edge of town keeps several kinds of birds in separate fenced sections and records all sorts of details in a daily notebook. At the beginning of the month, the farmer counted 300 chickens in the main coop, 200 turkeys in the larger back enclosure, and 80 guinea fowls near the feed shed. The farm also has 12 nesting boxes for the chickens, 9 water troughs, 4 storage bins of cracked corn, and 16 fence posts recently replaced after a storm. On ordinary days, the birds are fed twice, once at 6 a.m. and once at 4 p.m., using 50 kg of feed in the morning and 45 kg in the evening, although the exact amount varies by weather. The chickens lay an average of 140 eggs a day when healthy, the turkeys much fewer, and the guinea fowls are known more for noise than egg production. Last market day, the farmer sold 36 trays of eggs, each tray holding 30 eggs, and paid $84 for disinfectant, $125 for medicine that did not help, and $60 for repairs to a gate hinge. A delivery truck brought 18 sacks of feed on Monday and 22 more on Thursday, each sack weighing 25 kg, and the helper spent 3 hours stacking them in the shed.

Then a strange, incurable disease hit the farm. From that point on, every single day the farmer lost 20 chickens, 8 turkeys, and 5 guinea fowls. The veterinarian visited 2 times during the week, the farmhands checked the coops every 4 hours, and the farmer kept notes for all 7 days. No new birds were bought, hatched, borrowed, or moved in from neighboring farms during that week, even though a nearby breeder had offered 40 ducklings and 15 geese for sale. The farmer also considered separating the sick birds into 3 quarantine pens, each with room for 25 birds, but that did not change the daily losses. By the end of the week, 14 feed scoops had gone missing, 7 light bulbs had been replaced in the barn, and 2 water lines had to be cleared.

After a week, how many birds will be left in the poultry?

During a three-day reporting period in California, a public health dashboard compiled results from multiple testing sites, including 18 drive-through centers, 7 hospital labs, and 12 community clinics. On the first day of the report, technicians processed 24,000 test samples, of which 21,300 were negative, 700 were inconclusive and had to be retested later, and the total number of confirmed positive Coronavirus cases entered into the statewide system for that day stood at 2000. Some counties also noted that 300 test kits were delayed in transit, 120 staff members were working double shifts, and 45 data-entry corrections from the previous week were still under review, but those administrative details did not change the official starting total for that day. 

On the second day, several counties expanded testing hours from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m., mobile units visited 9 additional neighborhoods, and 6,500 more people were screened. The number of cases increased by 500 on the second day, while 50 patients were reported as recovered. At the same time, officials mentioned 80 hospital admissions, 35 patients discharged for non-COVID reasons, 14 ventilators newly installed, and 900 precautionary quarantine notices sent out after contact tracing. A separate memo also listed 250 antibody tests, 60 delayed lab confirmations, and 40 duplicate records removed from a different non-case file, but the official update for this problem is still that the number of cases increased by 500 on day two, with 50 recoveries. 

On the third day, news reports described a sharp surge after a weekend backlog was cleared: 11 counties uploaded late lab packets, 3 reporting systems were synchronized, and 2 overnight batches from private labs were added before noon. The total number of new cases spiked to 1500 with 200 recoveries. In the same bulletin, there were also references to 130 patients under observation, 75 ICU beds available statewide, 20 refrigerated transport units on standby, 400 phone calls answered by county hotlines, and 1,100 vaccine appointments scheduled for later that week. A regional breakdown mentioned 600 cases from urban sites, 500 from suburban testing centers, and 400 from rural clinics, while another unrelated operations note mentioned 90 volunteers, 30 canceled appointments, and 15 media briefings.

What's the total number of positive cases after the third day?

Early Saturday morning, Caleb and his dad drove out to Pine Hollow Lake for a fishing trip. They left the house at 6:15 a.m., stopped for gas for $24, bought 2 cups of hot chocolate and 1 coffee at the marina snack stand, and paid a $7 parking fee near dock number 4. Caleb packed a small red tackle box with 12 hooks, 8 sinkers, 3 extra bobbers, and a bag of worms that had 25 worms in it, although several were left unused by the end of the day. His dad brought a larger blue tackle bag with 4 spools of line, 2 nets, and a folding chair. The weather report said it would reach 68 degrees by noon, with winds of 9 miles per hour, and there were already 6 boats on the water when they arrived.

They fished from the shore for a while, then moved closer to the reeds near a wooden sign that warned people not to keep fish shorter than 10 inches. Caleb got a few bites before breakfast, lost 1 lure near a rock, and later saw 7 ducks swim past. His dad spent 15 minutes untangling a line and talking to another fisherman who said he had been there since 5:40 a.m. Caleb and his dad also counted 14 dragonflies, shared a packet of crackers with 18 crackers in it, and took a break at 9:30 to eat sandwiches. Caleb's dad said that on their last trip they had caught 11 fish total, but this time they were only counting trouts that each of them personally caught.

By the end of the trip, Caleb caught 2 trouts, and his dad caught three times as much as Caleb. How many more trouts did his dad catch compared to Caleb?

Christina is updating the reptile care page in her science notebook and wants to record the total length of all 3 of her pet snakes in inches. She keeps the snakes in separate glass enclosures lined up along one wall of her room. Each enclosure is 24 inches tall, 36 inches wide, and has a heat lamp that turns on for 12 hours a day. She bought substrate in 3 bags that weighed 10 pounds each, and she also labeled the tanks with feeding schedules: one snake eats every 7 days, another every 10 days, and the third every 14 days. Last month she spent $18 on bedding, $16 on frozen food, and $10 on a new water dish. She measured the room temperature at 78 degrees near the window and 82 degrees near the lamps. One tank has 2 artificial plants, another has 4 rocks, and the last has 1 hollow log. Christina also wrote down the lengths of the snakes for her records: 1 snake is 2 feet long. Another snake is 16 inches long. The last snake is 10 inches long. She considered rewriting all measurements in centimeters too, and she noticed that one ruler in her desk is 12 inches long while another measuring tape extends to 60 inches. She even compared the snakes to a shelf that is 4 feet long and to posters that are 18 inches wide. How many inches are all of her snakes combined?

Madeline was reorganizing the art cabinet in her room on a rainy Saturday afternoon before school started again. On the top shelf she had watercolor trays, on the middle shelf she had sticker books, and on the bottom shelf she kept her crayon boxes lined up by color theme. Last month she had bought 5 identical cardboard boxes of crayons during a back-to-school sale, even though the store also had packs of 12, 16, and 32. Each of Madeline's 5 boxes held 24 crayons. She wrote the purchase date on every box, counted the total colors, and noticed that some wrappers were peeled more than others. The crayons were used for class posters, a birthday banner, two thank-you cards, and a science project volcano label, although some markers and colored pencils were used too. 

While checking the boxes, she made several notes in her notebook. In 2 of the boxes, 5/8 of the crayons were not yet used. She almost mixed those up with two older half-empty marker cases that each had 18 markers, but those were separate and not part of the crayon count. In 2 other crayon boxes, only 2/3 of the crayons were used, which she wrote right after listing that her cousin had borrowed 7 colored pencils and returned 6. The last crayon box was not entirely used. It still had its plastic tray, a name label, and a corner taped shut, but she did not say anything more specific about how many crayons in that box had been used or unused. Also on the desk were 3 glue sticks, 11 sheets of construction paper, 4 paintbrushes, 2 erasers, and a receipt showing she had paid $4 per box after a $3 coupon on a set of craft supplies, but none of that changes the crayon inventory.

How many unused crayons did Madeline have?

Yesterday evening, David and William were invited to a large neighborhood party held in a rented hall with 12 round tables, 8 rectangular buffet tables, 96 paper plates, 84 cloth napkins, and 3 shelves of matching glassware. The hosts had spent all afternoon setting out snacks: 5 bowls of pretzels, 7 trays of fruit, 2 chocolate cakes, and 48 cupcakes. Music started at 6:30 p.m., dinner was served at 7:15 p.m., and dessert came out at 8:05 p.m. David arrived wearing a blue jacket, William arrived 10 minutes later carrying a gift bag with 3 ribbons on it, and together they chatted near the drink station where there were pitchers of lemonade, iced tea, and sparkling water. At one point, a stack of clean glasses was being moved from the kitchen area to the main room. During the confusion, David broke 2 glasses. William, who was nearby helping at the same time, broke 4 times the number of glasses David broke. Other guests spilled juice on 6 napkins, someone misplaced 9 forks, the caterer washed 24 unused glasses at the end of the night, and the host said there had originally been 60 glasses prepared for the party, with 18 placed on one table and 14 on another before the rest were set by the bar. How many glasses were broken?

During a huge Avengers archive project, SHIELD interns are trying to organize an absurdly detailed timeline binder with 48 tabbed sections, 12 color-coded dividers, and 365 daily incident logs from one training year. On one page, they list all kinds of unrelated notes: Thor has used 3 different hammers in simulation records, Captain America rotated through 5 uniform designs in one museum exhibit, Peter Parker submitted 9 lab reports late in a semester, and Tony Stark once reviewed 27 prototype suits, of which 8 were marked obsolete and 4 were kept for display. The page also mentions that Asgard sent 64 crates of ceremonial armor, each crate weighing 32 kilograms, and that the Avengers compound cafeteria serves breakfast from 7:00 to 9:30, lunch from 12:00 to 2:00, and dinner from 6:00 to 8:00. Another note says the archive team spent 14 hours labeling shelves, used 56 index cards, printed 224 photos, and discarded 18 duplicates. A side column compares famous age gaps in fictional biographies, including a 19-year training period, a 42-year diplomatic alliance, and a 108-year sleep cycle from a completely unrelated cosmic case file. 

Buried in the actual age summary, however, the archivist wrote the following: Thor is 13 times older than Captain America. Captain America is 7 times older than Peter Parker, and Ironman is 32 years older than Peter Parker. On the same record sheet, Thor's age is listed as 1456 years old, even though a nearby exhibit plaque separately mentions 1,460 candles ordered for a ceremonial celebration, with 4 extra in storage. The interns also note that Peter once won 2 science fairs, Captain America donated 11 shields to a museum fundraiser display, and Ironman paid for 75 replacement tablets after a lab accident involving 3 spilled chemical trays. 

How old is Ironman if Thor is 1456 years old?

At a big family photo day last weekend, Dallas, Darcy, and Dexter were all helping sort through old albums, school papers, and birthday decorations. On one table there were 12 framed photos, 8 loose pictures, 3 baby albums, and 2 boxes of holiday cards. Dallas had just finished a 6-mile bike ride and was wearing jersey number 14, Darcy was labeling 24 cupcakes for a school event, and Dexter was counting the 16 trading cards he wanted to bring to a friend's house. Their aunt kept mixing up years and ages because one album had pictures from 2 years ago, another from last year, and another from when Dallas was 9, Darcy was 6, and Dexter was 3. During the conversation, someone also mentioned that Dallas practices piano 4 days a week for 30 minutes, Darcy takes dance classes that cost $18 each, and Dexter has soccer on Tuesdays at 5:30.

To straighten things out, their mother stated the age relationships clearly: last year Dallas was 3 times the age of his sister Darcy. Darcy is twice as old as Dexter, who is 8 right now. The family also noted that Dallas's birthday is in October, Darcy's is in March, and Dexter's is in July, and that together they received 27 birthday cards this year, but none of that changed the age comparison being discussed.

How old is Dallas now?

In one monitored section of a forest reserve, biologists are cataloging animal activity before the autumn census. The section covers 12 square kilometers, includes 4 streams, 7 marked trails, 18 hollow logs, and 25 berry patches, and it is bordered by a meadow where deer are often seen at dawn. Last month, the team recorded 16 owls, 9 badgers, 14 hedgehogs, 22 squirrels, and 37 songbirds in the same area, though those numbers are not part of the current mammal tally. For this week’s report, the official count for the section is 100 weasels and 50 rabbits. The rangers also note that in nearby sections, there are 80 more rabbits and 40 fewer weasels than usual, but those neighboring areas are managed separately and are not included in this section’s count.

The reserve runs on a 7-day monitoring cycle, with checks every Monday, Wednesday, and Saturday. Feed stations were stocked with 60 kilograms of grain, 24 salt blocks were placed for larger herbivores, and 3 cameras at each of 5 observation posts captured over 900 images in total. Two interns worked 6 hours a day for 5 days entering old data, and one senior ranger drove 42 kilometers to inspect fencing after a storm. None of this changed the official starting count in this section: 100 weasels and 50 rabbits.

Then 3 foxes invade this region. One of the foxes is older and has a scar over its left eye, one has been seen near the eastern stream at least 11 times, and the third was first spotted at sunset near a fallen pine. Even though their hunting routes overlap with areas containing vole burrows, quail nests, and beetle-rich soil, the report specifically tracks only their effect on the weasel and rabbit populations in this section. Each fox catches an average of 4 weasels and 2 rabbits per week. Some weeks may vary slightly in field notes because of rain, temperature swings from 8°C to 17°C, or 2 nights of heavy wind, but the average rate used in the official summary remains the same for each fox.

After the foxes have been in the area for 3 weeks, during which time the reserve also hosted 2 school tours with 27 students each, repaired 6 signposts, replaced 14 meters of rope fencing, and counted 43 mushrooms along the north trail, how many rabbits and weasels will be left after 3 weeks?

At Apple’s New York store today, the staff had an unusually busy day with multiple product displays, accessory promotions, training sessions, and customer pickups all happening at once. The store opened at 9:00 a.m., closed at 8:00 p.m., and had 14 sales associates on the floor, 3 managers rotating shifts, and 2 technicians working the Genius Bar. A morning line of 47 customers formed before opening, 18 people came in just to ask about battery replacements, and 12 customers picked up online orders that had been paid for earlier in the week, including AirPods cases, chargers, and watch bands. None of those pickup-only transactions should be counted with today’s products sold for this question.

Inside the store, the merchandising team had arranged 6 front tables: 2 for iPhones, 1 for iPads, 1 for Apple TV devices, 1 for accessories, and 1 for seasonal promotions. One display wall showed 35 phone cases priced from $39 to $69, another had 24 chargers at $19 each, and a bundle promotion offered 2 HomePods for $598, though only a few customers asked about it. The store also demoed 9 MacBooks, 7 Apple Watches, and 4 Vision Pro headsets, but those demos were not part of the totals relevant here. During lunch, the café next door sent over 16 sandwiches and 20 coffees for the staff, and the receipt totaled $248 before tax.

As for the actual products sold today that matter for this calculation, Apple sold 100 iPhones at their New York store today for an average cost of $1000. They also sold 20 iPads for an average cost of $900 and 80 Apple TVs for an average cost of $200. Separately, 11 customers traded in old devices for store credit, 5 business clients asked for quotes on bulk orders for next month, and 3 schools inquired about educational pricing. The accessories department reported selling 60 cases, 40 screen protectors, and 25 charging cables, but those items are tracked in a different category and are not part of the products named above.

At the end of the day, one manager reviewed several figures: gross foot traffic of 312 visitors, 200 total receipts across all departments, 8 refunds processed from purchases made on previous days, and a customer satisfaction score of 4.8 out of 5 from 63 survey responses. Another manager noted that yesterday’s average selling price for iPhones alone had been $980 and that last Saturday the store sold 30 iPads, but those figures are only historical background. What was the average cost across all products sold today?

Melody kept a very detailed garden journal while growing sunflowers from two different seed packets, Packet A and Packet B, along the south fence of her yard. She planted 24 seeds from Packet A and 30 seeds from Packet B in early May, although only 18 from Packet A and 21 from Packet B sprouted within the first 10 days. The seed packets had different prices too: Packet A cost $4.80 and Packet B cost $3.60 at the garden center, where she also bought 3 bags of soil, 2 new trowels, and a 40-foot hose. She watered the flower beds every morning for 12 minutes and every evening for 8 minutes during the first 6 weeks, except on the 9 rainy days when she skipped watering. She measured stem thickness, leaf count, and bloom size, writing down numbers like 14 leaves, 17 leaves, 6-inch blooms, and 8-inch blooms for different plants on different dates. By midsummer, one especially tall sunflower from Packet A measured 192 inches tall. Melody compared that height to the sunflowers grown from Packet B and found that the sunflowers from Packet A were 20% taller than the sunflowers from Packet B. She also noted that the tallest Packet B plant had 11 leaves below the first flower head, that the row spacing was 18 inches, and that the compost pile behind the garden was 5 feet wide and 3 feet high. If the sunflowers from Packet A were 192 inches tall, how tall were the sunflowers from Packet B?

Mr. Grey is doing a long weekend shopping trip for his family and is trying to keep track of several gift ideas, store promotions, and receipts. He first stopped at a department store that opened at 9:00 a.m. and has a buy-2-get-1-half-off sale on selected winter scarves, though not on the brand he wanted. He looked at 5 belts priced at $18 each, compared 4 sweater styles marked $31, $34, $39, and $44, and even considered a watch that had been reduced from $120 to $96. In the clothing section, after checking sizes in medium, large, and extra-large, he finally purchased 3 polo shirts for $26 each. The cashier also mentioned that if he had bought 4 shirts instead of 3, he would have qualified for an extra store coupon, but he did not add another shirt.

Next, Mr. Grey went to a jewelry shop where display signs advertised earrings for $29 a pair, bracelets for $47, and a necklace-and-earring gift set for $135. He spent time comparing silver chains of 16-inch, 18-inch, and 20-inch lengths, and he asked about a loyalty program that gives 200 points after $250 in purchases. For the gifts he actually chose there, he purchased 2 necklaces for $83 each. He also paid attention to a sign saying that gift boxes were $4 each unless a purchase was over $100, in which case the first box was free, but he decided to reuse boxes he already had at home.

After that he visited an electronics store where he tested 3 game controllers, looked at 2 headphones costing $55 and $72, and saw a shelf of games priced at $40, $60, $75, $90, and $110. A clerk told him that some customers were bundling games with rechargeable batteries for an extra $18, and another sign said that spending $150 on electronics would earn a future $15 store credit next month. Mr. Grey bought 1 computer game for $90.

He paid for all of these actual gift purchases using his credit card. Because he used that card for all those items together, he received a $12 rebate. He also noticed on his statement a previous balance of $240, a minimum payment of $35, and a separate gas charge of $48 from earlier in the week, but those were unrelated to these gifts. What is the total cost of the gifts after the rebate?

Mary was organizing a pizza party for a Saturday game night in her apartment building's community room. She started planning on Wednesday, made a guest list of 18 people, and then revised it to 16 after two neighbors said they might arrive late. She checked three grocery flyers, compared family-size and party-size packages, and wrote a budget in her notebook with separate sections for food, drinks, paper plates, napkins, and decorations. The room rental deposit had already been paid earlier in the week, and she also still had 24 paper plates, 30 napkins, 2 unopened bags of ice, and 8 plastic cups left over from her cousin's birthday party, though she wasn't sure whether that would be enough. At one store, drinks were advertised as 2 boxes for $11 if purchased before noon, but that special was only for a different brand she did not choose. The pizza shop also had a coupon for $3 off every 4 boxes on weekday orders, but her order did not use that promotion. She thought about adding breadsticks for $5 per tray and salad bowls for $9 each, and she even wrote down prices for dipping sauce cups at 50 cents each, but she decided not to include those.

When she finally placed the order for the actual party items, Mary bought 5 boxes of drinks at $6 each box and 10 boxes of pizzas at $14 each box for her pizza party. The cashier packed the receipt into the bag along with a menu showing medium pizzas, large pizzas, and dessert pizzas, plus family bundles ranging from $22 to $48, but none of those bundle prices applied to Mary's purchase. Before leaving, Mary also glanced at a sign saying delivery would take 35 to 45 minutes and that reheating instructions were printed on the side of every pizza box. She paid $200 for all the items. How much change did she get back?

At a big family birthday gathering held on June 14, several relatives were comparing ages while planning cake candles, photo labels, and seating charts. Kris brought 24 cupcakes for the class party earlier that day, and there were also 24 paper plates left on the kitchen counter, 12 blue balloons, 12 silver balloons, 3 boxes of candles with 10 candles in each box, and a photo board showing pictures from the last 8 years. Herbert arrived 15 minutes late after riding in car number 10, while Kris had already helped set out 6 juice boxes, 4 bowls of fruit, and 2 trays of sandwiches. One aunt mentioned that Herbert used to be 10 centimeters shorter than Kris when they were little, and another cousin said Kris would turn 25 next year and had just finished a 24-page scrapbook this week. In the middle of all that, Grandma reminded everyone of the actual age relationship: Herbert is 10 years younger than Kris. If Kris is 24 years old now, how old will Herbert be next year?

At a large dinner party held in a community hall, 16 people are seated for the meal. The host had planned carefully: there are 4 round tables with 4 seats each, 16 cloth napkins folded at the place settings, 16 name cards, 8 candles on the sideboard, and 12 glass pitchers of water that were refilled twice during the evening. In the kitchen, the caterer prepared 40 dinner rolls for the guests, arranged in 5 baskets with 8 rolls in each basket, although 2 baskets were placed on the left buffet, 2 on the right buffet, and 1 stayed near the kitchen door. Earlier in the day, the bakery had also delivered 24 breadsticks, 18 croissants for breakfast the next morning, and 6 extra hamburger buns from another event, but those were kept separate and not counted as dinner rolls.

During dinner, the guests did not all eat the same amount of bread. Half the people at the party chose to eat 1 1/2 rolls each because they skipped appetizers, while the other half ate only 1/2 a roll each since they were saving room for dessert. For context, the appetizer trays held 32 stuffed mushrooms, 20 cheese squares, and 48 crackers, and dessert later included 2 sheet cakes cut into 24 slices each, plus 16 cups of coffee and 10 cups of tea. The soup course had been served in 16 bowls, and the main course included 9 platters of pasta, 7 platters of vegetables, and 4 serving spoons that kept getting moved around. Some guests stayed from 6:00 p.m. until 10:30 p.m., while others arrived 15 minutes late, and the cleanup crew packed 40 plates, 40 forks, 16 knives, and 32 wine glasses afterward.

Even though there were many other food items and supplies at the event, the only bread being counted for this question is the 40 dinner rolls set out for the 16 people at dinner. Half the people eat 1 1/2 rolls each. The other half eat 1/2 a roll each. How many dinner rolls are leftover?

Rosie has been keeping a very detailed running log for the week because she is training with a neighborhood fitness group, comparing her progress to a monthly chart, and also trying to decide whether to replace her worn-out shoes. Her training notebook includes all sorts of information: she stretches for 12 minutes before most runs and cools down for 8 minutes afterward, her water bottle holds 24 ounces, she usually runs a 2-mile loop in the park but sometimes adds a 1-mile out-and-back section, and her step counter estimated 9,600 steps on Monday, 4,800 on Tuesday, 9,500 on Wednesday, and 3,200 on Thursday. On Monday she started at 7:10 a.m., passed 3 traffic lights, and finished before breakfast. On Tuesday she ran after work, when the temperature was 68 degrees, and then bought 2 bananas for 90 cents each. On Wednesday she wore her blue shoes instead of her black ones, and on Thursday she only had time for a short outing because she had a dentist appointment at 4:20 p.m. Her friend Maya runs 5 miles per hour, her brother biked 14 miles on Wednesday, and the fitness group hopes to total 120 miles this month. Rosie also wrote down that the park track is 400 meters around, that 8 laps is a little under 2 miles, and that a sports drink costs $3 per bottle or $15 for a pack of 6.

What matters for Rosie's running total is that Rosie runs 6 miles per hour. She runs for 1 hour on Monday, 30 minutes on Tuesday, 1 hour on Wednesday, and 20 minutes on Thursday. If she wants to run 20 miles for the week, how many minutes should she run on Friday?

Gary had been comparing used cars for months before finally buying his first one. He looked at 14 listings in 3 different neighborhoods, test-drove 4 cars, and brought along his cousin twice to check for rust, tire wear, and strange engine noises. One car was listed for $5,800 but needed $900 in brake work, another was $6,400 with 118,000 miles, and a third seller dropped the price from $6,250 to $6,100 but would not include the snow tires. Gary eventually chose a different used car and bought it for $6,000. He paid for gas on the way home, spent $42 on registration paperwork, and later budgeted $75 per month for insurance, about $120 every 3 months for oil changes, and $480 per year for routine maintenance. His dad lent him the full purchase amount and told him he could pay back the entire $6,000 over 5 years. Gary even made a spreadsheet with columns for monthly fuel costs of $160, emergency repairs of $300 per year, and tire replacement after 2 more winters, although none of that changed the loan itself.

At first Gary considered following his dad's suggestion exactly. Since 5 years is 60 months, he wrote one possible monthly plan next to his phone bill of $55, gym membership of $25, and streaming subscriptions totaling $18 per month. But after getting a raise of $1.50 per hour and picking up 6 extra Saturday shifts in one season, he decided he wanted the debt gone much sooner. Instead of taking the full 5 years, Gary decided he would pay his dad back the full amount in 2 years, which is 24 months. Around the same time he was also comparing whether to spend $240 on seat covers, $90 on floor mats, and $35 each month on a car wash plan, but those choices were separate from the amount he owed his dad.

How much more is Gary spending per month to pay the loan off in 2 years instead of 5?

Sansa is a famous artist who works out of a bright downtown studio that opens at 9:00 a.m. and closes at 6:00 p.m. Her assistant keeps detailed records about everything in the shop: the rent is $1200 per month, the utility bill last month was $146, and she spent $38 on charcoal pencils, $24 on erasers, and $72 on frames during a weekend sale. Tourists often ask about her pricing chart because she sells portraits according to size, and the wall display includes several sample measurements such as 4-inch sketches, 8-inch portraits, 12-inch studies, 16-inch portraits, and even a rare 20-inch commission that is not part of her regular daily routine. On Mondays she usually answers 18 emails before lunch, drinks 2 cups of tea, and reorganizes 14 paint tubes by color. She has 6 brushes for watercolor, 9 brushes for acrylic, and 3 special brushes she uses only for hair details in royal portraits.

Her most popular standard portrait sizes are still the 8-inch and 16-inch versions. She sells an 8-inch portrait for $5, and a 16-inch portrait for twice the price of the 8-inch portrait. On a typical day, even though she may have to stretch 7 canvases, sharpen 11 pencils, greet 23 visitors, reject 2 damaged frames, and spend 45 minutes preparing backgrounds, her actual sales pattern is very consistent: she sells three 8-inch portraits and five 16-inch portraits per day. Last Tuesday one customer ordered 2 extra mat boards, another asked whether a 16-inch portrait uses twice as much paint as an 8-inch one, and a collector compared her prices with a nearby gallery charging $12, $15, and $21 for unrelated pieces. Her assistant also noted that over a 3-day art fair she handed out 60 business cards, wrapped 18 packages, and received 9 online inquiries, none of which changed the standard number of portraits she sold per day.

If she sells three 8-inch portraits and five 16-inch portraits per day, how many does she earns every 3 days?
